kingdom-of-airgialla.t: Confederation of mid-Ulster peoples bound to the Uí Néill as hostage-givers, which survived under the MacMahons as Oriel until the settlement of Monaghan in 1591.
kingdom-of-airgialla.o: Airgialla means 'hostage-givers', and the name describes a group of peoples in mid-Ulster, in modern Armagh, Monaghan, Tyrone, Fermanagh and Louth, who owed hostages and military service to the Uí Néill. Tradition says the Three Collas destroyed Emain Macha, the royal centre of the Ulaid, and settled their descendants in the conquered land.
kingdom-of-airgialla.r: Airgialla was a federation of many small kingdoms, such as the Uí Chremthainn and the Uí Méith, under an over-king. Its people held the lands around Armagh, whose church became the primatial see of Ireland. In the 12th century Donnchad Ua Cerbaill, king of Airgialla, extended his realm into Louth and founded Mellifont Abbey in 1142, the first Cistercian house in Ireland.
kingdom-of-airgialla.e: Anglo-Norman settlement took Louth, and the MacMahons, Mac Mathghamhna, became rulers of the remaining kingdom, known in English as Oriel, centred on Monaghan. After the execution of Hugh Roe MacMahon in 1590, the English divided the lordship among MacMahon chiefs in 1591, creating County Monaghan.
kingdom-of-airgialla.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.t: The last independent Georgian kingdom in the east, created by Erekle II, which placed itself under Russian protection in 1783 and was annexed in 1801.
kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.o: Erekle II, king of the Kingdom of Kakheti since 1744, succeeded his father Teimuraz II in the Kingdom of Kartli in 1762, uniting eastern Georgia under one crown for the first time since the 15th century. He had gained prestige fighting for Nader Shah in India and against Dagestani raiders.
kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.r: Erekle II, ruling from Tbilisi, modernised the army, encouraged trade and crafts and drew tribute from the khanates of Ganja and Erivan. In 1783 he signed the Treaty of Georgievsk with Catherine the Great, accepting a Russian protectorate. Russia failed to defend him, and in 1795 Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar defeated the Georgians at Krtsanisi and sacked Tbilisi.
kingdom-of-kartli-kakheti.e: After Erekle's death in 1798, his son George XII asked for closer union with Russia. When George died in 1800, Emperor Paul I and then Alexander I annexed the kingdom in 1801, deposing the Bagratid dynasty and making it a Russian province.

kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.t: The Artaxiad dynasty turned Armenia into a major power, and under Tigranes the Great it briefly ruled an empire stretching from the Caspian to the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.o: Artaxias, a Seleucid governor, broke away after the Seleucid Empire lost the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE and proclaimed himself king of Greater Armenia. He united the Armenian-speaking lands, set boundary stones that still survive, and founded a new capital, Artaxata, on the Araxes, according to legend on the advice of Hannibal.
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.r: The kingdom combined an Iranian-style monarchy and great noble houses with Hellenistic court culture; Greek plays were staged at Artaxata. Tigranes II, the Great, ruling from 95 BCE, seized northern Mesopotamia, Syria and Cilicia, took the title King of Kings and built Tigranocerta, settling it with deportees. Wealth came from farming, horses and trade routes between Parthia and the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.e: Lucullus defeated Tigranes at Tigranocerta in 69 BCE, and in 66 BCE he submitted to Pompey, keeping only Armenia. His successors were caught between the Roman Republic and the Parthian Empire; Artavasdes II was killed in Egypt. After rival puppet kings, the line ended about 12 CE.
kingdom-of-armenia-artaxiad.re: Armenian paganism with Iranian and Greek influence

kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.t: The Napoleonic kingdom of southern Italy under Joseph Bonaparte and Joachim Murat, which abolished feudalism in the south.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.o: After the Bourbon Kingdom of Naples joined the coalition against France, Napoleon sent an army in 1806. King Ferdinand IV fled to Sicily under British protection, and Napoleon made his brother Joseph Bonaparte king of Naples.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.r: Joseph abolished feudalism in 1806, closed monasteries and introduced French administration. In 1808 he became king of Spain and was succeeded by Joachim Murat, Napoleon's brother-in-law, who introduced the Napoleonic Code, built roads and fought brigandage in Calabria. The kingdom never controlled Sicily, which the Bourbons held with British help.
kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815.e: Murat abandoned Napoleon in 1814, but in 1815 he declared war on Austria with the Rimini Proclamation calling for Italian independence. Defeated at Tolentino in May 1815, he fled; landing in Calabria in October, he was captured and shot. Ferdinand returned to Naples.

kingdom-of-ceredigion.t: Early Welsh kingdom on Cardigan Bay, named after its legendary founder Ceredig, which grew into Seisyllwg in the 8th century.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.o: Welsh tradition says the kingdom was founded by Ceredig, a son of Cunedda, who came from the north to drive Irish settlers out of Wales in the 5th century, and that the land took its name from him. This story was recorded centuries later and is regarded with caution by historians, but Ceredigion as a district between the Dyfi and the Teifi is ancient.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.r: Little is known of its rulers before the 8th century beyond genealogies. The kingdom covered the coastal lowlands and hills of modern Ceredigion, a region of small farms and cattle-rearing, and its church centres included Llanbadarn Fawr, associated with St Padarn, which became one of the leading monasteries of Wales.
kingdom-of-ceredigion.e: Around 730 its king Seisyll ap Clydog conquered the neighbouring Kingdom of Ystrad Tywi, creating an enlarged realm known as Seisyllwg. This later passed to Hywel Dda and became part of Deheubarth. The name survives in the modern county of Ceredigion.

kingdom-of-di-206-bc.t: The northernmost of the Three Qins, given in 206 BCE to the former Qin officer Dong Yi and lost to Liu Bang within months.
kingdom-of-di-206-bc.o: Dong Yi was a Qin commander who urged Zhang Han to surrender to Xiang Yu in 207 BCE. As a reward, Xiang Yu made him King of Di, ruling the old Shang commandery in northern Shaanxi from Gaonu near modern Yan'an, one of three kingdoms meant to contain Liu Bang.
kingdom-of-di-206-bc.r: Di was a thinly populated frontier region on the Loess Plateau, facing the Xiongnu. Its king had no local support, and the kingdom existed only a few months.
kingdom-of-di-206-bc.e: When Liu Bang broke out of Hanzhong in 206 BCE, Dong Yi surrendered and his kingdom became Han territory. Like Sima Xin of the Kingdom of Sai, he later returned to Xiang Yu and killed himself after the Chu defeat on the Si River near Chenggao in 203 BCE.

kilwa-sultanate.t: The richest Swahili city-state of the Middle Ages, which controlled the gold trade of southern Africa from its island capital.
kilwa-sultanate.o: The Kilwa Chronicle traditionally dates the sultanate to c. 957, when Ali ibn al-Hasan, a prince said to come from Shiraz in Persia, bought the island of Kilwa Kisiwani from a local ruler. Archaeology suggests a gradual rise from a fishing and trading settlement, with stone building and coinage appearing by the 11th century.
kilwa-sultanate.r: Kilwa grew rich by taking control of Sofala, the port for gold from Great Zimbabwe. Under the Mahdali dynasty, from the late 13th century, Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman built the vast palace of Husuni Kubwa and enlarged the Great Mosque. Ibn Battuta, visiting in 1331, called Kilwa one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Its rulers minted copper coins and traded ivory, gold and slaves for Indian cloth and Chinese porcelain.
kilwa-sultanate.e: Dynastic quarrels weakened Kilwa in the 15th century, and in 1505 a Portuguese fleet under Francisco de Almeida sacked the city and built a fort there. Trade collapsed, and the town later fell under Omani rule. Its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

kingdom-of-qocho.t: A Uyghur kingdom of the Turfan oasis where Buddhism, Manichaeism and Christianity flourished and whose rulers submitted early to Genghis Khan.
kingdom-of-qocho.o: After the Uyghur Khaganate fell in 840, Uyghur groups moved south-west to the Tian Shan oases. By 856 they controlled Turfan and Beshbaliq, with Qocho (Gaochang) as a winter capital, establishing a kingdom under rulers with the title idiqut.
kingdom-of-qocho.r: The Uyghurs adapted to oasis life, with irrigated fields, vineyards and cotton. The court first favoured Manichaeism, but Buddhism became dominant, and the Bezeklik caves were decorated with murals of Uyghur donors. The Uyghur script, derived from Sogdian, was used for a large literature of Buddhist and other texts, and Uyghur scribes later served the Mongols.
kingdom-of-qocho.e: The kingdom became a vassal of the Qara Khitai, and in 1209 the idiqut Barchuq Art Tegin submitted to Genghis Khan. Under the Mongols it remained a privileged vassal until rule passed to the Chagatai Khanate in the 14th century.
kingdom-of-qocho.re: Buddhism, Manichaeism, Church of the East

kingdom-of-lalangina.t: A Betsileo kingdom of the southern Malagasy highlands, one of several small states absorbed by the expanding Merina Kingdom.
kingdom-of-lalangina.o: Lalangina was one of four main Betsileo kingdoms that took shape in the southern highlands of Madagascar in the 18th century, in the region around modern Fianarantsoa. Its ruling dynasty claimed descent from immigrant nobles, and its history is known mainly from oral tradition.
kingdom-of-lalangina.r: Betsileo kings ruled over farming villages that built extensive terraced rice fields in the highland valleys, and royal authority was tied to ancestral tombs and rituals. Lalangina competed with neighbouring kingdoms, including the Kingdom of Isandra, for land and cattle.
kingdom-of-lalangina.e: Around 1811 the Merina Kingdom under Andrianampoinimerina and his son Radama I absorbed the Betsileo kingdoms, and Lalangina came under Merina rule. The Betsileo remain one of Madagascar's largest peoples.

kydonia.t: Leading city of western Crete for much of antiquity, a rival of Knossos and Gortyn, on the site of modern Chania.
kydonia.o: Kydonia stood on a Minoan site on the north-west coast of Crete. Herodotus records that Samian exiles fleeing Polycrates settled there in 524 BCE and built temples, before Aeginetans defeated them in 519 BCE and settled the city in their turn. By the classical period it was an independent Cretan polis named after its legendary founder Kydon.
kydonia.r: Kydonia was governed, like other Cretan cities, by annual officials called kosmoi and a council of elders, with a warrior aristocracy and dependent rural labourers. It struck silver coins, traded across the Aegean and supplied mercenaries, including famous archers. In the Hellenistic period it fought repeated wars with Knossos, Gortyn and Polyrrhenia.
kydonia.e: Rome intervened in Crete during the wars against the Cretan pirates. Quintus Caecilius Metellus besieged and took Kydonia in 69 BCE on his way to conquering the island, which became part of the province of Crete and Cyrene. Kydonia remained a free city under Rome and survives as Chania.

kutrigurs.t: Nomads of the steppe west of the Don whose raid under Zabergan in 559 reached the outskirts of Constantinople.
kutrigurs.o: The Kutrigurs are named by Procopius and Agathias in the 6th century as a Hunnic or Bulgar people of the steppe between the Don and the Dnieper, kin to the Utigurs to their east. They emerged from the remnants of the Hunnic Empire and the Oghur peoples who arrived after 463.
kutrigurs.r: As pastoral nomads under chiefs, they lived on herding and raids into the Balkans, sometimes as Byzantine allies against the Gepids. In 559 their khan Zabergan crossed the frozen Danube, raided Thrace and Greece and threatened Constantinople, until the aged general Belisarius repelled him. Justinian then turned the Utigurs against them.
kutrigurs.e: Weakened by war with the Utigurs, the Kutrigurs fell under the Avars in the 560s; many joined the Avar Khaganate in Pannonia. Others later joined Kubrat's Old Great Bulgaria.

kingdom-of-dotawo.t: The last Christian Nubian kingdom on the Nile, a rump of Makuria centred at Gebel Adda and Qasr Ibrim that survived into the late 15th century.
kingdom-of-dotawo.o: Dotawo was the Old Nubian name used in documents for the realm of Makuria. After Dongola was abandoned around 1365 amid Mamluk interventions and Arab raids, the surviving court moved north to Daw, generally identified with Gebel Adda in Lower Nubia, and the reduced kingdom is known by this name.
kingdom-of-dotawo.r: The kingdom is known mainly from Old Nubian letters and legal documents found at Qasr Ibrim and from scattered Arabic notices. It kept the Nubian Church with its bishops, Greek and Old Nubian liturgy, and a court with eparchs and officials in the tradition of Makuria, but its territory and resources were small.
kingdom-of-dotawo.e: The last known king, Joel, is attested in 1484. Dotawo then disappears from the record, probably absorbed during the spread of Islam and Arab tribes and the rise of the Funj Sultanate, which ended Christian Nubia.

kamiros.t: Farming city on the west coast of Rhodes, one of the island's three ancient cities, whose terraced streets survive in remarkable condition.
kamiros.o: Kamiros was settled by Dorian Greeks in the early Iron Age on a slope above the west coast of Rhodes, facing Anatolia across the sea. It was one of the three Rhodian cities, with Lindos and Ialysos, and a member of the Dorian Hexapolis.
kamiros.r: Unlike Lindos, Kamiros relied mainly on farming of grain, figs, olives and wine. Its cemeteries have yielded rich finds of Archaic pottery and jewellery, giving its name to the 'Kamiran' style of East Greek ware. The city fell under the Achaemenid Empire and then belonged to the Delian League. Its acropolis held a temple of Athena Kameiras.
kamiros.e: In 408 BCE Kamiros joined Lindos and Ialysos to found the city of Rhodes and lost its political independence. It continued as a town; after earthquakes it was rebuilt in the Hellenistic period, and its houses and cistern can still be seen.
kamiros.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Kameiras

kingdom-of-changshan.t: Zhang Er's kingdom in Hebei, carved from Zhao by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, which fell to his former friend Chen Yu within a year.
kingdom-of-changshan.o: Zhang Er had been chancellor of the revived state of Zhao during the rebellion against the Qin dynasty. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Changshan, ruling most of Zhao from Xiangguo (near Xingtai), while the Zhao king Zhao Xie was moved north to the Kingdom of Dai (206 BC).
kingdom-of-changshan.r: The kingdom was dominated by the bitter quarrel between Zhang Er and Chen Yu, once sworn friends, who had fallen out during the siege of Julu. Chen Yu, given only a few counties, felt cheated by the settlement.
kingdom-of-changshan.e: In 205 BCE Chen Yu, with troops from Tian Rong of Qi (206 BC), drove Zhang Er out; Zhang fled to Liu Bang, and Zhao Xie was restored as King of Zhao. After Han Xin defeated Zhao at Jingxing in 204 BCE, Liu Bang made Zhang Er King of Zhao.

kingdom-of-glywysing.t: Kingdom of south-east Wales between the Usk and the Tawe, home of the great monasteries of Llantwit and Llancarfan, which became Morgannwg.
kingdom-of-glywysing.o: Glywysing took its name from Glywys, a legendary 5th-century king whose descendants, according to the Lives of the Welsh saints, included St Cadoc. It grew from the post-Roman communities of the Glamorgan lowlands, once the territory of the Silures, and was often joined with the neighbouring Kingdom of Gwent under a single dynasty.
kingdom-of-glywysing.r: The Llandaff charters, a collection of land grants, show a society of kings, churchmen and landowners trading estates and gifts. Meurig ap Tewdrig and his descendants ruled across Glywysing and Gwent from the 7th century. The monasteries of Llantwit Major, founded by St Illtud, and Llancarfan, founded by St Cadoc, were leading centres of learning. Asser says Hywel ap Rhys submitted to Alfred.
kingdom-of-glywysing.e: In the 10th century Morgan Hen ruled both Glywysing and Gwent, and from around 942 his combined realm became known as Morgannwg, from which the name Glamorgan derives. The region later fell to the Normans under Robert Fitzhamon in the 1090s.

kingdom-of-amathus.t: Cypriot kingdom on the south coast that kept the island's pre-Greek Eteocypriot language alive into the 4th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.o: Amathus was founded c. 1050 BCE on a hill near modern Limassol. Ancient writers regarded its people as autochthonous Cypriots, and the city preserved the Eteocypriot language, written in the Cypriot syllabary, alongside Greek. It also had close links with Phoenicia, and its rulers paid tribute to Assyria in the 7th century BCE.
kingdom-of-amathus.r: The acropolis held a palace and a major sanctuary of the Cypriot goddess later called Aphrodite, with a giant stone vase now in the Louvre. The kingdom grew rich from copper and agriculture. It was loyal to Persia: in 498 BCE it refused to join the revolt led by Onesilus of Salamis and was besieged.
kingdom-of-amathus.e: King Androcles sent ships to help Alexander the Great at Tyre in 332 BCE. The monarchy was ended under Ptolemy I c. 312 BCE, and Amathus continued as a city under the Ptolemaic Empire and Rome. It declined after the 7th century CE and was abandoned.

kingdom-of-the-rugians.t: A small East Germanic kingdom north of the Danube in Lower Austria, known chiefly from the Life of Saint Severinus and destroyed by Odoacer in 487.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.o: The Rugii originally lived on the Baltic coast, where Tacitus places them. After migrating south and serving under the Huns, they settled after Attila's death in 453 on the north bank of the Danube opposite the Roman province of Noricum, in the area later called Rugiland, in modern Lower Austria.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.r: The Rugian kings were Arian Christians who dominated the remaining Roman towns of Noricum Ripense, collecting tribute and controlling trade across the Danube. Eugippius' Life of Saint Severinus portrays King Flaccitheus, his son Feletheus and the harsh Queen Giso, whom the saint rebuked. Their power depended on balancing Ostrogoths, Heruli and the Roman population.
kingdom-of-the-rugians.e: In 487 Odoacer, ruler of Italy, attacked Rugiland and captured Feletheus and Giso; in 488 his brother crushed their son Fredericus, and the Roman population of Noricum was evacuated to Italy. Surviving Rugians joined Theodoric's Ostrogoths and went with them to Italy, keeping a separate identity there into the 540s.

kingdom-of-kuku.t: A Kabyle kingdom in the Djurdjura mountains whose founder, Ahmed Belkadi, defeated Hayreddin Barbarossa and briefly ruled Algiers.
kingdom-of-kuku.o: Ahmed Belkadi, a judge from a family that had served the Hafsids in Bejaia, established himself in Greater Kabylia around 1515 after the Spanish captured Bejaia, with his stronghold at Kuku in the Djurdjura mountains.
kingdom-of-kuku.r: Belkadi first allied with the Barbarossa brothers, then turned against Hayreddin, defeated him and held Algiers from about 1520 until he was killed around 1527. His successors ruled the Kabyle highlands, sometimes allied with the Regency of Algiers, sometimes with Spain, and competed with the Kingdom of Ait Abbas. Rule depended on mountain tribal alliances.
kingdom-of-kuku.e: The dynasty declined in the 17th century as Kabyle tribes asserted their independence and Algiers extended its influence. By around 1638 the kingdom had broken up, though Greater Kabylia stayed largely self-governing until the French conquest.

kingdom-of-lazica.t: A western Georgian kingdom on the Black Sea coast, heir of ancient Colchis, over which Byzantium and Persia fought the long Lazic War of the 6th century.
kingdom-of-lazica.o: The Lazi, a Kartvelian people of the old Kingdom of Colchis, rose to dominance on the eastern Black Sea coast in the 2nd century CE. Arrian, touring the coast for Emperor Hadrian in the 130s, recorded a Lazi king holding power by Roman appointment, and the Lazi gradually united neighbouring tribes.
kingdom-of-lazica.r: Kings ruled from the fortress of Archaeopolis, modern Nokalakevi, over a land of forests, river valleys and coastal forts. Lazica was a client of the Roman Empire and then the Byzantine Empire, and King Tzath I was baptised in Constantinople in 522, making Christianity official. The kingdom controlled trade routes and timber vital to Black Sea navies.
kingdom-of-lazica.e: In 541 the Lazi invited Persian help, sparking the Lazic War; after King Gubazes II was murdered by Byzantine officers, a peace of 562 returned Lazica to Byzantium. Arab raids in the 7th century weakened it, and its lands passed into the Kingdom of Abkhazia.

kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.t: A brief sub-kingdom in the east Midlands created for Penda's son Peada, notable as the place where Christianity first entered Mercian lands.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.o: The Middle Angles were a group of peoples in the east Midlands, around the Fens and the Nene and Welland valleys. Around 653 Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia made his son Peada their king. Peada married Alhflaed, a daughter of Oswiu of Northumbria, and accepted baptism as a condition of the marriage.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.r: Peada brought four priests, including Cedd and Diuma, who preached among the Middle Angles, the first Christian mission in Mercian territory. Tradition links Peada to the foundation of Medeshamstede, later Peterborough Abbey. The many small peoples of the region, listed in the Tribal Hidage, kept their own identities.
kingdom-of-the-middle-angles.e: After Penda's death in 655 Oswiu let Peada rule southern Mercia, but he was murdered in 656, allegedly through his wife's treachery. The Middle Angles were absorbed into Mercia, though they kept a bishopric at Leicester.

kazakh-khanate.t: The khanate of the Kazakh steppe, founded by Kerei and Janibek, which shaped Kazakh identity and law for nearly four centuries.
kazakh-khanate.o: Around 1465 the sultans Kerei and Janibek, descendants of Urus Khan of the White Horde, broke away from Abu'l-Khayr's Uzbek Khanate and led their followers to Moghulistan's western pastures in the Chu valley. Their people became known as Kazakhs, 'free wanderers', and after Abu'l-Khayr's death they took over most of the steppe.
kazakh-khanate.r: The khanate was a nomadic confederation led by Genghisid sultans, with clan elders and judges (biys). Under Qasim Khan in the early 16th century it may have numbered a million people. Tauke Khan in the late 17th century issued the code of law known as Zhety Zhargy. The city of Turkistan, with the mausoleum of Ahmad Yasawi, was a political and spiritual centre.
kazakh-khanate.e: Divided into the Senior Juz, Middle Juz and Junior Juz in the 18th century, the Kazakhs suffered Dzungar invasions and turned to Russia. Russia abolished the khans' power in the 1820s, and Kenesary Kasymov's revolt ended in 1847.

kingdom-of-the-franks.t: The Frankish realm founded by Clovis, the most lasting of the barbarian kingdoms and the common ancestor of France and Germany.
kingdom-of-the-franks.o: Clovis succeeded his father Childeric I as king of the Salian Franks at Tournai in 481. He destroyed the Domain of Soissons in 486, defeated the Alemanni, accepted Catholic baptism at Reims and in 507 crushed the Visigothic Kingdom at Vouillé, taking Aquitaine. He made Paris his capital and absorbed the other Frankish kingdoms.
kingdom-of-the-franks.r: The Merovingian kings divided the realm among their sons as private inheritance, creating Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy. Gallo-Roman bishops, counts and a Frankish warrior aristocracy ran it together. From the 7th century real power passed to the mayors of the palace, and Charles Martel halted an Umayyad army near Tours in 732.
kingdom-of-the-franks.e: In 751 Pippin the Short deposed the last Merovingian, Childeric III, and became king. His son Charlemagne conquered Saxony and Lombard Italy and was crowned emperor in 800, ruling the Carolingian Empire. In 843 the Treaty of Verdun split the realm into West Francia, Middle Francia and East Francia.

kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.t: The mountain-based Kongo kingship of Kibangu, one of the rival courts that emerged from Kongo's civil wars and eventually reunited the kingdom in 1709.
kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.o: After the Kingdom of Kongo's defeat by Portugal at the Battle of Mbwila in 1665, the kingdom split among rival royal houses, and the capital Sao Salvador was abandoned in 1678. One faction made its base on the fortified mountain of Kibangu, east of the old capital, where a line of claimants maintained the title of king of Kongo.
kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.r: The Kibangu kings ruled a small territory but kept the full ceremony and Catholic identity of the Kongo monarchy, hosting Italian Capuchin missionaries. Garcia III and later Pedro IV ruled from there. Pedro IV pursued reconciliation among the rival houses, while the prophet Kimpa Vita and her Antonian movement challenged him by reoccupying Sao Salvador; he had her burnt in 1706.
kingdom-of-kongo-dia-ntotila-kibangu.e: In 1709 Pedro IV's forces retook Sao Salvador, ending the separate Kibangu court and restoring a single, though much weakened, Kingdom of Kongo.

kingdom-of-asturias.t: The first Christian kingdom in Iberia after the Muslim conquest, born at Covadonga and seen as the cradle of the Reconquista.
kingdom-of-asturias.o: After 711 the Visigothic noble Pelagius led a revolt in the mountains of Asturias and defeated a Muslim force at Covadonga, traditionally in 718 or 722. His small realm, based at Cangas de Onís, grew under Alfonso I, son of Duke Peter of the Duchy of Cantabria, who raided the Douro valley and absorbed Cantabria.
kingdom-of-asturias.r: Alfonso II the Chaste made Oviedo the capital and modelled his court on the Visigothic kingdom of Toledo. Under him the tomb of St James was proclaimed at Compostela, starting a great pilgrimage. Ramiro I built the pre-Romanesque churches of Monte Naranco. Alfonso III the Great resettled the Douro frontier, taking Porto in 868 and Coimbra in 878, and sponsored chronicles of a Gothic restoration.
kingdom-of-asturias.e: In 910 Alfonso III was deposed by his sons, who divided the realm into León, Galicia and Asturias. With Fruela II's death in 924 the court settled at León, and the Kingdom of Asturias gave way to the Kingdom of León.

kingdom-of-provence.t: Short-lived Carolingian kingdom of the lower Rhône, carved out for the youngest son of Lothair I.
kingdom-of-provence.o: When Lothair I divided Middle Francia in 855, his youngest son Charles, still a boy, received Provence and the duchy of Lyon, stretching from the Mediterranean up the Rhône valley.
kingdom-of-provence.r: Charles suffered from epilepsy, and the kingdom was effectively run by Count Girart of Vienne, his guardian, who defended it against the ambitions of Charles the Bald and fought Viking raiders who had sailed up the Rhône. Vienne and Lyon were its main centres.
kingdom-of-provence.e: Charles died childless in 863, and his brothers Lothair II and the emperor Louis II divided the kingdom between them. The region later re-emerged as the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy under Boso in 879.

kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.t: The last Herodian kingdom, briefly reuniting Herod the Great's realm under Agrippa I and surviving as a Roman client under Agrippa II until about 100.
kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.o: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great and friend of Caligula, received the former Tetrarchy of Philip with the title king in 37. Caligula added Galilee and Peraea in 39, and Claudius, whom Agrippa had helped to the throne, gave him Judea and Samaria in 41, restoring his grandfather's kingdom.
kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.r: Agrippa I courted Jewish opinion in Jerusalem, began a third city wall and, according to Acts, executed the apostle James; he died suddenly at Caesarea in 44, and Judea returned to Roman procurators. His son Agrippa II received Chalcis and from 53 the northern lands, renaming Caesarea Philippi as Neronias. He supervised the Temple, appointed high priests and heard the apostle Paul at Caesarea.
kingdom-of-herod-agrippa.e: Agrippa II urged his people not to revolt in 66 and fought on Rome's side in the Jewish War. He kept his kingdom afterwards; its end is dated by his death, placed by some sources around 92-93 and by others around 100, after which the territory was annexed to Syria.

kanesh.t: Kanesh, a central Anatolian city-kingdom near Kayseri that hosted the largest Assyrian trading colony, and whose name gave the Hittite language its own title.
kanesh.o: Kanesh, at Kültepe, was a native Anatolian city by the late 3rd millennium BCE. From c. 1950 BCE merchants from Assur settled in a trading quarter, the karum, below its citadel, bringing tin and woollen textiles by donkey caravan to exchange for Anatolian silver and gold.
kanesh.r: Local kings and queens ruled the citadel and taxed the trade under treaties with Assur, while the merchants kept their own court and over 23,000 letters and contracts in Old Assyrian. The archives record Anatolian personal names that are the earliest evidence of Hittite, which its speakers later called nesili after Nesa, the local name of Kanesh.
kanesh.e: Around 1750 BCE Pithana and his son Anitta of Kussara captured Nesa and made it their seat. The trade colony faded c. 1700 BCE and the city lost importance as power shifted towards Hattusa and the Hittite Empire.

kingdom-of-sussex.t: The kingdom of the South Saxons on the English Channel coast, among the earliest Anglo-Saxon realms and the last major one to accept Christianity.
kingdom-of-sussex.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says that Aelle and his three sons landed in 477 and fought the Britons near the shore, later storming the Roman fort of Anderitum (Pevensey) in 491. Bede names Aelle as the first overlord of the southern English. Settlement was hemmed in by the dense Weald forest, which isolated the kingdom from its neighbours.
kingdom-of-sussex.r: Sussex was small and inward-looking, with a farming economy on the coastal plain and the chalk downs. Its kings often stood under Mercian or West Saxon overlordship. Paganism lasted until Wilfrid of York converted the South Saxons in the 680s, founding a monastery and bishopric at Selsey on land given by King Aethelwealh. Several kings sometimes ruled at once.
kingdom-of-sussex.e: Caedwalla of Wessex overran Sussex in the 680s, and in the 8th century it fell under Offa of Mercia. After Ecgberht's victory at Ellendun in 825, Sussex submitted to the Kingdom of Wessex and became a shire. The name survives in the modern counties of East and West Sussex.

kazikumukh-khanate.t: A Lak khanate in the mountains of central Dagestan whose ruler Surkhay Khan briefly controlled Shirvan in the 1720s.
kazikumukh-khanate.o: When the shamkhals moved to Tarki around 1642, the Lak heartland at Kumukh became a separate state under its own rulers, who took the title khan. The khanate kept the prestige of Kumukh as an old centre of Islam in Dagestan.
kazikumukh-khanate.r: The khans ruled Lak villages known for craftsmen, traders and seasonal workers, and drew wealth from raids and mercenary service. Surkhay Khan I joined the rebel Hajji Davud in sacking Shamakhi in 1721, an event that helped trigger Peter the Great's Persian campaign, and briefly ruled Shirvan as an Ottoman vassal. Nader Shah later defeated him.
kazikumukh-khanate.e: The khanate accepted Russian protection in 1820. Its khans, such as Aslan Khan, sided with Russia against the Caucasian Imamate, and in 1860 the Russian Empire abolished it. Its lands became the Kazikumukh district of the Dagestan Oblast, the heart of today's Lak region.

kingdom-of-slavonia.t: Habsburg crown land between the Drava and Sava rivers, reconquered from the Ottomans in 1699 and rebuilt with new settlers and baroque towns.
kingdom-of-slavonia.o: Habsburg armies drove the Ottomans out of Slavonia in the Great Turkish War, and the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 confirmed the conquest. The reclaimed land was divided between a civilian part, organised as the counties of Požega, Virovitica and Srijem, and a southern strip along the Sava placed in the Military Frontier.
kingdom-of-slavonia.r: Slavonia was depopulated by war, so the crown and new landowners brought in German, Hungarian, Slovak and Serb settlers. Osijek's fortress, Tvrđa, was rebuilt in the 1710s and 1720s, and the bishopric of Đakovo revived Catholic life, while Orthodox Serbs were organised around Sremski Karlovci. From 1745 the civil counties were placed under the Croatian ban and Sabor.
kingdom-of-slavonia.e: Slavonia remained formally a separate kingdom within the Lands of the Hungarian Crown until the Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868 joined it with Croatia as the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia. The eastern part, Srijem, was divided between Croatia and Serbia after 1945.

khanate-of-kazan.t: A Tatar khanate on the middle Volga, successor to Volga Bulgaria, whose conquest by Ivan the Terrible in 1552 opened the East to Russia.
khanate-of-kazan.o: Around 1438 Ulugh Muhammad, a deposed khan of the Golden Horde, settled in the former lands of Volga Bulgaria and established a khanate with Kazan as its capital. His son Mahmud consolidated it as an independent state.
khanate-of-kazan.r: Kazan ruled Tatars, Chuvash, Mari, Udmurts and Bashkirs, with a farming and trading economy linked to the Volga route. The khan shared power with a council of leading princely clans and religious leaders. The city had mosques, madrasas and a strong merchant community. Rival factions favoured Moscow or the Crimean Khanate, and Russian-backed khans such as Shah Ali were repeatedly installed.
khanate-of-kazan.e: After several failed campaigns, Ivan IV besieged and stormed Kazan in 1552, annexing the khanate to Muscovy. Its Tatar population survived, and Kazan remained the centre of Tatar culture, now the capital of Tatarstan.

kingdom-of-mauretania.t: The Berber kingdom of the Moors in Morocco and western Algeria, ending with Juba II's learned court at Caesarea.
kingdom-of-mauretania.o: The Mauri, Berber peoples of northern Morocco, were united under kings by the late 3rd century BCE; the first well-known king, Baga, provided an escort to Masinissa in 206 BCE. The kingdom lay west of the Mulucha (Moulouya) river and included old Phoenician towns such as Lixus and Tingis.
kingdom-of-mauretania.r: The kings mixed Berber, Punic and later Roman and Greek culture. Bocchus I handed Jugurtha of Numidia to Sulla in 105 BCE, gaining western Numidia. After Bocchus II bequeathed the kingdom to Rome, Augustus installed Juba II in 25 BCE with his wife Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Cleopatra VII. Juba, a scholar, rebuilt Iol as Caesarea, and the kingdom exported purple dye, citrus wood and wild animals.
kingdom-of-mauretania.e: In 40 CE Caligula summoned Juba's son Ptolemy to Rome and had him executed. After a revolt led by Aedemon, Claudius annexed the kingdom, dividing it in 42 CE into Mauretania Tingitana and Mauretania Caesariensis.

kingdom-of-dayuan.t: The ancient kingdom of the Ferghana valley, famed in China for its 'heavenly horses', which provoked the Han dynasty's longest-range war.
kingdom-of-dayuan.o: Dayuan, the Chinese name for the farming people of the Ferghana valley, was described by the envoy Zhang Qian around 128 BCE as a land of over 70 walled towns and several hundred thousand people. Its population may have included descendants of Greek settlers from Alexander's era, though this is debated.
kingdom-of-dayuan.r: The people grew rice, wheat and grapes, made wine and bred tall, fast horses that the Han court prized as 'blood-sweating' heavenly horses. A king ruled with nobles from the capital Ershi. In 104 BCE Dayuan refused to supply horses, and Emperor Wu sent the general Li Guangli, who after two campaigns besieged Ershi in 102 BCE, forcing the nobles to kill their king Wugua and hand over horses.
kingdom-of-dayuan.e: Dayuan remained a tributary of the Han for a time and appears in Chinese records into the 3rd century CE. Thereafter Ferghana was ruled by local dynasties that became the later Principality of Ferghana, still noted for its horses.

kingdom-of-aragon.t: The Pyrenean kingdom that conquered the Ebro valley, joined Catalonia to form the Crown of Aragon and kept its own laws until 1707.
kingdom-of-aragon.o: Aragon began as a small Carolingian-era county around Jaca. In 1035 Sancho III of Navarre left it to his son Ramiro I, who ruled as king in practice. His heirs Sancho Ramírez and Peter I expanded south, taking Huesca in 1096, and Alfonso I the Battler captured Zaragoza in 1118.
kingdom-of-aragon.r: The kingdom developed strong traditions of noble privilege: its Cortes, its fueros and the Justicia de Aragón, a judge who guarded the laws even against the king. Its economy rested on Ebro valley farming, wool and the many Muslim farmers, later called mudéjares and Moriscos, who stayed on the land. Zaragoza became its capital.
kingdom-of-aragon.e: The marriage of Petronila to Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona created the Crown of Aragon. Aragon kept its institutions under Habsburg Spain until Philip V abolished them by the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 after the War of the Spanish Succession.

kingdom-of-brycheiniog.t: Welsh kingdom of the Usk valley, founded according to legend by the Irish-descended Brychan, whose royal crannog at Llangorse was stormed by the Mercians in 916.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.o: Brycheiniog took its name from Brychan, a 5th-century ruler of Irish and British descent whose many saintly children are celebrated in Welsh and Cornish tradition. Ogham-inscribed stones in the region support Irish settlement in the post-Roman period. The kingdom occupied the upper Usk valley and the uplands around modern Brecon.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.r: Its kings were often under pressure from larger neighbours. Asser records that Elisedd ap Tewdwr submitted to Alfred of Wessex in the 880s. The royal crannog on Llangorse Lake, an artificial island built in the 890s, is the only one known in Wales; in 916 the Mercians under Æthelflæd attacked it and carried off the king's wife. Tewdwr ab Elisedd later witnessed English royal charters.
kingdom-of-brycheiniog.e: Brycheiniog lost its independence in the 11th century, coming under the rulers of Deheubarth and Morgannwg. In 1093 the Norman Bernard de Neufmarché defeated and killed Rhys ap Tewdwr near Brecon and created the Norman lordship of Brecknock, which later became the county of Brecknockshire.

kingdom-of-rhos.t: Early kingdom of the north Welsh coast east of the Conwy, guarded by the fortress of Deganwy, which became a cantref of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-rhos.o: Rhos lay between the River Conwy and the Clwydian hills, on the coast of modern Conwy county. Welsh tradition linked it with the sons of Cunedda, and in the 6th century Gildas denounced Cuneglasus, often identified as a king of Rhos, as the charioteer of the Bear's Stronghold, possibly the hillfort of Bryn Euryn near Colwyn Bay.
kingdom-of-rhos.r: The fortress of Deganwy, on twin hills above the Conwy estuary, was associated with Maelgwn Gwynedd and with the rulers of Rhos, and excavation has found imported Mediterranean pottery of the 5th and 6th centuries. The kingdom was closely tied to the Kingdom of Gwynedd and its kings were probably a junior branch of Maelgwn's dynasty.
kingdom-of-rhos.e: In 822 the Mercians destroyed Deganwy and took Rhos for a time. Rhos was later firmly part of the Kingdom of Gwynedd as a cantref of the Perfeddwlad, contested with English kings, until the conquest of 1283.

kingdom-of-vungu.t: A small kingdom north of the lower Congo River, remembered in Kongo tradition as the homeland of the founders of the Kingdom of Kongo.
kingdom-of-vungu.o: Vungu lay in the Mayombe region north of the Congo River and is known chiefly from oral traditions recorded by Portuguese and later writers. These say that the founder of Kongo, Lukeni lua Nimi, was a younger son of a Vungu ruler who crossed the river in the 14th century to conquer lands to the south.
kingdom-of-vungu.r: Very little is known of its government. Like neighbouring Kikongo-speaking polities it was probably ruled by a sacred king drawn from leading lineages, with authority tied to ancestral and territorial spirits. Its prestige rested largely on its role as the ancestral source of Kongo kingship, which later Kongo rulers acknowledged in ceremony.
kingdom-of-vungu.e: Vungu was gradually overshadowed by larger coastal kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Loango and the Kingdom of Kakongo, and it faded from the record by around 1700. Its memory survives mainly in Kongo origin traditions.

kel-ewey.t: A powerful Tuareg confederation of the Aïr mountains, masters of the salt caravans between the Sahara and Hausaland.
kel-ewey.o: The Kel Ewey are thought to have entered the Aïr massif in the 15th or 16th century, displacing earlier Tuareg groups such as the Kel Gres southward. They established themselves in the central and eastern Aïr around Timia and Iferouane, closely linked to the Sultanate of Agadez.
kel-ewey.r: The confederation was led by an anastafidet whose influence over the choice of sultan in Agadez was considerable. Society was hierarchical, with noble, vassal, religious and servile groups. The Kel Ewey organised the great caravans carrying salt and dates from Bilma and Fachi south to Hausaland, returning with millet and cloth.
kel-ewey.e: French troops occupied Aïr after 1900. In 1916 to 1917 Kaocen ag Mohammed, of a Kel Ewey section, led a major revolt and besieged Agadez, but French forces crushed the uprising in 1917. The Kel Ewey remain a major Tuareg group in Niger.

kingdom-of-paphlagonia.t: Paphlagonia, a kingdom of the forested Black Sea hinterland, ruled by local dynasts under Persia and later a pawn of Pontus and Rome.
kingdom-of-paphlagonia.o: The Paphlagonians lived between Bithynia and Pontus, along the Black Sea coast and the forested mountains behind it, with Gangra as an inland seat. By the early 4th century BCE they had kings, such as Corylas, mentioned by Xenophon, who were nominally subject to the Achaemenid Empire.
kingdom-of-paphlagonia.r: The rulers commanded cavalry and controlled timber and the coastal towns. Thys defied Persia until Datames captured him c. 380 BCE. Later kings, often called Pylaemenes, sought alliances with Rome while Pontus pressed them.
kingdom-of-paphlagonia.e: Mithridates VI of the Kingdom of Pontus occupied Paphlagonia in the 2nd century BCE. After Rome's victory it was divided among client rulers; when Deiotarus Philadelphus died in 6 BCE, his kingdom was annexed to Roman Galatia.

kingdom-of-maravi.t: The Chewa confederacy of the Kalonga at the southern end of Lake Malawi, which controlled the ivory trade of the lower Zambezi and gave Malawi its name.
kingdom-of-maravi.o: According to tradition, the Phiri clan migrated from the Luba lands of the Congo basin and settled south-west of Lake Malawi in the late 15th century. Their leader took the title Kalonga and set up his capital at Mankhamba, near the lake. Related chiefs spread out to found the Kingdom of Undi and the Kingdom of Lundu.
kingdom-of-maravi.r: The Kalonga ruled a loose confederacy of chiefs bound by kinship and tribute. Wealth came from iron working, cloth and especially ivory, sold to the Portuguese and Swahili on the Zambezi. Religion centred on the rain shrines of the high god Chisumphi and on the Nyau masked societies. Kalonga Masula in the early 17th century extended Maravi power towards the coast and aided the Portuguese against the Zimba.
kingdom-of-maravi.e: After Masula's death the confederacy loosened, and by the early 18th century the Kalonga, Undi and Lundu ruled separately. Ngoni and Yao incursions in the 19th century completed the break-up. The name Maravi survives in modern Malawi.

kingdom-of-tamassos.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom built on rich copper mines, whose last king sold his realm to the king of Kition for fifty talents.
kingdom-of-tamassos.o: Tamassos lay in the Pediaios valley at the foot of the copper-rich Troodos mountains and was settled from the Bronze Age. Its copper may be the 'Temese' of Homer's Odyssey. By the 7th century BCE it was an independent kingdom; its king Admetus appears among the Cypriot rulers listed by Esarhaddon of Assyria.
kingdom-of-tamassos.r: The kingdom's wealth came from copper mining and smelting. Its royal tombs of the 6th century BCE are built of fine ashlar masonry imitating wooden houses, and a sanctuary of Apollo and the Mother of the Gods has yielded much sculpture. Tamassos used Greek and Phoenician alongside each other.
kingdom-of-tamassos.e: In the 4th century BCE King Pasicyprus sold Tamassos to Pumiyaton of the Kingdom of Kition for fifty talents. Alexander the Great later gave it to the king of Salamis. Tamassos survived as a town under Ptolemaic and Roman rule.

kingdom-of-surrey.t: A short-lived Saxon territory south of the Thames whose name, the 'southern district', survives as the county of Surrey.
kingdom-of-surrey.o: Surrey, Suthrige, probably began as the southern part of a larger Middle Saxon territory on both sides of the Thames. In the 7th century it lay between Kent, Wessex, Sussex and Mercia and was ruled by local leaders under one or another of them.
kingdom-of-surrey.r: The only known ruler is Frithuwold, a sub-king under Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia, who around 672 to 674 endowed Chertsey Abbey, founded by Bishop Eorcenwald. The charter shows estates, minsters and Mercian overlordship but no independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-surrey.e: Surrey never had a lasting royal line. Control passed between Mercia and Wessex, and in the 9th century it became a West Saxon shire, keeping its name and much of its boundary.

kingdom-of-the-suebi.t: A Germanic kingdom that ruled Gallaecia from Braga for over 170 years, one of the first barbarian realms in the former Roman West.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.o: The Suebi crossed the Rhine in 406 with the Vandals and Alans and entered Hispania in 409. In 411 they received lands in Gallaecia under their king Hermeric. After the Vandals left for Africa in 429, Rechila expanded south, taking Emerita Augusta in 439 and Seville in 441.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.r: The kingdom was centred on Bracara Augusta and ruled a Hispano-Roman majority through bishops and local elites. Rechiar became the first Catholic Germanic king around 448 and minted silver coins, but was defeated and killed by the Visigoth Theodoric II in 456. The Suebi later turned Arian, then returned to Catholicism under Martin of Braga's influence around 560. The Councils of Braga of 561 and 572 organised the church.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.e: King Miro was drawn into Visigothic conflicts and died in 583. In 585 the Visigothic king Leovigild overthrew the usurper Andeca and annexed the kingdom, ending Suebic rule. Its territory shaped the later Kingdom of Galicia.

kingdom-of-kinda.t: A central Arabian tribal kingdom that briefly united the Bedouin of Najd under Himyarite patronage and produced the poet Imru al-Qays.
kingdom-of-kinda.o: Kinda was a tribe from the borders of Hadramawt that moved into central Arabia. In the 5th century the Himyarite Kingdom installed its chief Hujr Akil al-Murar as king over the Ma'add tribes of Najd, giving Himyar indirect control of the interior. Qaryat al-Faw, a caravan town on the edge of the Empty Quarter, is often linked with the kingdom.
kingdom-of-kinda.r: Kindite kings ruled as overlords of shifting tribal alliances rather than through fixed institutions, collecting tribute and leading raids. Under al-Harith ibn Amr in the early 6th century, Kinda reached its peak and even held al-Hira for a time at the expense of the Lakhmid Kingdom, with Byzantine diplomatic support.
kingdom-of-kinda.e: After al-Harith was killed around 528, his sons divided the tribes and were defeated by the Lakhmids and rival tribes. The kingdom had collapsed by about 540. Its memory survives through Imru al-Qays, son of the last king Hujr, whose ode is one of the Mu'allaqat.

kingdom-of-tio.t: The Teke kingdom on the plateaus north of Malebo Pool, whose king signed the 1880 treaty that founded French rule on the Congo.
kingdom-of-tio.o: The Tio or Teke kingdom formed on the sandy plateaus north of Malebo Pool by the 15th century. Portuguese sources of the 16th century call it Anziku and describe wars with the Kingdom of Kongo for control of the Pool, the hub of river trade between the interior and the Atlantic coast.
kingdom-of-tio.r: The king, known as the Makoko, ruled from Mbe as a sacred figure whose power came from the national shrine of Nkwe Mbali and the royal nkobi, a box of sacred relics. Real power was shared with territorial lords who controlled trade at the Pool. The kingdom traded slaves, ivory and copper downriver in exchange for cloth, guns and shells, and was famed for its raffia textiles.
kingdom-of-tio.e: In 1880 Makoko Iloo I signed a treaty with Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza placing his lands under French protection, which gave France its foothold on the Congo and its new post of Brazzaville. The kingship survives as a ceremonial office in the Republic of the Congo.

kingdom-of-york.t: The Viking kingdom centred on Jorvik, a prosperous Anglo-Scandinavian town whose kings were often also rulers of Dublin.
kingdom-of-york.o: The Great Heathen Army captured York in 866 to 867, and in 876 Halfdan shared out the land of Northumbria south of the Tees among his followers. Danish kings ruled from York, with Guthfrith in the 880s accepting Christianity. Early in the 10th century the Norse dynasty of the Kingdom of Dublin took over.
kingdom-of-york.r: Jorvik grew into a major town of craftsmen and traders, with goods from Scandinavia to the Middle East, as the Coppergate excavations show. Its kings minted coins, some with Christian symbols, and cooperated with the archbishops of York. Scandinavian settlement left hundreds of place-names across Yorkshire.
kingdom-of-york.e: Aethelstan seized York in 927, but Norse kings such as Olaf Guthfrithson, Amlaib Cuaran and Eric Bloodaxe returned repeatedly. Eric's expulsion and death in 954 ended the kingdom, and York became part of the Kingdom of England as an earldom.

klein-vrystaat.t: A tiny Boer republic on the Swazi border, created from a land grant by the Swazi king Mbandzeni.
klein-vrystaat.o: Around 1886 a group of Boer farmers who had obtained grazing and land concessions from the Swazi king Mbandzeni in the southwest of his kingdom set themselves up as an independent republic, the Little Free State, around the area of the later town of Piet Retief.
klein-vrystaat.r: Very little is recorded beyond its small Volksraad and a population of a few dozen farming families. Its existence was one example of the concessions that left much of the Swazi Kingdom in the hands of outsiders.
klein-vrystaat.e: Klein Vrystaat was incorporated into the South African Republic in 1891.

kingdom-of-matamba.t: An Mbundu kingdom east of Ndongo, often ruled by women, which Queen Njinga made the base of her long resistance to Portugal.
kingdom-of-matamba.o: Matamba lay in the upper Kwango valley and was a tributary of the Kingdom of Kongo in the early 16th century. It was ruled by queens in the later 16th century. Around 1631 Njinga Mbande, driven out of the Kingdom of Ndongo, conquered Matamba and made it the centre of her state.
kingdom-of-matamba.r: Njinga ruled with the support of Imbangala warriors, trading captives to the Dutch during their occupation of Luanda and later to the Portuguese after the peace of 1656. She accepted Christian missionaries, and Santa Maria de Matamba became her capital. After her death in 1663 her sister Barbara and later rulers continued the line, and the kingdom served as a slave-trading intermediary between the interior and Portuguese Angola.
kingdom-of-matamba.e: Matamba remained independent through the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes at war with Portugal or the Kingdom of Kasanje. Portuguese forces finally occupied it in 1909, and it was absorbed into Portuguese Angola.

kingdom-of-the-hwicce.t: An Anglo-Saxon sub-kingdom of the lower Severn valley around Worcester, ruled by its own kings under Mercian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.o: The Hwicce took shape in Gloucestershire, Worcestershire and western Warwickshire after the West Saxon victory at Dyrham in 577 opened the region to English settlement. By the 7th century the area was ruled by a local dynasty, possibly installed or confirmed by Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.r: Hwiccan kings such as Osric and Oshere founded minsters including Bath, Gloucester and Pershore, and a bishopric was created at Worcester around 680 to serve the people. The territory was rich in salt from Droitwich and in farmland, and its charters are among the earliest English documents.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.e: Hwiccan rulers were downgraded from kings to ealdormen in the late 8th century under Offa. The kingdom's boundaries survived as the medieval diocese of Worcester, preserving its outline for centuries.

kingdom-of-kourion.t: Cypriot kingdom on a clifftop above the south coast, remembered for the sanctuary of Apollo Hylates and for its king's betrayal at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE.
kingdom-of-kourion.o: Kourion arose in the Episkopi area of southern Cyprus, near a Late Bronze Age settlement, in the 11th century BCE. Its Greek inhabitants claimed descent from settlers from Argos. By the 7th century BCE it was one of the island's city-kingdoms, listed among the Cypriot rulers who paid tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon.
kingdom-of-kourion.r: The kings ruled a fertile territory along the Kouris river. The sanctuary of Apollo Hylates, god of the woodland, was its chief cult centre, and rich tombs yielded the gold and silver of the so-called Kourion treasure. Kourion followed the Cypriot syllabary and Greek institutions, under Assyrian and then Achaemenid overlordship.
kingdom-of-kourion.e: In the Ionian Revolt, King Stasanor deserted to the Persians at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE. Later King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre. The monarchy was abolished under Ptolemy I c. 312 BCE, and Kourion flourished as a Roman and early Christian city until earthquakes in the 4th century CE.
kingdom-of-kourion.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Hylates

kingdom-of-corsica.t: The eight-month kingdom of Theodore von Neuhoff, a German adventurer crowned by Corsican rebels against Genoa in 1736.
kingdom-of-corsica.o: Corsicans had been in revolt against Genoese rule since 1729. In March 1736 Theodore von Neuhoff, a Westphalian baron, landed with arms and money from Tunis, and in April the rebel leaders crowned him king at the convent of Alesani, with a constitution limiting his power.
kingdom-of-corsica.r: Theodore set up a court at Cervione, created orders of knighthood, minted coins and issued titles, but failed to take the Genoese-held coastal towns. Promised foreign aid did not arrive, and his support among the rebel chiefs waned.
kingdom-of-corsica.e: In November 1736 Theodore left Corsica to seek help. His later attempts to return failed, and he ended in a London debtors' prison, dying in 1756. The revolt continued and later produced the Corsican Republic.

kingdom-of-syunik.t: A south Armenian mountain kingdom that outlasted the fall of Ani, home to the great monastery of Tatev.
kingdom-of-syunik.o: The Siunid family had governed the mountainous province of Syunik since antiquity. Around 987 Smbat, a prince of its Baghk branch, took the title king with the backing of Bagratid Armenia, forming a kingdom in the southern highlands between Lake Sevan and the Araxes.
kingdom-of-syunik.r: Kings ruled from fortresses such as Kapan over a land of deep valleys, mines and pasture. The monastery of Tatev, seat of the bishops of Syunik, held many villages and grew into a centre of learning. The kingdom acknowledged the kings of Ani and later paid tribute to the Seljuk Empire while defending its fortresses.
kingdom-of-syunik.e: Seljuk conquests stripped away fortress after fortress in the 12th century, and in 1170 the Eldiguzids took Baghaberd, ending the kingdom. Local princely families such as the Orbelians later restored Armenian rule in Syunik under Georgian and Mongol overlords.

kingdom-of-henan.t: A short-lived kingdom around Luoyang, one of Xiang Yu's Eighteen Kingdoms, whose king Shen Yang surrendered to Liu Bang in 205 BCE.
kingdom-of-henan.o: In Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE, Shen Yang, a former official of Zhao and associate of Zhang Er, was rewarded for welcoming Chu forces at the Yellow River by being made King of Henan, with his capital at Luoyang.
kingdom-of-henan.r: The kingdom held the strategic Luoyang basin, the gateway between the Guanzhong region and the eastern plain. It lasted too briefly for any distinctive government to develop.
kingdom-of-henan.e: When Liu Bang emerged from the west in 205 BCE, Shen Yang surrendered without a fight, and his kingdom became Henan Commandery. Its loss opened the route east for Liu Bang's ill-fated march on Pengcheng, capital of Western Chu.

kwanyama-kingdom.t: The largest Ovambo kingdom, straddling the Angola–Namibia border, whose last king Mandume ya Ndemufayo fought both Portugal and South Africa.
kwanyama-kingdom.o: Oukwanyama formed by the 18th century on the floodplains around the Kunene and Cuvelai rivers, under kings drawn from a royal matriclan. It grew into the most populous of the Ovambo kingdoms, with its royal seat in the area of modern Ondjiva.
kwanyama-kingdom.r: Kings held wide power over land and justice, ruling through district headmen and maintaining armed retainers. The economy combined millet farming, cattle, salt and iron, and in the 19th century the kingdom traded cattle and captives for guns and horses with Portuguese and Boer traders. German and Finnish missionaries worked in the kingdom from the 1880s.
kwanyama-kingdom.e: Mandume ya Ndemufayo, king from 1911, resisted Portuguese advances, but after the Portuguese victory at Mongua in 1915 he withdrew south. He was killed fighting South African forces in 1917, and the kingdom was divided between Portuguese Angola and South West Africa.

kathiri-sultanate.t: The sultanate of the Kathiri tribe in Wadi Hadramawt, which ruled Seiyun and Tarim for centuries and was absorbed into South Yemen in 1967.
kathiri-sultanate.o: The Kathiri tribe rose in Hadramawt in the late 14th and 15th centuries, taking control of the valley's towns. In the 16th century Sultan Badr Abu Tuwayriq expanded Kathiri rule across Hadramawt and into Dhofar, using firearms and troops obtained through Ottoman contacts.
kathiri-sultanate.r: Kathiri sultans ruled from Seiyun, whose mud-brick palace still dominates the town, and from Tarim, the religious centre of the valley's sayyid families and Shafi'i scholarship. Their power depended on tribal alliances and later on remittances from Hadrami emigrants in Java, Singapore and Hyderabad. In the 19th century they lost the coast and much of the valley to the Qu'aiti Sultanate.
kathiri-sultanate.e: An agreement of 1918 with the Qu'aiti and Britain placed the sultanate within the British sphere, later the Aden Protectorate. In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over Hadramawt, abolished the sultanate and incorporated it into South Yemen.

kingdom-of-norway-1814.t: The brief independent Norway of 1814, which adopted the Eidsvoll constitution, still in force, before entering union with Sweden.
kingdom-of-norway-1814.o: When the Treaty of Kiel in January 1814 transferred Norway from Denmark to Sweden, the Danish prince Christian Frederik, governor in Norway, led resistance. A constituent assembly at Eidsvoll adopted a liberal constitution on 17 May 1814 and elected him king.
kingdom-of-norway-1814.r: The constitution, inspired by the American and French revolutions, divided power between king, an elected parliament, the Storting, and independent courts, and gave the vote to a relatively broad group of men. The new state had little time to govern: the great powers backed Sweden's claim, and the country was blockaded.
kingdom-of-norway-1814.e: Sweden invaded in July 1814, and after a short war the Convention of Moss on 14 August preserved the constitution in return for union. Christian Frederik abdicated in October, and on 4 November the Storting elected Charles XIII king, beginning Sweden-Norway. 17 May remains Norway's national day.

kingdom-of-lihyan.t: The Lihyanite kingdom of al-Ula, whose kings taxed the incense road through the Hejaz and carved monumental statues at Dedan.
kingdom-of-lihyan.o: Lihyan succeeded the Kingdom of Dedan at the oasis of al-Ula, probably in the late 6th or 5th century BCE, after the Babylonian occupation of the Hejaz ended. Its kings ruled from Dedan and drew their wealth from caravans carrying incense from south Arabia towards the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-lihyan.r: Dadanitic inscriptions record a succession of Lihyanite kings, temple offerings and taxes paid to the god Dhu Ghabat. Large sandstone statues of kings and nobles from the sanctuary at al-Khuraybah show contact with Egyptian and Hellenistic art. Minaean traders from the Kingdom of Ma'in lived alongside the local population and kept their own officials.
kingdom-of-lihyan.e: Lihyan declined as the Nabataean Kingdom extended its control over the caravan trade and took Hegra (Mada'in Salih) to the north. By the 1st century BCE its independence had ended, though the dynasty's exact fate is uncertain. The Lion Tombs and statues at al-Ula are among the region's best-known monuments.

kingdom-of-serbia.t: Serbian kingdom that doubled its territory in the Balkan Wars, endured the First World War and became the core of Yugoslavia.
kingdom-of-serbia.o: Prince Milan Obrenović of the Principality of Serbia, independent since 1878, proclaimed himself king in 1882 with the support of Austria-Hungary. His reign brought defeat by Bulgaria at Slivnitsa in 1885 and domestic unrest, and he abdicated in 1889 in favour of his son Alexander.
kingdom-of-serbia.r: The unpopular Alexander Obrenović was murdered with his queen by army officers in the May Coup of 1903, and Peter I Karađorđević became king. Under the 1903 constitution and Nikola Pašić's Radical Party, Serbia became a parliamentary state, freed itself from Austrian economic control after the Pig War of 1906, and in the Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913 gained Kosovo and Vardar Macedonia.
kingdom-of-serbia.e: After the Sarajevo assassination, Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia in 1914. Overrun in 1915, its army retreated through Albania to Corfu and returned via the Salonika front in 1918. On 1 December 1918 Serbia joined the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, then called the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

kingdom-of-marion.t: Cypriot kingdom on the north-west coast that grew rich on copper trade with Athens until Ptolemy I destroyed it in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-marion.o: Marion grew near modern Polis Chrysochous in north-west Cyprus, close to the copper mines of Limni, in the early Iron Age. It emerged as a city-kingdom in the Cypro-Archaic period, facing Anatolia and the Aegean across the sea.
kingdom-of-marion.r: Marion exported copper and imported large quantities of Athenian painted pottery, found in its cemeteries. Its kings, some with Greek names such as Stasioikos and others possibly Phoenician, issued coins in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. Inscriptions use the Cypriot syllabary for Greek.
kingdom-of-marion.e: Its last king, Stasioikos II, sided with Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who destroyed Marion in 312 BCE and moved its people to Paphos. Ptolemy II refounded the site as Arsinoe c. 270 BCE, and the modern town of Polis stands there today.

kingdom-of-lower-egypt.t: The predynastic Nile Delta, remembered by later Egyptians as a kingdom of the red crown centred on Buto before unification with the south.
kingdom-of-lower-egypt.o: Later Egyptian tradition held that before unification the Delta formed a kingdom of its own, with its capital at Buto (Pe and Dep) and the red crown as its emblem. Archaeologically the region was home to the Buto-Maadi culture of the 4th millennium BCE, with settlements at Buto, Maadi and Tell el-Farkha.
kingdom-of-lower-egypt.r: Whether the Delta was ever a single kingdom is debated; many scholars see a cluster of chiefdoms and trading towns gradually absorbed by Naqada culture spreading from the south around 3400 to 3300 BCE. The Palermo Stone lists names of early northern kings, but they cannot be checked. Buto was home to the cobra goddess Wadjet, and Maadi traded copper, wine and oil with Canaan.
kingdom-of-lower-egypt.e: The north was brought under southern rule around 3100 BCE, remembered as its conquest by Narmer or Menes and the founding of Early Dynastic Egypt. The red crown and Wadjet survived as emblems of Lower Egypt in royal regalia and titles for three thousand years.

kingdom-of-qataban.t: An incense kingdom of south Arabia centred on Wadi Bayhan and its capital Timna, rival of Saba and Hadramawt for five centuries.
kingdom-of-qataban.o: Qataban emerges in Sabaean inscriptions of the 7th century BCE as a junior ally of the Kingdom of Saba. As Sabaean power waned, its rulers asserted independence by the 5th or 4th century BCE, ruling from Timna (modern Hajar Kuhlan) in Wadi Bayhan, at the start of the caravan route north.
kingdom-of-qataban.r: The kingdom taxed the incense trade and built irrigation systems in Wadi Bayhan. Its most famous text, the market law of Shahr Yagil Yuhargib on a stele at Timna, regulated trade and taxes. Qatabanians worshipped the god Amm and wrote Qatabanic. At its height it reached the Gulf of Aden coast and Wadi Markha.
kingdom-of-qataban.e: Qataban weakened in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE as sea trade grew. Timna was burnt, and around 175 CE the Kingdom of Hadramawt and the Himyarite Kingdom divided its lands. Excavations by American teams in the 1950s made Timna one of the best-known south Arabian sites.

kingdom-of-the-netherlands.t: The Dutch constitutional monarchy, shaped by the 1848 constitution, colonial empire, neutrality, war and post-war reconstruction into a founding EU member.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.o: The Kingdom of the Netherlands took its present shape when William I accepted Belgian independence in the Treaty of London of 1839. Constitutional revision in 1848, drafted under Johan Rudolf Thorbecke, introduced ministerial responsibility and direct elections, establishing parliamentary government.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.r: The colonial empire, above all the Dutch East Indies, brought wealth through the cultivation system, criticised in Multatuli's Max Havelaar. Society was organised in 'pillars' of Protestants, Catholics, socialists and liberals. The country stayed neutral in the First World War but was occupied by Germany from 1940 to 1945, while Queen Wilhelmina led the government from London.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.e: Indonesia became independent in 1949. After the North Sea flood of 1953 the Delta Works were built. The Netherlands co-founded NATO and the European Communities, and since 1954 the Kingdom has included Caribbean countries. Willem-Alexander became king in 2013.

kingdom-of-israel.t: The northern Kingdom of Israel, a wealthy Iron Age state centred on Samaria, home of prophets Elijah and Amos, conquered by Assyria.
kingdom-of-israel.o: After Solomon's death c. 930 BCE, the northern tribes rejected his son and made Jeroboam I king, splitting the United Kingdom of Israel. Jeroboam set up shrines at Bethel and Dan to rival Jerusalem. Omri founded a new capital at Samaria c. 880 BCE.
kingdom-of-israel.r: Israel was larger and richer than Judah, with olive oil, wine and trade links to Tyre. Ahab fielded 2,000 chariots at Qarqar in 853 BCE, and the Black Obelisk shows Jehu paying tribute to Shalmaneser III. The prophets Elijah, Amos and Hosea condemned its kings' religious and social policies.
kingdom-of-israel.e: After a revolt against the Assyrian Empire, Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria, which fell in 722 BCE; Sargon II deported over 27,000 people and made Israel a province. The exiles became the legend of the ten lost tribes, while the Samaritans claim descent from those who remained.

krivichs.t: A large East Slavic tribal union on the upper Dnieper, Dvina and Volga, whose towns became Smolensk and Polotsk.
krivichs.o: The Krivichs settled the forested watershed between the Dnieper, the Western Dvina and the upper Volga between the 6th and 8th centuries, mixing with the Baltic and Finnic peoples already there. Archaeologists link them with the culture of long burial mounds. The Primary Chronicle names their towns Smolensk, Polotsk and Izborsk.
krivichs.r: They were organised in clans and districts around fortified centres, governed by elders and tribal assemblies. Their lands lay on the river route from the Baltic to the Black Sea, so trade with Scandinavians brought silver and goods. According to the chronicle, the Krivichs joined the Ilmen Slavs and Finnic tribes in inviting Rurik and his Varangians to rule them.
krivichs.e: In 882 Prince Oleg took Smolensk on his way south to Kiev, and the Krivichs were drawn into Kievan Rus', paying tribute and serving in its armies. Their territory later formed the Principality of Polotsk and the Principality of Smolensk, and their name survives in Latvian as the word for Russians, krievi.

kingdom-of-albania-medieval.t: Angevin kingdom on the Albanian coast created by Charles I of Anjou in 1272 as a base for his ambitions against Byzantium.
kingdom-of-albania-medieval.o: Charles I of Anjou, king of Sicily, acquired claims to the Albanian coast through the Treaty of Viterbo of 1267. In 1272 Albanian nobles and the city of Durrës accepted him, and he proclaimed himself King of Albania (Regnum Albaniae).
kingdom-of-albania-medieval.r: The kingdom was governed by Angevin captains-general and marshals from Durrës, with Albanian nobles granted titles and privileges. It served as a bridgehead for Charles's planned attack on Byzantium, but the Angevin army was defeated at the siege of Berat in 1281. Thereafter it was reduced mostly to Durrës and its surroundings, held by the princes of Achaea and Taranto.
kingdom-of-albania-medieval.e: Albanian lords and the Serbian Empire took much of the land in the 14th century. In 1368 Karl Thopia seized Durrës, ending Angevin rule and founding the Principality of Albania (medieval).

kel-gres.t: A Tuareg confederation pushed south from Aïr that settled on the borderlands of Hausaland, mixing pastoral and agricultural life.
kel-gres.o: The Kel Gres lived in the Aïr mountains in the early modern period, with ties to the Sultanate of Agadez. Pressure from the Kel Ewey drove them south, and by the 18th century they had settled in the region between Tahoua and Madaoua on the northern edge of the Hausa kingdoms.
kel-gres.r: The Kel Gres combined camel and cattle herding with control over farming villages worked by dependent and servile groups. They traded in salt and livestock and were drawn into the wars of the Kingdom of Gobir and its neighbours, and later into rivalries with the Iwellemmeden Kel Dinnik. Muslim scholarly lineages had high prestige.
kel-gres.e: The French conquered the region around 1900, and Tuareg resistance during the First World War was suppressed by 1917. The Kel Gres are today part of Niger's Tuareg population.

kingdom-of-pengwern.t: A shadowy British kingdom of the Shropshire borderlands, remembered in the Welsh poems lamenting Cynddylan and the ruin of his hall.
kingdom-of-pengwern.o: Pengwern is known almost entirely from Welsh poetry, notably the Canu Heledd, a 9th or 10th century cycle of poems lamenting Cynddylan, a 7th century prince. Its centre is uncertain; later tradition placed it at Shrewsbury, while scholars suggest the Wrekin area or Din Gwrygon.
kingdom-of-pengwern.r: Nothing reliable is recorded of its government. The poems describe Cynddylan's hall at Eglwysau Bassa and his wars against the English, and he may have been an ally of Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia. The kingdom was probably one of several successors to the Cornovii tribal region.
kingdom-of-pengwern.e: Pengwern seems to have fallen to Mercian expansion in the mid 7th century; Cynddylan's death is lamented in the poems. Its lands became Mercian, while its memory survived in Welsh literature as a symbol of loss.

kingdom-of-saxony.t: Kingdom of the Albertine Wettins created under Napoleon, a German industrial heartland around Dresden, Leipzig and Chemnitz.
kingdom-of-saxony.o: Elector Frederick Augustus III of Saxony changed sides after Prussia's defeat at Jena and joined the Confederation of the Rhine in December 1806, taking the title King Frederick Augustus I. Napoleon also made him Duke of Warsaw in 1807.
kingdom-of-saxony.r: Saxony fought for Napoleon until Leipzig in 1813, and at the Congress of Vienna it lost about three-fifths of its territory to Prussia. A constitution followed the unrest of 1830, and the May Uprising in Dresden in 1849 was crushed with Prussian help. Textiles, machine building and mining made Saxony one of Germany's most industrialised regions, and Leipzig was a centre of publishing and music.
kingdom-of-saxony.e: Saxony sided with Austria in 1866, then joined the North German Confederation and in 1871 the German Empire. King Frederick Augustus III abdicated in November 1918, and the state became the Free State of Saxony.

kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.t: Early Welsh kingdom of the Tywi valley in Carmarthenshire, conquered around 730 by Ceredigion to form the realm of Seisyllwg.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.o: Ystrad Tywi, 'the vale of the Tywi', covered the fertile river valley and surrounding uplands of what is now Carmarthenshire, including the old Roman town of Moridunum, Carmarthen. After Roman rule ended around 410 it seems to have emerged as a separate territory, sometimes held by the kings of the neighbouring Kingdom of Dyfed.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.r: Very little is known about its rulers or government, and no secure king list survives. The Tywi valley was among the best farmland in south-west Wales, with major church sites such as Llandeilo Fawr, home of the gospel book now known as the Lichfield Gospels before it left Wales.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.e: Around 730 Seisyll ap Clydog of the Kingdom of Ceredigion conquered Ystrad Tywi, forming a larger kingdom named Seisyllwg after him. This passed in the 10th century to Hywel Dda and became part of Deheubarth, whose later princes ruled from Dinefwr in the Tywi valley.

kingdom-of-majorca.t: A Christian kingdom created after James I's conquest of Majorca, independent under its own dynasty from 1276 to 1344 and a realm of Aragon thereafter.
kingdom-of-majorca.o: James I of Aragon conquered Majorca from the Almohads in 1229, then Ibiza in 1235, and established a separate kingdom. On his death in 1276 he left Majorca, Roussillon, Cerdanya and Montpellier to his younger son James II, creating an independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-majorca.r: The kingdom was a Mediterranean trading state, with Palma and Perpignan as royal seats, merchant fleets reaching North Africa and a famed school of cartographers who made the Catalan Atlas. Ramon Llull, philosopher and missionary, was its most famous son. Its kings were forced to accept vassalage to the Crown of Aragon.
kingdom-of-majorca.e: Peter IV of Aragon seized the kingdom in 1343-1344, and James III was killed at Llucmajor in 1349 trying to retake it. Majorca remained a separate realm within the Crown until the Nueva Planta decree of 1715.

kingdom-of-han-206-bc.t: The remote kingdom Xiang Yu gave Liu Bang in 206 BCE, from which Liu fought his way out to defeat Xiang Yu and found the Han dynasty.
kingdom-of-han-206-bc.o: Liu Bang, a minor Qin official turned rebel, was first to enter the Qin heartland and accepted the surrender of Ziying. Xiang Yu, wary of him, made him King of Han in 206 BCE, ruling the isolated Hanzhong, Ba and Shu regions from Nanzheng. Liu Bang burned the plank roads behind him to show he had no ambitions.
kingdom-of-han-206-bc.r: With the chancellor Xiao He managing supplies and the general Han Xin commanding the army, the kingdom became a base for war. Xiao He kept the Qin records and grain stores, and Sichuan's resources fed the campaigns.
kingdom-of-han-206-bc.e: In 206 BCE Liu Bang conquered the Three Qins, then fought Western Chu for four years, losing at Pengcheng but recovering. After Xiang Yu's death at Gaixia in 202 BCE, Liu Bang took the title of emperor, and his kingdom gave its name to the Han Dynasty and to the Han Chinese.

kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.t: The first Armenian dynasty, the Orontids or Yervandunis, ruled Armenia as Persian satraps and then as kings for over three centuries before the Seleucids took over.
kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.o: After the fall of the Kingdom of Urartu, Armenian-speaking groups dominated the highlands. The Orontid family appears as governors of the satrapy of Armenia under the Achaemenid Empire, and the Behistun inscription of Darius I records fighting in Armenia in 521 BCE. The traditional start of the dynasty in the 6th century BCE is uncertain.
kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.r: The Orontids ruled as satraps closely tied to the Persian court, sending horses as tribute, while Xenophon described the villages and wheat beer of Armenia in 401 BCE. After Alexander the Great, they ruled as effectively independent kings from Armavir and then Yervandashat. Their culture blended Iranian religion and Aramaic administration with local traditions.
kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.e: Around 200 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus III defeated Orontes IV and divided the land between his generals Artaxias and Zariadres. After the Seleucid defeat at Magnesia in 190 BCE, Artaxias founded the Kingdom of Armenia (Artaxiad), which kept many Orontid traditions.

kingdom-of-gwent.t: Welsh kingdom between the Usk and the Wye, heir to the Roman town of Caerwent, which fell to the Normans after 1067.
kingdom-of-gwent.o: Gwent took its name from Venta Silurum, Caerwent, the Roman capital of the Silures. After Roman rule ended a kingdom formed in the land between the Usk and the Wye, with traditions of a founder named Caradog Freichfras. Its kings were often the same as those of the Kingdom of Glywysing, the two realms passing between branches of one dynasty.
kingdom-of-gwent.r: The Llandaff charters record grants by its kings to churches and show a landscape of royal estates and small monasteries. Brochfael ap Meurig submitted to Alfred of Wessex, according to Asser. The kingdom lay on the English border, and its rulers alternately fought and allied with the Mercians and later the English kings, while the fertile Usk valley and coastal levels provided its wealth.
kingdom-of-gwent.e: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn seized Gwent in the 1050s. After the Norman Conquest William FitzOsbern built Chepstow Castle from 1067 and pushed west. Its last king, Caradog ap Gruffudd, was killed at the battle of Mynydd Carn in 1081, and Gwent became Norman marcher lordships, later Monmouthshire.
