kingdom-of-orleans.t: Short-lived Merovingian kingdom of Clovis' son Chlodomer, which vanished when he fell in battle in 524.
kingdom-of-orleans.o: In the division of 511 Clovis' second son Chlodomer received lands along the Loire, with Orléans as his capital, together with Tours, Bourges and part of Aquitaine.
kingdom-of-orleans.r: Chlodomer ruled for only thirteen years. Little is known of his government beyond his wars against the Kingdom of the Burgundians, during which he had the captured King Sigismund and his family killed in 524.
kingdom-of-orleans.e: Chlodomer was killed later in 524 at the Battle of Vézeronce. His uncles Childebert I and Chlothar I murdered two of his young sons and divided his kingdom. The third son, Clodoald, escaped and became a monk; the town of Saint-Cloud near Paris is named after him.

krusevo-republic.t: Ten-day revolutionary government in the mountain town of Kruševo during the Ilinden Uprising of 1903, celebrated in North Macedonia as a founding moment.
krusevo-republic.o: On 2 August 1903, the feast of Saint Elijah, the Internal Macedonian-Adrianople Revolutionary Organisation launched the Ilinden Uprising against Ottoman rule in Macedonia. Rebels under Nikola Karev and Pitu Guli seized Kruševo, a prosperous mountain town of Slav, Aromanian and Greek-oriented Orthodox families, and proclaimed a provisional government.
krusevo-republic.r: Karev headed a council that included members of the different communities, and the town's administration, courts and supplies were reorganised for defence. The Kruševo Manifesto, attributed to the rebels, called on the local Muslim population to join the struggle against tyranny rather than against neighbours. The republic lasted about ten days.
krusevo-republic.e: An Ottoman army retook Kruševo around 12 August 1903; Pitu Guli died defending the Mečkin Kamen position and much of the town was burnt. Bulgaria and North Macedonia both claim the uprising, and the Ilinden memorial at Kruševo is a national symbol of North Macedonia.

kingdom-of-ngoyo.t: A small Kongo coastal kingdom around Cabinda whose port grew into one of the busiest Atlantic slave-trading harbours north of the Congo River.
kingdom-of-ngoyo.o: Ngoyo was one of three Kikongo-speaking kingdoms on the coast north of the Congo estuary, alongside the Kingdom of Loango and the Kingdom of Kakongo. Its people, the Woyo, recognised the seniority of Loango in early times but by the mid-16th century Ngoyo was ruled by its own king, the Mangoyo, from Mbanza Ngoyo.
kingdom-of-ngoyo.r: The king was a sacred figure who, by tradition, could not see the sea, and was elected by senior lineages. Royal officials managed trade at the port of Cabinda, where Dutch, English, French and Portuguese ships bought slaves, ivory and copper brought from the interior. The trade made local merchant families rich and weakened the crown.
kingdom-of-ngoyo.e: After the Atlantic slave trade ended, the kingdom declined. In 1885 local princes signed the Treaty of Simulambuco, placing the area under Portuguese protection, and it became the Cabinda exclave of Portuguese Angola.

kataghan-khanate.t: An Uzbek khanate of northern Afghanistan centred on Kunduz, a slave-raiding power under Murad Beg until absorbed by the Afghan Emirate.
kataghan-khanate.o: The Qataghan Uzbeks had settled in the region of Kunduz in the 17th and 18th centuries. In the early 19th century their leader Murad Beg built a powerful state from Kunduz, taking Balkh, Badakhshan and neighbouring Tajik districts around 1815 to 1820.
kataghan-khanate.r: Murad Beg ruled with an army of Uzbek horsemen and grew rich from raiding and slaving, deporting Tajiks of Badakhshan to the marshy Kunduz plain. The British traveller Alexander Burnes and William Moorcroft described his court in the 1820s and 1830s. Successors were weaker and paid tribute to Bukhara or Kabul.
kataghan-khanate.e: After Murad Beg's death in the 1840s the khanate declined. In 1859 Dost Mohammad Khan's son Muhammad Afzal Khan conquered Kunduz for the Emirate of Afghanistan, ending its independence.

kingdom-of-ormus.t: The island kingdom of Hormuz, which controlled the mouth of the Gulf and its horse and spice trade until Persia and England expelled the Portuguese.
kingdom-of-ormus.o: Arab and Persian traditions say the kingdom was founded in the 11th century on the mainland near modern Minab by a ruler from Oman. Around 1300, harried by Mongol-era raids, its king moved the capital to the barren island of Jarun, which took the name Hormuz.
kingdom-of-ormus.r: Hormuz lived by trade, taxing ships between India, Persia, Arabia and East Africa and shipping Arabian horses to India. Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta visited it. Kings controlled ports on both sides of the Gulf, including Qalhat, Muscat and Bahrain, and paid tribute to stronger mainland powers. Water and food had to be brought to the island.
kingdom-of-ormus.e: Afonso de Albuquerque attacked in 1507 and in 1515 made Hormuz a vassal of the Portuguese Empire, which built a fortress and controlled its customs. In 1622 an Anglo-Persian force under Shah Abbas I of the Safavid Empire captured the island, ending the kingdom; trade moved to Bandar Abbas.

kingdom-of-epirus.t: Kingdom of the Molossians in north-west Greece, whose Aeacid kings led the Epirote peoples and produced Pyrrhus, Rome's most famous Greek opponent.
kingdom-of-epirus.o: The Molossian kings claimed descent from Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, and were called Aeacids. Their kingdom in the mountains of Epirus emerges into history in the 5th century BCE; King Tharyps, educated at Athens, introduced Greek institutions and letters. The Molossians gradually led the other Epirote tribes, the Chaonians and Thesprotians, in an alliance.
kingdom-of-epirus.r: Kings ruled alongside an assembly and annual magistrates, swearing to govern by law. The economy rested on pastoralism, with Dodona's oracle of Zeus as the great religious centre. Alexander I, brother of Olympias and uncle of Alexander the Great, campaigned in southern Italy until his death in 331 BCE. Pyrrhus (297-272 BCE) made Ambracia his capital and won costly victories over Rome.
kingdom-of-epirus.e: After Pyrrhus died at Argos in 272 BCE, his successors struggled against Macedon and the Aetolians. The last of the royal line, Deidamia, was killed around 232 BCE and the monarchy was replaced by the Epirote League. Pyrrhus survives in the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'.

karystos.t: City of southern Euboea, forced into the Delian League by Athens and later famed for its green-veined Cipollino marble.
karystos.o: Karystos lay at the southern end of Euboea, below Mount Ochi. Greek tradition held that its people were Dryopes, later joined by Ionian settlers. It grew in the early Iron Age as a farming and seafaring community, controlling the channel between Euboea and Andros.
karystos.r: The Persians forced Karystos to submit in 490 BCE, and it fought on their side in 480 BCE. Athens then compelled it to join the Delian League c. 472 BCE. In the 4th century BCE it produced the physician Diocles, and later the writer Antigonus. Its green-veined marble, Cipollino, was quarried heavily in Roman times.
karystos.e: Karystos passed between Macedonian kings and Athens in the Hellenistic period and came under Roman control by 146 BCE. Its marble quarries remained important under the Empire, and the modern town keeps the ancient name.

kingdom-of-murcia.t: A Castilian frontier kingdom in south-eastern Spain, formed after the reconquest of Murcia and kept as a historical unit until 1833.
kingdom-of-murcia.o: After the Mudéjar revolt of 1264-1266, James I of Aragon conquered Murcia on behalf of his son-in-law Alfonso X of Castile, ending the Third Taifa of Murcia. Alfonso X resettled the territory with Castilians and Catalans and kept it as a separate kingdom within the Crown of Castile.
kingdom-of-murcia.r: Murcia was a frontier facing both the Emirate of Granada and the Crown of Aragon, which took its northern districts by the Treaty of Torrellas in 1304. The irrigated huertas produced silk, fruit and grain, the Mudéjar population declined, and Cartagena grew into the main naval base on the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-murcia.e: The kingdom was a historical title and administrative unit rather than a self-governing state. In 1833 Javier de Burgos's reform divided Spain into provinces, splitting the old kingdom into the provinces of Murcia and Albacete.

kingdom-of-tethba.t: A midland Irish kingdom spanning Longford and Westmeath, held by branches of the southern Ui Neill and later by the O'Farrells and O'Quinns.
kingdom-of-tethba.o: Tethba appears in the earliest Irish annals as a territory in the Irish midlands, divided by the River Inny into northern and southern parts. Its rulers in the early medieval period came from Cairpre and Maine, sons of Niall of the Nine Hostages, making it part of the southern Ui Neill world centred on Mide.
kingdom-of-tethba.r: Tethba was a small overkingship of several local peoples, often subordinate to the kings of Mide. Monasteries such as Ardagh and Clonmacnoise's daughter houses stood in or near its lands. In the 11th and 12th centuries local families, the Ui Cuinn and the Ui Fergail, rose to power in the northern part, later known as Annaly.
kingdom-of-tethba.e: After the Norman invasion much of southern Tethba was granted to Hugh de Lacy within the Lordship of Meath. Annaly survived under the O'Farrells until the 16th century, when it became County Longford.

klaipeda-region.t: The Memel Territory, detached from Germany after the First World War, seized by Lithuania in 1923 and annexed by Hitler in 1939.
klaipeda-region.o: The Treaty of Versailles separated the land north of the Neman, including the port of Memel (Klaipėda), from Germany, placing it under the Allies in 1920 with a French administration. In January 1923 Lithuanian irregulars staged the Klaipėda Revolt, and the Allies accepted Lithuanian sovereignty.
klaipeda-region.r: Under the Klaipėda Convention of 1924, the region was an autonomous part of the Republic of Lithuania, with its own parliament and directorate. Most inhabitants were German-speaking or bilingual Lietuvininkai, and conflicts between German parties and the Lithuanian governor were constant. The port was Lithuania's only outlet to the sea.
klaipeda-region.e: Nazi groups grew strong in the 1930s. In March 1939 Germany issued an ultimatum, and Lithuania ceded the region, which was annexed to the Reich on 23 March 1939. After the Second World War it became part of the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, and its German population fled or was expelled.

kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.t: A kingdom without a king, created by Germany and Austria-Hungary in occupied Poland during the First World War, which handed power to Pilsudski in 1918.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.o: After driving the Russians out of Congress Poland in 1915, the Central Powers proclaimed an independent Kingdom of Poland by the Act of 5 November 1916, hoping to recruit Polish soldiers. Its borders and future king were left undecided.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.r: A Provisional Council of State, including Jozef Pilsudski, was set up in 1917, but real power remained with the German governor-general in Warsaw. When Pilsudski's legionnaires refused an oath of loyalty to the Central Powers, he was interned at Magdeburg. A Regency Council of Archbishop Aleksander Kakowski, Prince Zdzislaw Lubomirski and Jozef Ostrowski then governed, building Polish courts, schools and offices.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.e: As Germany collapsed in November 1918, the Regency Council handed command of the army and then all authority to Pilsudski, freshly released, and dissolved itself. Its institutions passed to the Second Polish Republic.

kingdom-of-connacht.t: Western Irish province-kingdom whose O'Connor kings, Toirdelbach and Ruaidrí, became high kings before Anglo-Norman conquest reduced it.
kingdom-of-connacht.o: The Connachta, who gave the province its name, claimed descent from Conn of the Hundred Battles. By the 6th century their branches, the Uí Briúin and Uí Fiachrach, ruled the west, with kings inaugurated at Cruachan, the great ritual site of Rathcroghan in Roscommon. The Uí Briúin gradually took control of the over-kingship.
kingdom-of-connacht.r: Kings ruled through a network of subject kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Ui Maine. The Ua Conchobair, O'Connor, line rose in the 11th century; Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair, king from 1106 to 1156, built bridges and castles, divided Munster and claimed the high kingship. His son Ruaidrí became the last High King of Ireland and agreed the Treaty of Windsor with Henry II in 1175.
kingdom-of-connacht.e: Anglo-Norman lords led by the de Burghs received a grant of Connacht in 1227, and the O'Connors were confined to Roscommon. Splits between rival O'Connor branches in the 14th century weakened the kingship further, and the title faded out in the later 15th century.
kingdom-of-connacht.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-madanda.t: A small Shona kingdom in central Mozambique between the Buzi and Save rivers, on the edge of the Mutapa and Uteve world.
kingdom-of-madanda.o: Madanda emerged around 1500 as one of the Shona-speaking states between the Zimbabwe plateau and the coast, south of the Kingdom of Uteve. Its rulers were probably linked by origin to the Mutapa dynasty, but the kingdom appears only occasionally in Portuguese records.
kingdom-of-madanda.r: Little is known of its government. Like its neighbours, it was probably ruled by a sacred king advised by spirit mediums, and its people farmed, herded cattle and traded ivory and gold with Portuguese posts at Sofala and on the Zambezi.
kingdom-of-madanda.e: In the 19th century Madanda came under the domination of the Gaza Nguni state. In the 1890s its territory passed to the Mozambique Company and was absorbed into Portuguese Mozambique.

kalmar-union.t: Personal union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch, created by Queen Margaret I in 1397 and broken by Sweden's secession in 1523.
kalmar-union.o: Margaret I, daughter of Valdemar IV of Denmark and widow of Haakon VI of Norway, became ruler of Denmark and Norway and, after defeating King Albert of Mecklenburg in 1389, of Sweden too. In 1397 her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania was crowned king of all three realms at Kalmar.
kalmar-union.r: The union shared a monarch and foreign policy, but each kingdom kept its own laws, councils and nobility. Danish dominance and wars with the Hanseatic League and Holstein caused resentment in Sweden, where the Engelbrekt rebellion of 1434 began a century of conflict. Swedish regents of the Sture family often ruled in practice.
kalmar-union.e: Christian II reconquered Sweden in 1520 and executed some eighty nobles and clergy in the Stockholm Bloodbath, provoking a revolt led by Gustav Vasa, who was elected king of Sweden in 1523. The union ended, while Denmark and Norway continued together as Denmark-Norway.

kingdom-of-noricum.t: A Celtic kingdom in the eastern Alps, famed for its iron and steel, that became a Roman ally and then a Roman province without a major war.
kingdom-of-noricum.o: Noricum grew out of a union of Celtic tribes in the eastern Alps, led by the Norici, during the 2nd century BCE. Its core lay in modern Carinthia and Styria, around the Magdalensberg and a centre the Romans called Noreia. In 113 BCE Rome defended it against the migrating Cimbri, who defeated a Roman army at Noreia.
kingdom-of-noricum.r: The kingdom was ruled by kings over a federation of tribes and was known across the Mediterranean for ferrum Noricum, a high-quality steel produced from local ores. Italian merchants settled at the Magdalensberg trading post, and Noricum minted its own silver coins. Close ties with Rome made it a client kingdom; its king Voccio sent cavalry to Julius Caesar in 49 BCE.
kingdom-of-noricum.e: Around 16 BCE Noricum was absorbed peacefully into the Roman Empire, becoming the province of Noricum with towns such as Virunum and Celeia. Roman rule lasted until the late 5th century, when the Life of Saint Severinus records the last Roman communities before their evacuation in 488.

knidos.t: Dorian port city on a Carian peninsula, home of Praxiteles's Aphrodite, the astronomer Eudoxus and a renowned school of medicine.
knidos.o: Dorian Greeks settled Knidos at the tip of a long peninsula in south-west Anatolia in the early first millennium BCE. It belonged to the Dorian Hexapolis with Kos, Halicarnassus and the three Rhodian cities of Lindos, Ialysos and Kamiros, which met at the sanctuary of Apollo at Triopion in Knidian territory.
knidos.r: Knidos was an oligarchy run by a council of sixty, and grew rich on trade, wine and its double harbour. When the Persian general Harpagus advanced c. 545 BCE, the Knidians tried to cut through their isthmus but submitted. The city later produced the astronomer Eudoxus, the physician Ctesias and Sostratus, architect of the Pharos of Alexandria; its treasury and clubhouse stood at Delphi.
knidos.e: Off Knidos in 394 BCE Conon's Persian-backed fleet destroyed Spartan sea power. In the 4th century BCE the city moved to the cape, where Praxiteles's nude Aphrodite drew visitors. It joined the Roman province of Asia in 129 BCE as a free city.

kingdom-of-ailech.t: Kingdom of the northern Uí Néill based at the stone fort of Grianan of Aileach, whose Cenél nEógain kings often held the high kingship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-ailech.o: Ailech emerged in the early medieval period as the kingdom of the northern Uí Néill, descendants of Niall of the Nine Hostages who expanded into the north-west in the 5th and 6th centuries. It took its name from the hilltop stone fort of Grianan of Aileach on the Inishowen peninsula, which served as a royal centre.
kingdom-of-ailech.r: The kingdom was dominated by the Cenél nEógain, who displaced the Cenél Conaill from the kingship in the 8th century and alternated the high kingship with the southern Uí Néill. Kings such as Áed Findliath and Niall Glúndub, killed fighting the Vikings of Dublin in 919, were among the most powerful in Ireland. The Mac Lochlainn line, notably Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn, held the high kingship in the 12th century.
kingdom-of-ailech.e: In 1101 Muirchertach Ua Briain of Munster demolished Grianan of Aileach in revenge for an earlier attack on Kincora. Power within Cenél nEógain passed from the Mac Lochlainns to the Ua Néill, and the kingdom of Ailech became the O'Neill kingdom of Tír Eógain, Tyrone.

kololo-kingdom.t: A Sotho conquest state on the upper Zambezi, visited by Livingstone, whose language still shapes Lozi speech.
kololo-kingdom.o: Sebetwane led the Kololo, a Sotho group displaced in the 1820s, on a long migration across Botswana. Around 1840 they conquered the Lozi kingdom of Barotseland on the upper Zambezi floodplain, setting up their capital at Linyanti in the Chobe swamps.
kololo-kingdom.r: Sebetwane ruled with skill, incorporating Lozi and other subjects and spreading his Sotho language, which became the basis of modern Silozi. The Kololo lived from cattle, Lozi labour and tribute in grain, fish and ivory. David Livingstone reached Sebetwane in 1851 and later travelled to the Atlantic and Indian Ocean coasts with Kololo porters provided by Sekeletu.
kololo-kingdom.e: Sebetwane died in 1851; under his sickly son Sekeletu, malaria thinned the Kololo and loyalty collapsed. After Sekeletu's death in 1863 a Lozi rising led by Sipopa killed most Kololo men in 1864, restoring the Lozi monarchy.

kingdom-of-cambrai.t: Small Frankish kingdom around Cambrai, ruled by Clovis' kinsman Ragnachar until Clovis eliminated him.
kingdom-of-cambrai.o: Cambrai was taken by the Salian king Chlodio in the mid 5th century, and by the 480s it was the seat of a separate Frankish king, Ragnachar, a relative of Clovis. Known almost only from Gregory of Tours.
kingdom-of-cambrai.r: Ragnachar joined Clovis against Syagrius and the Domain of Soissons in 486. Gregory portrays him as a debauched ruler who lost the loyalty of his warriors.
kingdom-of-cambrai.e: Around 509 Clovis bribed Ragnachar's followers with armlets of gilded bronze passed off as gold, defeated him and killed him and his brother Richar with his own axe. Cambrai was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Franks.

kingdom-of-prussia.t: Hohenzollern kingdom that rose from scattered lands to a great power, defeated Austria and France and united Germany under its rule.
kingdom-of-prussia.o: Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg crowned himself King in Prussia at Königsberg on 18 January 1701, with Emperor Leopold I's consent. The title rested on the Duchy of Prussia, outside the Empire, but it was applied to all Hohenzollern lands, including Brandenburg, Pomerania and territories in the Rhineland and Westphalia.
kingdom-of-prussia.r: Frederick William I built a large army and efficient bureaucracy. Frederick II seized Silesia in 1740 and survived the Seven Years' War, then gained West Prussia in the First Partition of Poland. After defeat at Jena in 1806, the Stein and Hardenberg reforms modernised the state. Prussia gained the Rhineland in 1815, led the Zollverein, and under Bismarck defeated Denmark, Austria and France.
kingdom-of-prussia.e: In 1871 King William I became German Emperor, and Prussia formed the dominant state of the German Empire. William II abdicated in November 1918, and Prussia became the Free State of Prussia, abolished by the Allies in 1947.

kushano-sasanian-kingdom.t: Sasanian princes who ruled the former Kushan lands of Bactria and Gandhara as 'Kushanshahs', blending Persian, Kushan and Buddhist traditions.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.o: After Ardashir I founded the Sasanian Empire, he and his son Shapur I conquered Bactria and much of the Kushan Empire in the mid-3rd century. Government of the region was entrusted to Sasanian princes who took the title Kushanshah, King of the Kushans, ruling from Balkh.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.r: The Kushanshahs issued gold and copper coins in the Kushan style, often showing the god Oesho (Shiva) with the bull Nandi, alongside Sasanian crowns and Middle Persian or Bactrian legends. They held trade routes through the Hindu Kush, and Buddhist monasteries in Bactria continued to flourish under them. At times they acted nearly independently of the main Sasanian court.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.e: In the mid-4th century the Chionites and the Kidarite Kingdom overran Bactria, ending Kushano-Sasanian rule. Their coinage strongly influenced the coin types of these later Hunnic rulers.

kingdom-of-loango.t: The Vili kingdom of the Loango coast, a major Atlantic trading power known for its raffia cloth, copper and ivory and later for slaves.
kingdom-of-loango.o: Loango emerged among the Vili north of the Congo River, probably by the 15th century, and by the mid-16th century had shaken off any dependence on the Kingdom of Kongo. Its king, the Maloango, ruled from Mbanza Loango (Buali) near Loango Bay, the kingdom's main harbour.
kingdom-of-loango.r: The Maloango was a sacred ruler chosen from princes of the royal matrilineage, assisted by ministers responsible for trade, war and the coast. Loango exported fine raffia cloth, used as currency in the region, together with copper from the Mindouli mines, ivory and dyewood. From the 17th century Dutch, English and French ships bought slaves at Loango Bay in large numbers.
kingdom-of-loango.e: The end of the slave trade and long interregnums left the crown weak in the 19th century. In 1883 the coast came under French protection, and the area became part of the French Congo. The Maloango title survives as a traditional office.

kingdom-of-waterford.t: A Norse town-kingdom at the mouth of the Suir, the oldest city in Ireland, until its storming by the Anglo-Normans in 1170.
kingdom-of-waterford.o: Vikings raided the south-east in the 9th century, and in 914 a large fleet under Ragnall established a base at Waterford, Vedrafjordr. The settlement grew into a fortified trading town ruled by Norse kings or jarls, sometimes linked to the Kingdom of Dublin.
kingdom-of-waterford.r: Waterford traded wine, slaves and goods across the Irish Sea and to France. Its rulers became Christian and accepted bishops consecrated at Canterbury from 1096. Irish overkings of Munster, especially the O'Briens, often controlled the town, and Reginald's Tower recalls its Norse defences.
kingdom-of-waterford.e: In 1170 Strongbow and Raymond le Gros stormed the town, and Strongbow married Aoife, daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, there. Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171 and made it a royal city in the Lordship of Ireland.

kingdom-of-iarmumu.t: The early medieval kingdom of West Munster around Killarney's lakes, ruled by the Eoganacht Locha Lein, rivals of the Munster kings at Cashel.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.o: Iarmumu took shape in south-west Ireland by the 6th century, when the Eoganacht Locha Lein, a branch of the dynasties ruling Munster, established themselves around Loch Lein, the Lower Lake at Killarney. Their territory covered much of later Kerry and west Cork, absorbing earlier peoples such as the Corcu Duibne.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.r: The kings of Iarmumu sometimes claimed the kingship of all Munster, but were usually excluded from the rotation of Cashel's Eoganacht branches. Inisfallen on Loch Lein became an important monastery, later home of the Annals of Inisfallen. Cattle wealth and client peoples supported the dynasty.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.e: By the 8th and 9th centuries the dynasty weakened, and other lineages gained ground in Kerry, notably the Ui Donnchada. In the 12th century the area fell within the Kingdom of Desmond under the MacCarthys, with the O'Donoghues as local lords around Killarney.

kingdom-of-khotan.t: The jade-rich Buddhist kingdom of the southern Silk Road, whose Saka-speaking kings lasted more than a thousand years until the Kara-Khanid conquest.
kingdom-of-khotan.o: Khotan, Yutian in Chinese, grew in the oasis watered by rivers from the Kunlun Mountains on the southern edge of the Taklamakan. Its own legends trace the founding to Indian and Chinese settlers, including a son of the emperor Ashoka. It appears in Han records from the 2nd century BCE, already trading the white and green jade of its rivers.
kingdom-of-khotan.r: Khotan's people spoke Khotanese, an Eastern Iranian Saka language preserved in many Buddhist texts. Its kings, of the Visa dynasty, made it a major centre of Mahayana Buddhism, and tradition says a Chinese princess smuggled silkworm eggs to it in her headdress. Under the Tang Dynasty it was one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi; in the 10th century King Li Shengtian kept close ties with Dunhuang.
kingdom-of-khotan.e: After a long war, the Muslim Kara-Khanid Khanate conquered Khotan around 1006. Its Buddhist culture was replaced by Islam and the Turkic language, but manuscripts from Khotan and Dunhuang preserve Khotanese literature.

kingdom-of-rhufoniog.t: Small early Welsh kingdom between the Conwy and Clwyd valleys, named in legend after a son of Cunedda, later a cantref of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.o: Welsh tradition, preserved in genealogies written down centuries later, says the district took its name from Rhufon, one of the sons of Cunedda who came from the north to settle north Wales in the 5th century. The story is a later origin legend, but Rhufoniog existed as a distinct territory in the uplands of what is now Denbighshire.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.r: Very little is known of its rulers or government. It was one of several small early kingdoms of north Wales whose local dynasties appear in medieval genealogies, and its territory included the hills around Denbigh. Farming and cattle-rearing were the mainstay of a thinly settled land.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.e: By the 9th century Rhufoniog had been absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd and later formed one of the cantrefi of the Perfeddwlad, the borderland between Gwynedd and England contested by Welsh princes and English kings until 1283.

kingdom-of-great-britain.t: The kingdom created by the union of England and Scotland in 1707, which became Europe's leading maritime and commercial power in the 18th century.
kingdom-of-great-britain.o: The Acts of Union of 1707, passed by the Kingdom of England and the Kingdom of Scotland, merged them into one kingdom with a single Parliament at Westminster, while Scotland kept its own law, church and education. The two countries had shared a monarch since 1603.
kingdom-of-great-britain.r: Great Britain developed cabinet government under Robert Walpole and the Hanoverian kings from 1714. It defeated Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1745. Trade, the Bank of England and naval power built an empire in North America, the Caribbean and India, and the Seven Years' War brought Canada. The American colonies were lost in 1783, while the Industrial Revolution began.
kingdom-of-great-britain.e: The Acts of Union of 1800 joined Great Britain with the Kingdom of Ireland to form the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland on 1 January 1801.
kingdom-of-great-britain.re: Christianity; Church of England, Church of Scotland

kingdom-of-meirionnydd.t: Early Welsh kingdom between the Mawddach and the Dyfi, named after a grandson of Cunedda, which gave its name to the later county of Merioneth.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.o: According to Welsh genealogical tradition, Meirionnydd took its name from Meirion, a grandson of Cunedda, who was granted the land between the rivers Mawddach and Dyfi in the 5th century. Like other Cunedda stories, this is a later legend, but a separate royal line for Meirionnydd is recorded in medieval genealogies.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.r: Little is recorded of its government. The kingdom covered a mountainous coastal region including Cadair Idris, with farming on the valley floors and the coast, and its people were linked by sea with the rest of Cardigan Bay. Its kings appear to have been subordinate to the more powerful rulers of the Kingdom of Gwynedd for much of their history.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.e: Meirionnydd was absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd, probably by the 10th century, becoming one of its cantrefi. After the English conquest of 1283 it formed the core of the county of Merioneth, and the name survives in the region of Meirionnydd today.

kingdom-of-buellt.t: Small Welsh kingdom around Builth Wells, ruled by a dynasty claiming descent from Vortigern, and later the place where Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed.
kingdom-of-buellt.o: Buellt lay in the middle Wye and Irfon valleys around modern Builth Wells. The Historia Brittonum of about 829 says Ambrosius granted Buellt and Gwrtheyrnion to Pascent, son of Vortigern, and names Fernmail as the ruler of both in the author's own day. Among its wonders it lists Carn Cabal, a cairn said to bear the footprint of Arthur's hound.
kingdom-of-buellt.r: Little is recorded of its government. It was a small upland kingdom of river valleys and hill grazing, generally ruled together with the Kingdom of Gwrtheyrnion and lying between the larger realms of the Kingdom of Powys, the Kingdom of Brycheiniog and the south-western kingdoms.
kingdom-of-buellt.e: Buellt was absorbed by larger Welsh kingdoms in the 10th century and later became a cantref contested between Welsh princes and Norman lords, with a castle at Builth. In 1282 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, last native Prince of Wales, was killed near Cilmeri in Buellt.

kingdom-of-mukish.t: Mukish, the kingdom of Alalakh in the Amuq plain, best known for King Idrimi, whose statue tells the story of an exiled prince who won back a throne.
kingdom-of-mukish.o: Alalakh, at Tell Atchana near Antakya, was a town of the fertile Amuq plain by the early 2nd millennium BCE. In the 18th century BCE Abba-El of Yamhad granted it to his brother Yarim-Lim, making it a dependent kingdom of Aleppo. Leonard Woolley's excavations from 1937 recovered palaces and archives from this period.
kingdom-of-mukish.r: Alalakh's palace archives record a society of nobles who owned chariots, free farmers and dependent labourers, written in Akkadian with many Hurrian names. After a Hittite destruction c. 1600 BCE, Idrimi, a refugee prince from Aleppo, took the city and ruled Mukish as a vassal of the Mitanni Empire, as his inscribed statue relates.
kingdom-of-mukish.e: Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire conquered Mukish in the 14th century BCE and gave some of its land to Ugarit. Alalakh was abandoned around 1200 BCE, during the collapse of the Late Bronze Age, and its region later formed part of Patina.

kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.t: Nemanjić Serbia as a kingdom, which gained its own church, grew rich on silver mines and expanded south to become the Balkans' leading power.
kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.o: Stefan, son of Stefan Nemanja and ruler of the Grand Principality of Serbia, was crowned king in 1217 with a crown sent by Pope Honorius III, earning the name Stefan the First-Crowned. In 1219 his brother Sava obtained an autocephalous Serbian archbishopric from the Patriarch at Nicaea.
kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.r: The king ruled through royal courts that moved between residences, with nobles holding land in return for service. Uroš I invited Saxon miners, opening silver mines at Brskovo and Novo Brdo that made Serbia rich and supplied Ragusa's trade. Royal foundations such as Mileševa, Sopoćani and Gračanica have celebrated frescoes. Milutin (1282–1321) took northern Macedonia from Byzantium, and Stefan Dečanski crushed Bulgaria at Velbazhd in 1330.
kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.e: Stefan Dušan, who took the throne in 1331, conquered much of Byzantine Macedonia, Albania and Epirus and in 1346 was crowned emperor at Skopje, turning the kingdom into the Serbian Empire.

kingdom-of-bithynia.t: Bithynia, a Hellenistic kingdom of north-western Anatolia that invited the Galatians in, sheltered Hannibal and was bequeathed to Rome.
kingdom-of-bithynia.o: The Bithynians, a people of Thracian origin, lived south of the Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara. Their dynast Zipoetes I resisted Lysimachus and the Seleucid Empire, and in 297 BCE he took the title king, founding a dynasty that lasted over two centuries.
kingdom-of-bithynia.r: Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia as his capital in 264 BCE and invited Celtic warriors into Asia, who settled in Galatia. Prusias I expanded the kingdom, founded Prusa and sheltered Hannibal, who took poison at Libyssa in 183 BCE rather than be handed to Rome. The kings promoted Greek city life.
kingdom-of-bithynia.e: Nicomedes IV, restored to his throne by Rome, left Bithynia to the Roman Republic in his will in 74 BCE. The bequest provoked the Third Mithridatic War with the Kingdom of Pontus, and Bithynia became a Roman province.

kingdom-of-jibei.t: A fragment of the old state of Qi given to Tian An in 206 BCE, destroyed within months when Tian Rong reunited Qi by force.
kingdom-of-jibei.o: Tian An, a grandson of King Jian, the last king of the State of Qi, captured several towns north of the Ji River during the war against the Qin dynasty and followed Xiang Yu to Julu. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Jibei, with his capital at Boyang in central Shandong.
kingdom-of-jibei.r: Jibei was one of three kingdoms into which Xiang Yu split Qi, alongside the Kingdom of Jiaodong and Qi (206 BC), to weaken the powerful Tian clan. It lasted too short a time for any government to take shape.
kingdom-of-jibei.e: Tian Rong, the Qi strongman excluded from Xiang Yu's settlement, attacked the three kingdoms in 206 BCE, killed Tian An and reunited Qi under himself, provoking Xiang Yu's invasion of Qi.

kingdom-of-yong.t: The kingdom of Zhang Han, the Qin general turned king, who guarded the western Wei valley against Liu Bang until his capital was flooded in 205 BCE.
kingdom-of-yong.o: Zhang Han was the Qin general who crushed Chen Sheng's rising, then surrendered to Xiang Yu after the defeat of Qin forces at Julu. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Yong, ruling the western Guanzhong region from Feiqiu, west of Xianyang, as the main barrier against Liu Bang in Hanzhong.
kingdom-of-yong.r: Yong was one of the Three Qins, with the Kingdom of Sai and the Kingdom of Di (206 BC). Like them, it lacked local loyalty because Xiang Yu had slaughtered the Qin soldiers Zhang Han had led.
kingdom-of-yong.e: Later in 206 BCE Liu Bang's general Han Xin crossed the mountains by the Chencang route and defeated Zhang Han. Besieged in Feiqiu, Zhang held out until 205 BCE, when the Han army flooded the city and he killed himself.

khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.t: The short-lived Soviet-backed republic that replaced the Khanate of Khiva in 1920 before being divided among the new national republics.
khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.o: In early 1920 the Red Army, with the Turkmen leader Junaid Khan's enemies and the reformist Young Khivans, overthrew the Khanate of Khiva. In April 1920 the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic was proclaimed, with Khiva as capital.
khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.r: Officially independent and allied with Soviet Russia, it was governed by Young Khivans and later communists, under strong influence from Moscow. It nationalised the khan's estates, opened schools and fought Junaid Khan's Turkmen forces. Purges in 1921 and 1922 removed many of the original leaders, and it became the Khorezm Soviet Socialist Republic in 1923.
khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.e: In the national delimitation of 1924 the republic was divided among the Uzbek SSR, the Turkmen SSR and the new Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast, later Karakalpakstan.

kingdom-of-the-gepids.t: East Germanic kingdom in the Tisza plain and Transylvania that rose after Attila's empire collapsed and was destroyed by Lombards and Avars in 567.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.o: The Gepids, a Gothic-related people, were subjects of Attila's Huns. In 454 their king Ardaric led the revolt that crushed Attila's sons at the River Nedao, and the Gepids took over the lands east of the Danube in the Tisza plain and Transylvania.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.r: Gepid kings ruled a mixed population of Germanic, Sarmatian and local peoples, and adopted Arian Christianity. Rich princely graves such as those at Apahida show their wealth. They seized Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) on the Sava, a key city, and competed with the Ostrogoths, Byzantium and the Lombards for the middle Danube. Kings Thurisind and Cunimund fought the Lombards in the 550s and 560s.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.e: In 567 the Lombards under Alboin, allied with the newly arrived Avars, destroyed the kingdom; Cunimund was killed and Alboin made his skull into a drinking cup. The Gepid lands passed to the Avar Khaganate.

kingdom-of-mapungubwe.t: Southern Africa's first class-divided kingdom, ruled from a hilltop above the Limpopo and famed for its golden rhinoceros.
kingdom-of-mapungubwe.o: The kingdom grew out of the earlier settlement at K2 (Bambandyanalo) near the confluence of the Shashe and Limpopo rivers. Around 1075 the ruling group moved onto Mapungubwe Hill, separating itself physically from commoners below. Wealth came from cattle, farming on the floodplain and a growing trade in ivory and gold with Swahili merchants on the Indian Ocean coast.
kingdom-of-mapungubwe.r: Archaeology is the only source. The elite lived and were buried on the hilltop with gold-foil objects, including the famous golden rhinoceros, while ordinary people lived in the valley. Glass beads from India and the Middle East, Chinese celadon and locally worked gold show a link through coastal ports such as Sofala to the wider Indian Ocean economy. Sacred leadership and rainmaking probably underpinned royal authority.
kingdom-of-mapungubwe.e: Mapungubwe was abandoned in the early 13th century, possibly as a cooler, drier climate undermined floodplain farming. Power and trade shifted north to the Kingdom of Zimbabwe, which inherited many of its institutions. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage landscape in South Africa.

kingdom-of-powys.t: Kingdom of mid and north-east Wales and the Marches that long faced Mercia across Offa's Dyke, until it split into two lordships after 1160.
kingdom-of-powys.o: Powys arose in the territory of the Cornovii after Roman rule ended around 410, its name perhaps from the Latin pagenses, country people. Its early kings claimed descent from Cadell Ddyrnllug and, according to the Pillar of Eliseg, from Vortigern and Magnus Maximus. Its first centre may have been at Wroxeter or Pengwern before the English advance pushed it westward.
kingdom-of-powys.r: Powys bordered the Mercians and suffered heavily from their expansion; Selyf ap Cynan fell at the battle of Chester around 615, and Offa built his dyke along the frontier in the 8th century. Cyngen ap Cadell raised the Pillar of Eliseg near Llangollen to honour an ancestor who won back land from the English. Later kings ruled from Mathrafal, and its society rested on cattle and kin-based law.
kingdom-of-powys.e: Cyngen died on pilgrimage to Rome in 854, and Powys passed to Rhodri the Great of the Kingdom of Gwynedd. A native dynasty returned under Bleddyn ap Cynfyn in the 1060s, but after Madog ap Maredudd died in 1160 the kingdom split into Powys Fadog and Powys Wenwynwyn.

kingdom-of-commagene.t: Commagene, a small kingdom on the upper Euphrates whose king Antiochus I built the colossal god-statues on the summit of Nemrut Dağı.
kingdom-of-commagene.o: Commagene, the former Kummuh, lay between the Taurus mountains and the Euphrates. Its governor Ptolemaeus broke away from the Seleucid Empire c. 163 BCE. His successor Mithridates I Callinicus married a Seleucid princess, uniting Persian and Macedonian royal lines.
kingdom-of-commagene.r: Antiochus I Theos ruled from Samosata and devised a royal cult in which Greek and Persian gods were merged. On Nemrut Dağı he built a burial mound flanked by giant statues of himself with Zeus-Oromasdes, Apollo-Mithras and Heracles-Artagnes. Commagene grew rich from its fertile valleys and river crossings.
kingdom-of-commagene.e: Rome annexed Commagene in 17 CE, restored it to Antiochus IV in 38 CE, and finally absorbed it into the province of Syria in 72 CE under Vespasian.

karelo-finnish-soviet-socialist-republic.t: Soviet union republic created after the Winter War from Karelia and lands taken from Finland, downgraded to an autonomous republic in 1956.
karelo-finnish-soviet-socialist-republic.o: After the Winter War, the Soviet Union in March 1940 combined the Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic with most of the territory ceded by Finland, creating a full union republic with Petrozavodsk as capital. Otto Wille Kuusinen, former head of the Finnish Democratic Republic, became its head of state.
karelo-finnish-soviet-socialist-republic.r: Its status as a union republic was partly intended as a framework for absorbing Finland. Finnish was promoted alongside Russian, though Finns and Karelians were a minority among Russians. The republic depended on forestry, mining and fishing. Finnish forces occupied much of it, including Petrozavodsk, during the Continuation War of 1941-1944.
karelo-finnish-soviet-socialist-republic.e: After the war Finland was clearly not to be annexed, and the republic's role faded. In 1956 it was downgraded to the Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic within the Russian SFSR. Today it is the Republic of Karelia in Russia.

kingdom-of-the-swedes.t: Early kingdom of the Svear around Lake Mälaren and Uppsala, whose kings ruled the trading town of Birka and later united the Swedish lands.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.o: Tacitus wrote of the Suiones in the 1st century, and by the 6th century the Svear had a power centre at Old Uppsala, where great royal mounds were raised. Rich boat graves at Vendel and Valsgärde show a wealthy warrior elite. Later sagas trace the kings to the legendary Yngling dynasty.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.r: Kingship was tied to the pagan cult at Uppsala, described by Adam of Bremen, and to assemblies of free men at the thing. Birka, founded in the 8th century on Lake Mälaren, linked the kingdom to trade routes east to Rus' and the Byzantine and Abbasid worlds. Rimbert's life of Ansgar records kings Björn and Anund receiving the Frankish missionary around 830 and 850.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.e: Eric the Victorious, who defeated a rival at Fýrisvellir in the 980s, and his son Olof Skötkonung extended Svear rule over the Geats. This union of the Svear and Götar is regarded as the start of the medieval Kingdom of Sweden, and the Uppsala kingship gave Sweden its name.

kingdom-of-hana.t: Hana, a kingdom of the middle Euphrates centred on Terqa, which filled the gap left by Mari's fall and preserved its old traditions.
kingdom-of-hana.o: After the Babylonian Empire destroyed Mari c. 1760 BCE, local rulers at Terqa, a few kilometres upstream and long the seat of the god Dagan, created the kingdom of Hana. It controlled the Euphrates valley between the Khabur river and the Babylonian frontier.
kingdom-of-hana.r: Its kings, such as Isharlim and Kashtiliashu, issued land contracts in a distinctive Hana style and kept the Mari-era cult of Dagan. Excavations at Tell Ashara found a scribe's house with a jar of cloves, which must have travelled from south-east Asia. Some rulers bore names suggesting links with the Kassites.
kingdom-of-hana.e: Hana fell under the Mitanni Empire in the 15th century BCE and later the Assyrian Empire, surviving as a province and a regional name. Its successor on the middle Euphrates was the Land of Suhu.

kingdom-of-lithuania.t: The only crowned kingdom in Lithuanian history, created when Mindaugas accepted Catholic baptism and a royal crown from the Pope.
kingdom-of-lithuania.o: Mindaugas had united the Lithuanian lands by the 1240s but faced a coalition of rivals backed by the Livonian Order. To split his enemies he accepted baptism in 1251, and Pope Innocent IV authorised his coronation, which took place in July 1253, probably in Vilnius.
kingdom-of-lithuania.r: As king, Mindaugas ruled a mainly pagan land with a small Catholic church and a bishop appointed for Lithuania. He granted lands, including parts of Samogitia, to the Livonian Order in return for its support. The kingdom brought Lithuania into the diplomatic world of Latin Europe while Mindaugas extended his power over Black Ruthenia.
kingdom-of-lithuania.e: After the Samogitians crushed the Livonian Order at Durbe in 1260, Mindaugas broke with the order and seems to have abandoned Christianity. He was murdered in 1263 by his nephew Treniota and Daumantas, and the royal title lapsed. The state continued as the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; his coronation is marked by a Lithuanian national holiday.

kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.t: A tiny Jutish kingdom on the Isle of Wight, the last part of England to accept Christianity, ended by the violent conquest of Caedwalla in 686.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.o: Bede reports that the Isle of Wight, like Kent and part of Hampshire, was settled by Jutes. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle claims that Cerdic and Cynric took the island in 530 and gave it to their kinsmen Stuf and Wihtgar, but the story is largely legendary.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.r: The Wihtwara lived from farming and the sea under their own kings, sometimes dependents of greater neighbours. In 661 Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia gave the island to the South Saxon king Aethelwealh. The island was still pagan in the 680s.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.e: In 686 Caedwalla of the Kingdom of Wessex conquered the island, killed King Arwald and had his two young brothers executed after baptism, as Bede recounts. The island became part of Wessex and was converted by Wilfrid's clergy.

kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.t: A kingdom proclaimed among the Mapuche by a French adventurer in 1860, which never won recognition but survives as a claim of French pretenders.
kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.o: Orélie-Antoine de Tounens, a lawyer from the Dordogne in France, travelled to Chile in 1858 and went to Araucanía, the independent Mapuche lands south of the Biobío. In November 1860 he proclaimed himself King Orélie-Antoine I of Araucanía and, days later, added Patagonia, claiming support from Mapuche chiefs.
kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.r: The kingdom existed largely on paper. Orélie-Antoine issued a constitution, a flag and decrees, and some Mapuche leaders, such as Quilapán, seem to have seen him as a potential ally against Chilean expansion. He had no army, administration or international recognition, and Chile regarded the scheme as a threat to its sovereignty.
kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.e: Chilean authorities arrested him in January 1862, declared him insane and deported him to France. He returned several times without success and died in France in 1878. Chile carried out the Occupation of Araucanía by 1883. French claimants still use his title.

kingdom-of-ndongo.t: The Mbundu kingdom of the Ngola, whose title gave Angola its name and whose queen Njinga fought the Portuguese for decades.
kingdom-of-ndongo.o: Ndongo was formed by Mbundu chiefdoms between the Kwanza and Lukala rivers in the late 15th century under a ruler titled the Ngola. Initially a tributary of the Kingdom of Kongo, it asserted independence in the 1550s, and a Portuguese embassy reached its capital Kabasa in 1560.
kingdom-of-ndongo.r: The Ngola ruled through regional lords (sobas) who paid tribute in cattle, salt, cloth and slaves. From 1575, when Paulo Dias de Novais founded Luanda, Ndongo faced constant war with Portuguese Angola and its Imbangala allies, who sought slaves for the Atlantic trade. Njinga Mbande, who became ruler in 1624, negotiated, converted, fought and allied with the Dutch, later ruling from the Kingdom of Matamba.
kingdom-of-ndongo.e: Ndongo was split between Njinga's party and a Portuguese-backed puppet king, Ngola Hari. When his successor rebelled, the Portuguese stormed the fortress of Pungo Andongo in 1671, ending the kingdom. The Ngola title gave Angola its name, and Njinga is a national heroine.

kingdom-of-greece.t: The Greek monarchy from 1832 to 1973, which more than doubled Greece's territory and lived through the National Schism, occupation, civil war and dictatorship.
kingdom-of-greece.o: Under the London Conference of 1832, Britain, France and Russia made Otto of Bavaria king of independent Greece, replacing the First Hellenic Republic. He arrived at Nauplia in 1833 with Bavarian regents, and Athens became the capital in 1834. A revolt in September 1843 forced him to grant a constitution.
kingdom-of-greece.r: Otto was deposed in 1862 and replaced by George I, whose long reign added the Ionian Islands (1864), Thessaly (1881) and, through the Balkan Wars, Macedonia, Epirus and Crete. Politics were shaped by the Great Idea of uniting Greeks and by the clash between Eleftherios Venizelos and King Constantine I. Defeat in Asia Minor in 1922 brought a population exchange with Turkey.
kingdom-of-greece.e: The monarchy was replaced by the Second Hellenic Republic in 1924 and restored in 1935, followed by the Metaxas dictatorship, Axis occupation and civil war. After the 1967 coup, Constantine II went into exile; the junta abolished the monarchy in 1973, confirmed by referendum in 1974.

kingdom-of-yugoslavia.t: First united state of the South Slavs, a monarchy torn by rivalry between Serbs and Croats and destroyed by the Axis invasion of 1941.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.o: As Austria-Hungary collapsed, the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs joined the Kingdom of Serbia and Montenegro to form the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, proclaimed in Belgrade on 1 December 1918 under the Karađorđević dynasty. Its borders, confirmed by the post-war treaties, joined lands with very different histories, faiths and economies.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.r: The centralist Vidovdan Constitution of 1921 favoured Serbian dominance and was opposed by Stjepan Radić's Croatian Peasant Party. After Radić was shot in parliament in 1928, King Alexander imposed a dictatorship in 1929 and renamed the country Yugoslavia. He was assassinated in Marseille in 1934, and Prince Paul's regency created the Banovina of Croatia in 1939.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.e: In March 1941 the government signed the Tripartite Pact, but officers overthrew it two days later. Germany and its allies invaded on 6 April 1941 and the army capitulated within eleven days. King Peter II went into exile, and the country was partitioned among the Independent State of Croatia and occupying powers.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.re: Serbian Orthodox and Catholic Christianity, Sunni Islam

keos.t: Cycladic island state of four small cities nearest to Attica, home of the poets Simonides and Bacchylides.
keos.o: Keos lies off the tip of Attica and had a major Bronze Age town at Ayia Irini. In the early Iron Age Ionian Greeks settled it, and the island was organised as a tetrapolis of four cities, Ioulis, Karthaia, Koressia and Poiessa, which sometimes acted together as one state.
keos.r: Keos was famous for its poets: Simonides and his nephew Bacchylides, both from Ioulis, wrote for patrons across Greece in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. Strabo records a Keian law said to require citizens over sixty to drink hemlock. The island exported ruddle, a red earth pigment, and paid tribute in the Delian League.
keos.e: Keos joined the Second Athenian League but revolted in the 360s BCE and was subdued. In the 3rd century BCE Koressia became a Ptolemaic naval base renamed Arsinoe. The island passed under Roman control by 146 BCE.

kingdom-of-abkhazia.t: A western Georgian kingdom whose rulers, though Abkhaz in origin, built a Georgian church and culture and through Bagrat III united Georgia in 1008.
kingdom-of-abkhazia.o: Around 778 Leon II, ruler of the Principality of Abasgia, broke from the Byzantine Empire with Khazar help, took the title king and joined Abasgia to Egrisi, the old lands of Lazica. He moved his capital to Kutaisi, shifting the state's centre into the Georgian-speaking interior.
kingdom-of-abkhazia.r: Over the 9th century the kings replaced Greek with Georgian in church and government and separated the western Georgian church from Constantinople. Under George II and Constantine III the kingdom expanded into Kartli and fought the Armenian Bagratids. Churches such as Mokvi and Bedia show its wealth, and the kingdom controlled the Black Sea coast and Rioni valley.
kingdom-of-abkhazia.e: In 978 the throne passed to Bagrat III, son of the Bagratid Gurgen and an Abkhazian princess. In 1008 he inherited Kartli as well, founding the united Kingdom of Georgia.

kadi-burhan-al-din-state.t: The sultanate of a judge and poet who seized the Eretnid throne and held central Anatolia against the Ottomans, Mamluks and Turkmen.
kadi-burhan-al-din-state.o: Kadi Burhan al-Din Ahmad was a jurist from Kayseri who served the Eretnids as judge and vizier. As the dynasty weakened he became the real power, and in 1381, after the death of Ala al-Din Ali, he declared himself sultan in Sivas.
kadi-burhan-al-din-state.r: He spent his reign fighting: against the Ottomans, whom he defeated at Kirkdilim in 1392, against the Mamluks, the Aq Qoyunlu, Mutahharten of Erzincan and the beys of Amasya. He was also a poet whose divan of Turkish verse is one of the earliest in Anatolia, and his court historian Astarabadi wrote the Bazm u Razm, a chronicle of his reign in Persian.
kadi-burhan-al-din-state.e: In 1398 he was killed by the Aq Qoyunlu chief Qara Yuluk Osman. Sivas surrendered to Bayezid I, but Timur destroyed it in 1400.

kingdom-of-lydia.t: Lydia, the western Anatolian kingdom of Sardis, where the first coins were struck and Croesus became a byword for wealth.
kingdom-of-lydia.o: Greek tradition traced a Heraclid dynasty in Lydia, then called Maeonia, back to c. 1200 BCE, but the kingdom becomes historical with Gyges, who seized the throne c. 680 BCE and founded the Mermnad dynasty. He fought the Cimmerians and sent gifts to Delphi.
kingdom-of-lydia.r: From Sardis the Mermnad kings ruled the Hermus valley and subdued most Greek cities of Ionia. Electrum from the river Pactolus underpinned the first coinage in the late 7th century BCE, and Croesus introduced separate gold and silver coins. The huge burial mound of Alyattes stands at Bin Tepe.
kingdom-of-lydia.e: After a war with the Median Empire ended by the eclipse of 585 BCE, Croesus attacked Persia and was defeated by Cyrus, who took Sardis c. 546 BCE. Lydia became a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire, and Sardis its western capital.

kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.t: The short-lived sea realm of Somerled, who seized the southern Hebrides from the kings of Man and founded the dynasty of the Lords of the Isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.o: Somerled, a Norse-Gaelic warlord of Argyll married to a daughter of Olaf I of Man, challenged his brother-in-law Godred of the Kingdom of the Isles. After a sea battle in 1156 the Hebrides were divided, and in 1158 Somerled drove Godred from Man, ruling Argyll, Kintyre and the southern isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.r: Somerled's power rested on galley fleets and the loyalty of Gaelic and Norse-Gaelic kindreds. He acted as an independent ruler, sometimes allied with and sometimes against the Scottish king, and is linked with the founding of Saddell Abbey in Kintyre.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.e: Somerled was killed in 1164 at Renfrew while invading the Kingdom of Scotland. His realm was divided among his sons, ancestors of the MacDougalls, MacDonalds and MacRuairis, whose descendants later formed the Lordship of the Isles.

keraite-khanate.t: A powerful Christian steppe khanate in central Mongolia, whose ruler Toghrul was Genghis Khan's patron and rival, and later the model for legends of Prester John.
keraite-khanate.o: The Keraites were a large tribal union living along the Orkhon and Tuul rivers in central Mongolia, probably of Mongolic speech with strong Turkic influences. Syriac sources record that their ruler converted to the Church of the East around 1007, together with many of his people.
keraite-khanate.r: The khanate was a confederation of clans under a ruling family, with Christian priests and Nestorian practices alongside steppe customs. Its rulers, among them Marghuz Buyruk, fought the Tatars, Naimans and Merkits. Toghrul, sworn brother of Temüjin's father, became the most powerful khan of central Mongolia and received the title Ong Khan from the Jin dynasty (1115-1234) in 1196 after the campaign against the Tatars.
keraite-khanate.e: Toghrul helped the young Temüjin rise but turned against him; in 1203 Temüjin defeated the Keraites, and Toghrul was killed by Naimans while fleeing. The Keraites joined the Mongol Empire; the Keraite princess Sorghaghtani Beki was mother of Möngke, Kublai and Hülegü.

kingdom-of-italy-medieval.t: The medieval Kingdom of Italy, contested by Italian magnates after 888 and then held by the German emperors, whose authority waned as the cities grew.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.o: When the Carolingian Empire broke up in 888, Italian nobles elected Berengar of Friuli as King of Italy. For seventy years rival magnates and outsiders, among them Guy and Lambert of Spoleto, Louis of Provence, Rudolf of Burgundy and Hugh of Arles, fought for the crown, which was traditionally received at Pavia.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.r: In 951 Otto I of Germany took the title, and from his imperial coronation in 962 the crown was tied to the German emperors, often crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy. Arduin of Ivrea was the last native king (1002–1014). Imperial rule relied on bishops and counts, but the communes grew independent; the Lombard League defeated Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176, and the Peace of Constance in 1183 recognised their self-government.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.e: After the 13th century the kingdom survived mainly as a legal framework of imperial fiefs. Charles V was the last emperor crowned King of Italy, at Bologna in 1530. Imperial claims in Italy ended with the French Revolutionary Wars and the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801.

kara-khanid-khanate.t: The first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam as a state religion, which brought Transoxiana under Turkic rule and produced classic works of Turkic literature.
kara-khanid-khanate.o: The Kara-Khanid dynasty emerged in the mid-9th century among the Karluk Yabgu, Chigil and Yagma tribes after the fall of the Uyghur Khaganate, with centres at Balasagun and Kashgar. Around 934 the ruler Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam, and his successors made it the religion of the state.
kara-khanid-khanate.r: The khanate had a dual structure, with a senior khagan and a junior co-ruler, and appanages held by members of the royal clan. In 999 it took Bukhara from the Samanid Empire, bringing Transoxiana under Turkic rule. The Kara-Khanids built mosques and madrasas, and their court produced Yusuf Balasaguni's Kutadgu Bilig and Mahmud al-Kashgari's dictionary of Turkic languages.
kara-khanid-khanate.e: Dynastic rivalry split the khanate around 1042 into the Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate and the Western Kara-Khanid Khanate, which became vassals of the Seljuks and the Qara Khitai.

kingdom-of-navarre.t: The Basque Pyrenean kingdom of Pamplona, which under Sancho III dominated Christian Spain and survived in part until 1841.
kingdom-of-navarre.o: Around 824, after the Basques defeated a Frankish army at the second Battle of Roncevaux, Íñigo Arista became ruler of Pamplona, allied with his kinsmen the Banu Qasi. In 905 Sancho Garcés I founded the Jimena dynasty and pushed south into the Ebro valley and La Rioja.
kingdom-of-navarre.r: Sancho III the Great, from 1004 to 1035, controlled Aragon, Castile and the Pyrenean counties, the dominant power of Christian Iberia. After a period of partition between 1076 and 1134, the kingdom revived. Sancho VII fought at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. French dynasties ruled from 1234, and Charles III the Noble built the palace of Olite. Basque, Romance and Latin were spoken, and the kingdom kept its own fueros and cortes.
kingdom-of-navarre.e: In 1512 Ferdinand the Catholic conquered Upper Navarre, joined to Castile in 1515, while Lower Navarre north of the Pyrenees remained with the Albret family. Its kings became kings of France in 1589. Spanish Navarre kept its own institutions until the law of 1841 made it a province.

khanate-of-kokand.t: An Uzbek khanate of the Ferghana valley that grew to rule Tashkent and the Kyrgyz and Kazakh steppes before Russia annexed it in 1876.
khanate-of-kokand.o: Around 1709 Shahrukh Bi, leader of the Ming Uzbek tribe, broke away from the Khanate of Bukhara and established a separate state in the eastern Ferghana valley. His successors built Kokand as their capital, and Narbuta Bi strengthened the state in the late 18th century.
khanate-of-kokand.r: Alim Khan, who took the title khan around 1800, created a standing army and conquered Tashkent in 1809, followed by Umar Khan, a patron of poetry whose wife Nodira was a celebrated poet. The khanate controlled the trade routes to Kashgar and dominated Kyrgyz and Kazakh nomads, building forts such as Ak-Mechet on the Syr Darya. Rivalry between settled Sarts and nomadic Kipchaks caused civil wars.
khanate-of-kokand.e: Russia took Ak-Mechet in 1853 and Tashkent in 1865. After a revolt against the pro-Russian Khudayar Khan in 1875, General Skobelev crushed resistance and Russia annexed the khanate in 1876 as the Ferghana Oblast of the Turkestan Governorate-General.

kingdom-of-ui-failge.t: Irish midland kingdom of the O'Connor Faly, which resisted English expansion from its bogland strongholds until the plantation of Offaly in 1556.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.o: The Uí Failge, 'descendants of Failge', claimed descent from Rus Failge, a son of the legendary Leinster king Cathair Mór. From the early medieval period they held a kingdom in the north-west of the Kingdom of Leinster, in what is now County Offaly, which takes its name from them. From the 11th century their rulers were the Ua Conchobair Failge, O'Connor Faly.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.r: Their territory of bog, esker and woodland was hard for invaders to penetrate. After the Anglo-Norman invasion the FitzGeralds of Kildare took their eastern lands, but the O'Connors Faly held the rest, raiding the Pale and taking protection payments known as black rent. Their stronghold at Daingean, set among bogs, was their main fortress in the 16th century.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.e: After Brian O'Connor Faly rebelled and surrendered in the 1540s, the English took Daingean. In 1556 the government of Mary I shired the kingdom as King's County, with Daingean renamed Philipstown, and planted it with English settlers, ending the kingdom.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.t: Medieval Croatian kingdom of the Trpimirović dynasty, which reached from the Drava to the Adriatic before passing to the Hungarian crown.
kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.o: Around 925 Tomislav, ruler of the Duchy of Croatia, also held the Duchy of Pannonian Croatia and was addressed as king in papal letters. He had defeated Hungarian raids and the army of Simeon I of Bulgaria, uniting the Croats in one kingdom.
kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.r: Kings ruled with a council of nobles and bans, from royal seats such as Knin, Biograd na Moru and Nin. Petar Krešimir IV (1058–1074) brought the Byzantine Dalmatian towns under his control, and Demetrius Zvonimir was crowned by a papal legate in 1076, tying Croatia to the Reformed papacy. The Baška tablet records Zvonimir's gift in Glagolitic script.
kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.e: After Zvonimir died without heirs, Ladislaus I of Hungary claimed the throne. The last king, Petar Snačić, fell at Gvozd in 1097, and in 1102 Coloman was crowned king of Croatia, beginning the Kingdom of Croatia (1102-1526) in union with Hungary.

kingdom-of-kucha.t: The largest oasis kingdom of the northern Tarim Basin, a Buddhist centre famous for its music, the Kizil caves and the great translator Kumarajiva.
kingdom-of-kucha.o: Kucha, Qiuci in Chinese, was an Indo-European-speaking oasis state between the Tianshan Mountains and the Taklamakan desert, recorded from the 2nd century BCE among the kingdoms of the Western Regions. Its rulers, later known in Chinese by the surname Bai, balanced between the Xiongnu, the Han Dynasty and later steppe powers.
kingdom-of-kucha.r: Kuchean, now called Tocharian B, was written in Brahmi script. Kucha's monasteries, including the painted caves at Kizil, made it a leading centre of Buddhism, and the translator Kumarajiva was born there in 344; in 384 the Former Qin general Lü Guang took the city and carried him east. Kuchean musicians and instruments shaped the court music of the Sui and the Tang Dynasty.
kingdom-of-kucha.e: The Tang conquered Kucha in 648 and made it the seat of the Anxi Protectorate. When Tang control collapsed in the late 8th century, Uyghurs moved in, and after 840 Kucha became part of the Kingdom of Qocho and was gradually Turkicised.

kingdom-of-gododdin.t: British kingdom of Lothian centred on Edinburgh, celebrated in the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin, which fell to Northumbria in the 7th century.
kingdom-of-gododdin.o: Gododdin was the post-Roman kingdom of the Votadini, whose name became Guotodin and then Gododdin in Welsh. Its centre was Din Eidyn, the rock of Edinburgh, and it stretched across Lothian and the eastern Borders. Welsh tradition also linked the district of Manaw Gododdin, around the head of the Forth, with Cunedda, legendary founder of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-gododdin.r: The kingdom is best known from Y Gododdin, attributed to the poet Aneirin, which mourns a war band feasted for a year by Mynyddog Mwynfawr at Din Eidyn and then slaughtered at Catraeth, usually identified as Catterick, around 600. The poem portrays an aristocratic warrior society bound by loyalty, mead and gifts. Hillforts such as Traprain Law and Edinburgh Castle Rock were key centres.
kingdom-of-gododdin.e: The Anglian kingdom of Bernicia, later Northumbria, expanded northward in the 7th century. Irish annals record the siege of Etin in 638, generally taken as the Northumbrian capture of Edinburgh. Lothian remained English until it passed to the Scottish kings in the 10th and 11th centuries.

kingdom-of-kazembe.t: The eastern Lunda kingdom of the Luapula valley, a wealthy trading state visited by Portuguese explorers and David Livingstone.
kingdom-of-kazembe.o: Around 1740 a Lunda general sent east by the Mwata Yamvo of the Lunda Empire conquered the Luapula valley south of Lake Mweru. His successors, bearing the title Mwata Kazembe, built an independent kingdom that still paid tribute to the Lunda court.
kingdom-of-kazembe.r: The Kazembe ruled from a large capital through Lunda aristocrats who governed local chiefs. The kingdom traded copper from Katanga, ivory and slaves with Portuguese from Tete and Swahili-Arab merchants from the east coast. The Portuguese explorer Francisco de Lacerda died there in 1798, and Livingstone visited in 1867–68. The annual Mutomboko ceremony commemorates the conquest.
kingdom-of-kazembe.e: In the late 19th century Msiri's Yeke state took Katanga and Swahili-Arab traders eroded Kazembe's power. British South Africa Company forces occupied the capital in 1899, and the kingdom was absorbed into Northern Rhodesia. The Mwata Kazembe remains a traditional ruler in Zambia.

kingdom-of-germany.t: The German kingdom at the heart of the Holy Roman Empire, an elective monarchy whose kings claimed the imperial crown for more than eight centuries.
kingdom-of-germany.o: The kingdom grew out of East Francia. Its kings, from Henry the Fowler in 919, were elected by the great nobles. When Otto I was crowned emperor in Rome in 962, the German crown became joined with the imperial title and with kingship of Italy and later Burgundy, a link that defined the Holy Roman Empire.
kingdom-of-germany.r: German kings were elected, from 1356 by the seven prince-electors under the Golden Bull, and crowned at Aachen. Royal power weakened during the Investiture Controversy and after the fall of the Hohenstaufen, while princes, bishops and free cities gained autonomy. From 1438 the Habsburgs held the crown almost without break, governing with the Imperial Diet.
kingdom-of-germany.e: The Reformation and the Thirty Years' War, ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, left Germany a federation of nearly sovereign states. Under Napoleonic pressure, Francis II abdicated on 6 August 1806, dissolving the Empire and the German kingdom with it.
kingdom-of-germany.re: Catholic Christianity, Lutheranism and Calvinism after 1517

kingdom-of-ulaid.t: The ancient over-kingdom of Ulster, linked in legend with Emain Macha and the Ulster Cycle, which shrank to Antrim and Down before the Anglo-Normans.
kingdom-of-ulaid.o: The Ulaid, probably Ptolemy's Voluntii, gave their name to Ulster. Irish tradition remembers them as rulers of the whole north from Emain Macha, Navan Fort near Armagh, the setting of the Ulster Cycle tales of Conchobar mac Nessa and Cú Chulainn. In the 5th century, according to tradition, the Three Collas and the Uí Néill drove them east of the River Bann.
kingdom-of-ulaid.r: In historic times the kingdom was an over-kingship shared between the Dal Fiatach of Down and the Dal nAraidi of Antrim. Kings such as Báetán mac Cairill and Congal Cáech challenged the Uí Néill, but defeat at Mag Rath in 637 ended their hopes of wider supremacy. The kingdom's monasteries, including Bangor, Movilla and Nendrum, were among the great centres of early Irish learning.
kingdom-of-ulaid.e: Viking raids and Uí Néill pressure confined the Ulaid to Antrim and Down. In 1177 John de Courcy captured Downpatrick and defeated Ruaidrí Mac Duinn Sléibe, and the Ulaid lands became the Anglo-Norman Earldom of Ulster.

kingdom-of-kartli.t: The central Georgian kingdom around Tbilisi, a Persian vassal for much of its history, which produced Georgia's first printing press and a famous law code.
kingdom-of-kartli.o: Kartli, the historic core of eastern Georgia, emerged as a separate kingdom during the break-up of the Kingdom of Georgia in the late 15th century. Constantine II, the last king to claim all Georgia, was left by about 1490 with Kartli alone, and his descendants ruled it from Tbilisi.
kingdom-of-kartli.r: Kartli lay on the front line between the Ottoman and Safavid empires and was usually a Safavid vassal; several kings, such as Rostom, converted to Islam to hold the throne. Simon I fought both empires and died an Ottoman captive. Vakhtang VI, regent and king in the early 18th century, compiled a law code, edited the Georgian chronicles and set up a printing press in Tbilisi in 1709.
kingdom-of-kartli.e: After Vakhtang VI sought Russian help and fled to Russia in 1724, the Ottomans occupied Kartli until 1735. Teimuraz II regained the throne in 1744, and on his death in 1762 his son Erekle II united Kartli with Kakheti.

kingdom-of-mercia.t: The great midland kingdom that dominated England in the 8th century under Aethelbald and Offa, whose Dyke still marks the Welsh border.
kingdom-of-mercia.o: Mercia, the 'border people', arose among Angles in the upper Trent valley. Later genealogies place its first kings, Icel and Creoda, in the 6th century, but the first well-attested ruler is the pagan Penda, who fought Northumbria and East Anglia from the 620s to his death at the Winwaed in 655.
kingdom-of-mercia.r: Mercian kings ruled from Tamworth, with a bishopric at Lichfield, and dominated client kingdoms such as the Hwicce and the Magonsaete. Offa took the title king of the English, issued a reformed silver penny, corresponded with Charlemagne and built Offa's Dyke. He briefly created an archbishopric at Lichfield.
kingdom-of-mercia.e: Defeat by Wessex at Ellendun in 825 and the Viking conquests of the 870s split Mercia. Its western half, under Aethelred and Aethelflaed, the Lady of the Mercians, allied with Wessex. After Aethelflaed's death in 918 it was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons.

kingdom-of-finland-1918.t: The short-lived attempt to make independent Finland a monarchy under a German prince, abandoned when Germany lost the First World War.
kingdom-of-finland-1918.o: After the civil war, conservative politicians wanted a strong monarchy tied to Germany, whose troops had helped the Whites win. On 9 October 1918 a rump parliament, without the Social Democrats, elected Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse as king of Finland. Pehr Evind Svinhufvud served as regent.
kingdom-of-finland-1918.r: The kingdom existed largely on paper. Frederick Charles never came to Finland, and no coronation took place. German influence over the army and the economy was strong, and the monarchists hoped the throne would secure German protection against Soviet Russia.
kingdom-of-finland-1918.e: Germany's defeat in November 1918 made a German king impossible. Frederick Charles renounced the throne on 14 December 1918, and Mannerheim replaced Svinhufvud as regent. The constitution of 1919 created the Republic of Finland, and the monarchy project was abandoned.

khanate-of-khiva.t: The Uzbek khanate of Khwarazm, ruled from the walled city of Khiva for four centuries, notorious for its slave markets and finally a Russian protectorate.
khanate-of-khiva.o: In 1511 Ilbars and Balbars, descendants of Arab Shah of the Shibanid line, took Khwarazm after the Safavids had briefly seized it from Muhammad Shaybani. The Arabshahid dynasty ruled at first from Urgench and later from Khiva, which became the capital in the 17th century as the Amu Darya changed course.
khanate-of-khiva.r: The khanate ruled Uzbek tribes, Turkmen and settled Sarts along the irrigated lower Amu Darya. The khan and historian Abu'l-Ghazi Bahadur wrote a genealogical history of the Turks. Slave trading of Persians and Russians captured by Turkmen raiders was central to the economy. From 1804 the Qungrat dynasty, whose founders had been inaks, ruled as khans, building much of Itchan Kala.
khanate-of-khiva.e: Russian forces captured Khiva in 1873 and made it a protectorate. In 1920 the Red Army and the Young Khivans deposed the last khan, Said Abdullah, creating the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic.

kingdom-of-lindsey.t: A small Anglian kingdom in north Lincolnshire centred on Roman Lincoln, briefly fought over by Northumbria and Mercia before Mercian absorption.
kingdom-of-lindsey.o: Lindsey took its name from the Roman Lindum (Lincoln), and Anglian settlers established a kingdom there in the late 5th or 6th century. A list of its kings survives in a collection of royal genealogies, tracing them to Woden, ending with Aldfrith in the late 8th century.
kingdom-of-lindsey.r: The kingdom lay between the Humber and the Witham, bounded by fen and sea, and was too small to stand alone. Paulinus preached at Lincoln around 628 under Northumbrian protection, building a stone church. A separate bishopric of Lindsey was founded in 678.
kingdom-of-lindsey.e: Northumbria and Mercia contested Lindsey until the Battle of the Trent in 679 left it permanently Mercian. Its kings faded into dependent rulers and disappeared by about 800. The district was later settled by Danes and formed part of Lincolnshire.

kingdom-of-paeonia.t: Ancient kingdom of the Axios (Vardar) valley north of Macedon, whose kings minted fine silver coins before falling under Macedonian control.
kingdom-of-paeonia.o: The Paeonians held the Axios and Strymon valleys from early times; Homer lists them as allies of Troy. In 511 BCE the Persian general Megabazus deported many of them to Asia. A kingdom with its own coinage emerged in the 4th century BCE, centred on Bylazora and Astibos (Štip).
kingdom-of-paeonia.r: Kings such as Lyppeios, Patraos and Audoleon issued silver coins showing Apollo and horsemen, and Audoleon was honoured at Athens. The economy rested on herding, farming and the trade route along the Axios. The Paeonians worshipped the sun and a Dionysus called Dyalos, and were famed riders. Philip II of Macedon forced them into dependency after 358 BCE, and they served in Alexander's army.
kingdom-of-paeonia.e: Celtic invasions in 279 BCE weakened the kingdom. In 217 BCE Philip V of Macedon took Bylazora, ending its independence, and after 168 BCE Paeonia became part of Roman Macedonia.

kingdom-of-hejaz.t: The Hashemite kingdom proclaimed by Sharif Hussein during the Arab Revolt, which held Mecca and Medina until conquered by Ibn Saud.
kingdom-of-hejaz.o: In June 1916 Hussein ibn Ali, head of the Sharifate of Mecca, launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire with British support, encouraged by the Hussein-McMahon correspondence. He proclaimed himself King of the Arab Lands; the Allies recognised him as King of the Hejaz. His sons Faisal and Abdullah led Arab forces north.
kingdom-of-hejaz.r: The kingdom controlled the Hejaz, its holy cities, the pilgrimage and the port of Jeddah, financed largely by British subsidies and pilgrim fees. Hussein refused to accept the post-war mandates in Syria, Palestine and Iraq, quarrelled with Britain and declined to sign the Treaty of Versailles. In March 1924, after Turkey abolished the caliphate, he declared himself caliph.
kingdom-of-hejaz.e: Ibn Saud's Ikhwan took Ta'if and then Mecca in late 1924. Hussein abdicated in favour of his son Ali, who surrendered Jeddah in December 1925. The Hejaz became part of the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd, while Hussein's sons ruled the Kingdom of Iraq and the Emirate of Transjordan.
