kingdom-of-hengshan.t: Wu Rui's kingdom in the middle Yangtze, created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, whose ruler switched to Liu Bang and became the first King of Changsha.
kingdom-of-hengshan.o: Wu Rui, a Qin magistrate of Po county who was popular with the Yue peoples, joined the rebellion against the Qin dynasty and sent troops with his son-in-law Ying Bu. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Hengshan, with his capital at Zhu near modern Huanggang in Hubei.
kingdom-of-hengshan.r: Hengshan straddled the Yangtze east of the Kingdom of Linjiang, controlling rice lands and river trade. Wu Rui's support among the Baiyue peoples of the south gave him a following beyond the Chinese population.
kingdom-of-hengshan.e: Wu Rui supported Liu Bang against Xiang Yu, and after the Han victory in 202 BCE he was moved to become King of Changsha. His family held Changsha until 157 BCE, one of the few non-Liu kingdoms to survive under the Han Dynasty.

kingdom-of-cilicia.t: Cilicia, a vassal kingdom of the Syennesis dynasty at Tarsus that kept its own kings under Persia until 401 BCE.
kingdom-of-cilicia.o: After the fall of the Assyrian Empire, local rulers in the Cilician plain and Rough Cilicia formed a kingdom with Tarsus as its capital, drawing on the lands of Que and Hilakku. Babylonian records call part of it Pirindu, and Neriglissar of the Chaldean Empire fought its king Appuashu in 557 BCE.
kingdom-of-cilicia.r: Its kings bore the title or name Syennesis. One Syennesis mediated, with a Babylonian envoy, the peace between Lydia and the Median Empire after the eclipse battle of 585 BCE. Under the Achaemenid Empire the kingdom kept its own rulers, paid tribute in silver and white horses and supplied ships to the Persian fleet.
kingdom-of-cilicia.e: In 401 BCE Syennesis and his wife Epyaxa supported Cyrus the Younger in his revolt. After its failure the Persians abolished the kingship and turned Cilicia into an ordinary satrapy.

kingdom-of-castile.t: The medieval kingdom of Castile, which took Toledo, crushed the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa and became the dominant power of Christian Iberia.
kingdom-of-castile.o: The County of Castile had been raised to a kingdom by Ferdinand I, who also ruled the Kingdom of León. At his death in 1065 he divided his realms, leaving Castile to his eldest son Sancho II. After Sancho's murder in 1072 his brother Alfonso VI reunited Castile and León.
kingdom-of-castile.r: Castile was a frontier society of free settlers, town councils with their own fueros and mounted warriors, later organised in military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago. Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085. Alfonso VIII, defeated at Alarcos in 1195, led the coalition that destroyed the Almohad army at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Burgos, on the pilgrim road to Santiago, prospered on trade and wool.
kingdom-of-castile.e: Castile and León were separated again from 1157, but in 1230 Ferdinand III, already king of Castile, inherited León, creating the lasting union known as the Crown of Castile, which absorbed most of al-Andalus within a generation.

kingdom-of-pergamon.t: Hellenistic kingdom of the Attalid dynasty in western Anatolia, a great centre of art and learning that was bequeathed to Rome in 133 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.o: Philetaerus, an officer guarding Lysimachus' treasure of 9,000 talents at the citadel of Pergamon, changed sides to Seleucus I in 282 BCE and kept the fortress and money. His nephew Eumenes I asserted independence from the Seleucids. Attalus I took the title of king around 238 BCE after defeating the Galatians.
kingdom-of-pergamon.r: The Attalids built Pergamon into a showpiece capital of terraces, temples and theatre, with a library second only to Alexandria's, traditionally linked to the development of parchment. The Great Altar of Zeus celebrated victory over the Galatians. Loyal alliance with Rome brought Eumenes II wide lands in Asia Minor after the Peace of Apamea in 188 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.e: Attalus III died in 133 BCE leaving his kingdom to Rome. Aristonicus, claiming to be a royal son, led a revolt that was crushed by 129 BCE, and the kingdom became the Roman province of Asia. The Pergamon Altar is now in Berlin.

kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.t: Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy, ruled from Milan by his stepson Eugène de Beauharnais, which gave northern Italians a modern state and a common army.
kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.o: When Napoleon became emperor of the French, the Italian Republic (1802–1805) was turned into a kingdom. On 26 May 1805 Napoleon crowned himself king of Italy in Milan Cathedral with the Iron Crown of Lombardy, and appointed his stepson Eugène de Beauharnais as viceroy.
kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.r: The kingdom grew to include Venetia in 1806, the Marche in 1808 and South Tyrol in 1810, and for a time Istria and Dalmatia, which passed to the Illyrian Provinces in 1809. It had departments and prefects on the French model, the Napoleonic Code, public schools and an efficient tax system. Its conscript army fought in Spain and Russia, where tens of thousands died in 1812.
kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.e: After Napoleon's defeats, Eugène signed an armistice in April 1814. A riot in Milan killed the finance minister Giuseppe Prina, and Austrian troops took over; the territory became the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia and other restored states.

kingdom-of-main.t: The Minaean kingdom of al-Jawf, whose merchants ran the incense trade from Yemen to Egypt and even the Greek island of Delos.
kingdom-of-main.o: Ma'in arose in the al-Jawf valley north of Marib, in a region of city-states once subject to the Kingdom of Saba. By the 6th or 5th century BCE it was independent, its kings ruling from Qarnawu with Yathill (Baraqish) as a second major city.
kingdom-of-main.r: Ma'in was above all a trading state. Minaean merchants organised incense caravans to Gaza and Egypt, kept a colony at Dedan in the Hejaz, and left inscriptions as far away as Delos. Inscriptions list Minaean men marrying foreign wives from Gaza and Egypt. The main god was Wadd, and the kings governed with councils drawn from leading families. The language was Minaic.
kingdom-of-main.e: Ma'in depended on caravan trade and lost importance as Ptolemaic and Roman shipping in the Red Sea grew. Around 100 BCE it was absorbed by the Kingdom of Saba. The walls of Baraqish still stand in al-Jawf.

kingdom-of-saba.t: Biblical Sheba: the incense kingdom of Marib whose great dam, temples and caravans made it the leading power of ancient south Arabia.
kingdom-of-saba.o: Sabaean inscriptions begin around the 8th century BCE, when rulers titled mukarrib governed from Marib in the Yemeni desert margin. The early Marib Dam captured seasonal floods to irrigate two vast oases. In the 7th century BCE Karib'il Watar conquered the Kingdom of Awsan and imposed Sabaean supremacy over much of south-western Arabia.
kingdom-of-saba.r: Saba grew rich on frankincense and myrrh carried north along the caravan routes to Gaza and Mesopotamia. Society was organised in tribes and communes bound to the king; the national god Almaqah was worshipped at the Awwam temple near Marib. Sabaic, written in the Ancient South Arabian script, became the region's prestige language. Its fame gave rise to the story of the Queen of Sheba.
kingdom-of-saba.e: From the 1st century BCE Saba lost ground as sea trade bypassed the caravans and the Himyarite Kingdom rose in the highlands. After centuries of rivalry, Shammar Yahrish of Himyar absorbed Saba around 275 CE, keeping the title King of Saba and Dhu Raydan. The Marib Dam finally failed in the 6th century.

kingdom-of-munster.t: Southern Irish over-kingdom ruled from the Rock of Cashel by the Eóganachta and later by the Dál Cais of Brian Bóruma, until it split in two in 1118.
kingdom-of-munster.o: Munster, Mumu in Irish, was one of the ancient provinces of Ireland. From around the 5th century the Eóganachta dynasties, tracing descent from Conall Corc, the legendary founder of Cashel, established an over-kingship over the province, displacing earlier Érainn peoples such as the Corcu Loigde.
kingdom-of-munster.r: Kings ruled from Cashel through a confederation of Eóganacht branches, collecting tribute from many subject peoples. Several were also churchmen or patrons of learning, such as Feidlimid mac Crimthainn, king and abbot, who died in 847. Cathal mac Finguine, who died in 742, challenged the Uí Néill for supremacy. In the 10th century the Dál Cais of Thomond took the kingship, and Brian Bóruma, king of Munster from 978, became High King of Ireland in 1002.
kingdom-of-munster.e: In 1101 Muirchertach Ua Briain gave the Rock of Cashel to the Church. In 1118 Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair of the Kingdom of Connacht divided Munster by the Treaty of Glanmire into Desmond, under the MacCarthys, and Thomond, under the O'Briens.

kingdom-of-manyika.t: A Shona kingdom of the eastern highlands, ruled by the Mutasa, whose goldfields drew Portuguese traders and later British and Portuguese rivals.
kingdom-of-manyika.o: Manyika emerged around 1490 in the highlands that now straddle the Zimbabwe–Mozambique border, as a tributary state on the edge of the Mutapa realm. Its rulers, who bore the title Mutasa, soon became effectively independent, controlling the alluvial gold of the region and the routes to the coast.
kingdom-of-manyika.r: The Mutasa ruled through a network of chiefs and kin, and rainmaking and ancestral spirit mediums supported royal authority. Gold was traded at Portuguese fairs such as Masekesa, and the kingdom was a frequent target of Portuguese, Barwe and Uteve ambitions. In the 19th century it suffered raids from the Gaza Nguni.
kingdom-of-manyika.e: In 1890 Mutasa signed an agreement with the British South Africa Company, which clashed with the Portuguese claim. Fighting at Macequece in 1891 and the Anglo-Portuguese treaty that year split Manyika between Southern Rhodesia and Portuguese Mozambique. Manyika remains a Shona dialect and regional identity.

kummuh.t: Kummuh, a Neo-Hittite kingdom on the upper Euphrates around Samosata, forerunner of later Commagene.
kummuh.o: Kummuh arose after the Hittite collapse c. 1180 BCE in the land on the right bank of the upper Euphrates around Samosata, modern Samsat. Assyrian texts mention it from the time of Tiglath-Pileser I, c. 1100 BCE, when it was a target of raids.
kummuh.r: Its kings ruled a farming land of river valleys and wrote inscriptions in Luwian hieroglyphs. Placed between the Assyrian Empire and the Kingdom of Urartu, they usually paid tribute to Assyria; Kushtashpi joined an Urartian alliance against Tiglath-Pileser III and then submitted again.
kummuh.e: In 708 BCE Sargon II deposed King Muwatalli for conspiring with Urartu, deported its people and made Kummuh an Assyrian province. The name survived as Commagene, later the Kingdom of Commagene.

kingdom-of-imereti.t: The western Georgian kingdom centred on Kutaisi that endured Ottoman pressure for centuries until the Russian Empire annexed it in 1810.
kingdom-of-imereti.o: In 1259-1260 David VI Narin, a co-king of the Kingdom of Georgia, rebelled against the Mongols and withdrew to Kutaisi, creating a separate western kingdom. George V the Brilliant reunited it with the rest of Georgia in 1330, but it broke away again in the 1380s and was finally independent after the division of 1490.
kingdom-of-imereti.r: The kings ruled from Kutaisi with the Gelati monastery as a royal shrine, but powerful vassals, the Dadiani of Mingrelia, the Gurieli of Guria and the dukes of Racha, often defied them. From 1555 Imereti was tributary to the Ottoman Empire, and the slave trade with Ottoman ports was a scourge. Solomon I defeated the Ottomans at Chikhori in 1757 and banned the slave trade.
kingdom-of-imereti.e: Solomon II accepted a Russian protectorate in 1804 but resisted direct rule, and in 1810 the Russian Empire deposed him and annexed Imereti. He died in exile at Trabzon in 1815.

kingdom-of-east-anglia.t: The kingdom of the East Angles in Norfolk and Suffolk, famed for the Sutton Hoo ship burial and for its martyred last king, Edmund.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.o: Angles settled Norfolk and Suffolk in the 5th century, and the Wuffingas dynasty, named after Wuffa, ruled by the 6th century. Its royal centre lay at Rendlesham in the Deben valley, close to the burial ground at Sutton Hoo.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.r: Raedwald, overlord of the southern English around 616, probably lies in the Sutton Hoo ship burial, with its gold and Byzantine silver. He kept both a Christian altar and a pagan one. Later kings founded the bishopric at Dunwich under Felix and monasteries such as Ely. Ipswich became one of the first post-Roman towns.
kingdom-of-east-anglia.e: East Anglia was often under Mercian overlordship in the 8th century. The Great Heathen Army killed King Edmund in 869 and the Danes later settled the land as the Danish Kingdom of East Anglia. Edmund's cult grew at Bury St Edmunds.

kingdom-of-shule.t: The oasis kingdom of Kashgar at the western end of the Tarim Basin, a crossroads where the Silk Roads met before climbing the Pamirs.
kingdom-of-shule.o: Shule, the Chinese name for Kashgar, was a city-state at the foot of the Pamirs, recorded by Han sources from the 2nd century BCE. Its people spoke an Eastern Iranian language related to Saka, and it controlled the routes west to Ferghana and Bactria and south towards India.
kingdom-of-shule.r: Shule was ruled by local kings who switched allegiance between the Xiongnu, Kushan, Han and later Turkic powers. In the 70s CE the Han general Ban Chao used it as his base for reconquering the Western Regions. Buddhism was strong, and the city's markets traded silk, horses and jade. Under the Tang Dynasty its kings of the Pei family ruled as one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi.
kingdom-of-shule.e: The Tibetan Empire took the Tarim garrisons around 790, ending Tang authority. In the 10th century Kashgar became the capital of the Kara-Khanid Khanate, whose rulers converted to Islam and turned the city into a centre of Turkic Muslim culture.

kingdom-of-colchis.t: The land of the Golden Fleece on the eastern Black Sea, an early Georgian kingdom whose gold, timber and Greek trading ports made it a bridge between the Caucasus and the Greek world.
kingdom-of-colchis.o: Colchis appears as Qulha in Urartian inscriptions of the 8th century BCE, when it emerged in the lowlands of the Rioni and its foothills, in part inheriting the lands of Diauehi. Greek colonists from Miletus founded ports such as Phasis and Dioscurias in the 6th century BCE, and the Argonaut legend fixed its fame.
kingdom-of-colchis.r: Power was held by kings and local sceptre-bearing chiefs ruling from towns such as Vani, whose rich burials hold fine gold jewellery. Colchians traded linen, timber, honey and slaves with the Greeks and paid tribute to the Achaemenid Empire. They spoke a Kartvelian language, and local coins called Colchian tetri circulated widely.
kingdom-of-colchis.e: In the 2nd century BCE the kingdom fragmented under local rulers, and about 101 BCE Mithridates VI annexed it to the Kingdom of Pontus. After Pontus fell to Rome, the coast passed under Roman influence and the western Georgian kingdom of Lazica later grew in the same lands.

kingdom-of-westphalia.t: Napoleonic kingdom ruled by his brother Jérôme, Germany's first state with a written constitution and equal rights for Jews.
kingdom-of-westphalia.o: After defeating Prussia, Napoleon created the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807 by the Peace of Tilsit, combining Hesse-Kassel, Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, Prussian lands west of the Elbe such as Magdeburg and Halberstadt, and parts of Hanover. He gave it to his youngest brother Jérôme Bonaparte, with Kassel as capital.
kingdom-of-westphalia.r: The constitution of November 1807, the first in Germany, abolished serfdom and guild privileges, introduced the Napoleonic Code and granted equal rights to Jews. A parliament of estates met. But heavy taxes, French demands for soldiers and losses in Russia made the regime unpopular, and Jérôme's court was known for extravagance. Revolts broke out in 1809.
kingdom-of-westphalia.e: After the battle of Leipzig in 1813 Russian troops took Kassel and Jérôme fled. The old rulers returned to Hesse-Kassel, Brunswick and Hanover, while Prussia recovered its lands.

kingdom-of-etruria.t: A Napoleonic kingdom created in Tuscany for a Spanish Bourbon prince in 1801, abolished six years later.
kingdom-of-etruria.o: By agreements between France and Spain in 1800–1801, including the Treaty of Aranjuez, the Grand Duchy of Tuscany was taken from its Habsburg-Lorraine ruler and turned into the Kingdom of Etruria for Louis of Bourbon-Parma, in exchange for the Bourbon claim to the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza.
kingdom-of-etruria.r: Louis I, in poor health, ruled from Florence under strong French influence; the State of the Presidi was added. After his death in 1803 his widow Maria Luisa of Spain governed as regent for their young son Charles Louis. The court was conservative and pious, and the kingdom paid heavily to support French troops.
kingdom-of-etruria.e: In 1807 Napoleon dissolved the kingdom under the Treaty of Fontainebleau and annexed Tuscany to France in 1808. In 1809 he made his sister Elisa grand duchess. Maria Luisa later received the Duchy of Lucca.

kingdom-of-the-thuringians.t: A Germanic kingdom in central Germany, briefly one of the great powers of the post-Roman west until the Franks destroyed it in 531.
kingdom-of-the-thuringians.o: The Thuringians appear around 400 in a Roman veterinary text that praises their horses. They likely descended in part from the Hermunduri and Angles, and formed a kingdom centred on the Thuringian basin, extending at its height from the Harz to the Danube and from the Werra to the Elbe.
kingdom-of-the-thuringians.r: In the early 6th century King Herminafrid married Amalaberga, niece of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, linking Thuringia to the Ostrogothic alliance system. Rich graves, horse burials and the trade in horses show an aristocratic warrior society. Little is known of its institutions, as it left no written records of its own.
kingdom-of-the-thuringians.e: After Theodoric's death removed Ostrogothic protection, the Frankish kings Theuderic I and Chlothar I defeated the Thuringians on the Unstrut in 531; Herminafrid was killed soon after at Zülpich. The north went to Saxon allies, the rest to the Franks, later forming the Duchy of Thuringia.

kingdom-of-galicia.t: The north-western Iberian kingdom centred on Santiago de Compostela, sometimes ruled by its own kings but usually joined with León and Castile.
kingdom-of-galicia.o: When Alfonso III of Asturias was deposed in 910, his son Ordoño II took Galicia as his kingdom. Galicia had been the core of the Kingdom of the Suebi and a part of the Asturian realm, and the cult of St James at Compostela had made it famous across Europe.
kingdom-of-galicia.r: Galicia was dominated by a powerful nobility and the church, above all the archbishops of Santiago such as Diego Gelmírez. It had its own kings at times, among them García II from 1065 to 1071, and Alfonso VII was crowned king of Galicia at Santiago in 1111. Galician-Portuguese became a major literary language, used for the troubadour lyric and the Cantigas de Santa Maria.
kingdom-of-galicia.e: From 1230 Galicia was permanently part of the Crown of Castile, though it kept the title of kingdom and from the 16th century its own Junta. The provincial reform of 1833 abolished it as an administrative unit, but Galicia today is an autonomous community.

kadesh.t: Kadesh, a fortified Syrian city on the Orontes that led resistance to Egypt and gave its name to the great chariot battle of 1274 BCE.
kadesh.o: Kadesh, at Tell Nebi Mend south of Homs, controlled the route through the Homs gap between the coast and inner Syria. In the 15th century BCE its king, backed by the Mitanni Empire, led the Canaanite and Syrian coalition that Thutmose III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom defeated at Megiddo.
kadesh.r: Its kings governed a compact territory of the upper Orontes and were courted by every great power. In the Amarna age King Aitakkama went over to the Hittite Empire and raided Egyptian vassals, and the Hittites kept Kadesh as a vassal kingdom.
kadesh.e: In 1274 BCE Ramesses II fought Muwatalli II outside the city in the Battle of Kadesh, after which the city stayed in Hittite hands. Kadesh was destroyed around 1200 BCE in the end of the Late Bronze Age and survived only as a village.

kingdom-of-wessex.t: The kingdom of the West Saxons, which survived the Viking onslaught under Alfred the Great and grew into the Kingdom of England.
kingdom-of-wessex.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle traces Wessex to Cerdic and Cynric, said to have landed in 495 and taken the kingship in 519. Early kings of the Gewisse operated in the upper Thames valley before expanding west and south. Archaeology suggests more complex origins than the Chronicle's story.
kingdom-of-wessex.r: Wessex was divided into shires under ealdormen, with royal estates, law codes from Ine around 694, and bishoprics at Winchester and Sherborne. Christianity arrived with Birinus in 635. Victory over Mercia at Ellendun in 825 made Ecgberht the leading southern king. Alfred built a network of fortified burhs, a navy and a revival of learning in English.
kingdom-of-wessex.e: Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878 and his successors reconquered the Danelaw. From 886 Wessex merged into the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons, and under Aethelstan in 927 it became the core of the Kingdom of England, with Winchester its royal centre.

kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.t: The Gaelic lordship of north-west Ulster, ruled from the 13th century by the O'Donnells, whose flight in 1607 ended independent Gaelic rule in Ulster.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.o: Tir Chonaill, the land of Conall, was named after Conall Gulban, a son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. His descendants, the Cenel Conaill, formed one branch of the northern Ui Neill and held much of present-day County Donegal. Columba of Iona belonged to this kindred, which also shared the high kingship in the early centuries.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.r: Cenel Conaill kings alternated the northern overkingship with Cenel nEogain until the 8th century. From the 13th century the O'Donnell family ruled from Donegal Castle, with a strong fleet, Scottish mercenaries and learned bardic families such as the O'Clerys. Franciscan Donegal Friary was a key patron foundation.
kingdom-of-tir-chonaill.e: Red Hugh O'Donnell joined Hugh O'Neill in the Nine Years' War against England. After defeat, Rory O'Donnell, Earl of Tyrconnell, left Ireland in the Flight of the Earls in 1607, and his lands were confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster under the Kingdom of Ireland.

karelians.t: Finnic people around Lake Ladoga and their stronghold of Korela, allies of Novgorod whose land was divided between Sweden and Rus' in 1323.
karelians.o: The Karelians emerged in the late Iron Age on the north-western shores of Lake Ladoga and the Karelian Isthmus. Their wealth came from the fur trade, and by the 12th century they were closely tied to Novgorod, joining its campaigns against the Finns and Swedes.
karelians.r: Karelian society was led by local chiefs and wealthy families who controlled fur collection from the north. Rich graves with silver ornaments and swords show a prosperous elite. In 1227 Prince Yaroslav Vsevolodovich of Novgorod had many Karelians baptised into Orthodox Christianity, and Korela became their main fortified centre.
karelians.e: In 1278 Novgorod campaigned against the Karelians and tightened its control over them. Sweden pressed from the west and founded Vyborg in 1293. The Treaty of Nöteborg in 1323 divided Karelia between Sweden and Novgorod, a border that shaped the later divide between Lutheran Finland and Orthodox Russia.

kingdom-of-uteve.t: A Shona kingdom behind the port of Sofala whose rulers, the Sachiteve, charged the Portuguese for passage to the gold fairs of the interior.
kingdom-of-uteve.o: Uteve emerged in the late 15th century when a branch of the ruling house in the Mutapa lands broke away and established itself between the Zimbabwe plateau and the coast. Its position astride the routes from Sofala to the inland goldfields made it a key intermediary for Swahili and then Portuguese traders.
kingdom-of-uteve.r: The king, called the Sachiteve (Quiteve to the Portuguese), was a sacred ruler bound by strict ritual; the Dominican friar Joao dos Santos, who lived at Sofala in the 1590s, described royal ceremonies and regicide when a king became infirm. Spirit mediums and ancestor cults were central. The Portuguese paid regular tribute, the curva, for the right to trade through the kingdom.
kingdom-of-uteve.e: Uteve was weakened by succession disputes and in the 19th century fell under the domination of the Gaza Nguni. By around 1890 its lands were included in the territory of the Mozambique Company within Portuguese Mozambique.

kalmyk-khanate.t: A khanate of Oirat Mongols who migrated to the Volga steppe, the westernmost Buddhist state in Europe.
kalmyk-khanate.o: In the early 17th century the Torghut, an Oirat Mongol tribe, under their leader Kho Orluk, migrated west from Dzungaria across the Kazakh steppe, reaching the lower Volga by about 1630 and driving out the Nogai Horde. Ayuka Khan later received the title of khan from the Dalai Lama.
kalmyk-khanate.r: The Kalmyks were pastoral nomads following Tibetan Buddhism, with monasteries and a code of law based on the Mongol-Oirat Code of 1640. As allies of Russia they guarded its southern frontier, fighting the Crimean Khanate, the Kazakh Khanate and Ottoman forces. Ayuka Khan, ruling from 1669 to 1724, was the khanate's most powerful leader.
kalmyk-khanate.e: Russian settlement and controls on the steppe pushed many Kalmyks to return east. In 1771 Ubashi Khan led some 150,000 across the steppe to Dzungaria, losing many on the way. Catherine the Great abolished the khanate, and those left on the Volga are the ancestors of today's Kalmyks.

kingdom-of-the-algarve.t: Portugal's southern coast, held as a nominally separate kingdom by the Portuguese crown from its conquest until 1910.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.o: Afonso III of Portugal completed the conquest of the Algarve by taking Faro in 1249. Castile disputed the territory until the Treaty of Badajoz of 1267, after which Portuguese kings styled themselves Kings of Portugal and the Algarve.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.r: The Algarve had no separate institutions: it was governed from Lisbon as part of the Kingdom of Portugal, though its title and arms were kept as a mark of conquest. Its ports, especially Lagos, served as bases for Henry the Navigator's voyages to Africa. Fishing, salt, figs and almonds sustained its economy.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.e: The title was later expanded under Manuel I to cover territories in Africa. The Kingdom of the Algarve ended in law with the Portuguese monarchy in the revolution of 1910 and became a region of the First Portuguese Republic.

kingdom-of-bernicia.t: The northern Anglian kingdom based on the fortress of Bamburgh, whose kings united with Deira to create Northumbria.
kingdom-of-bernicia.o: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle dates Bernicia to 547, when Ida took the kingship and built Bamburgh. Its people were Angles who settled the coast between the Tees and the Forth among the British population. The British name Bryneich suggests the kingdom took over an earlier British territory.
kingdom-of-bernicia.r: Bernicia's kings were warriors whose power rested on tribute and plunder. Aethelfrith defeated Aedan of Dal Riata at Degsastan in 603 and the Britons at Chester, then seized Deira. His son Oswald brought Aidan from Iona, who founded Lindisfarne in 635, and royal sites such as Yeavering show grand halls.
kingdom-of-bernicia.e: Under Oswiu, Bernicia and the Kingdom of Deira were joined permanently after 654, forming the Kingdom of Northumbria. Bamburgh remained a royal fortress and later the seat of the Earldom of Bamburgh.

karasids.t: A beylik on the Sea of Marmara and Aegean whose annexation gave the Ottomans the soldiers and ships to cross into Europe.
karasids.o: Around the end of the 13th century the Turkmen leader Karesi Bey took the former Byzantine region of Mysia, with Balikesir and Pergamon, as Byzantine defences in western Anatolia collapsed.
karasids.r: The Karasids raided across the Dardanelles into Thrace and the Aegean, sometimes as allies of Byzantine factions. Ibn Battuta met the ruler of Pergamon, Yakhshi Bey, in the 1330s. After Karesi Bey's death his sons, Demirhan and Yakhshi, divided the lands and quarrelled, opening the way to Ottoman intervention. The beylik's warriors and commanders, such as Haci Ilbey and Evrenos Bey, later served the Ottomans.
karasids.e: Orhan annexed the beylik, a process usually dated to around 1345, though resistance continued for some years. Its manpower and Dardanelles coast enabled the Ottoman crossing to Gallipoli in 1354.

kuban-cossack-host.t: The Cossack community of the Kuban, descended largely from the Zaporozhian Cossacks, which garrisoned the north-western Caucasus for Russia.
kuban-cossack-host.o: The Kuban Cossack Host was formed in 1860 by merging the Black Sea Cossack Host, made up of former Zaporozhian Cossacks resettled on the Kuban in 1792, with part of the Caucasus Line Cossack Host. It was centred on Yekaterinodar, modern Krasnodar.
kuban-cossack-host.r: Cossacks held land in stanitsas in return for military service, electing village atamans while the host's chief ataman was appointed by the tsar. They provided cavalry and the plastun scout units and settled lands cleared of Circassians after 1864. Many spoke a Ukrainian dialect, and the Kuban grew rich on grain. Their choir and traditions survive.
kuban-cossack-host.e: After 1917 the Kuban Rada declared autonomy and allied with the Whites. The Russian SFSR conquered the region in 1920, abolished the host and persecuted Cossacks. The host was revived as a cultural and service organisation in the 1990s.

knossos.t: Leading city-state of Iron Age Crete on the site of the great Minoan palace, rival of Gortyn until the Roman conquest of 67 BCE.
knossos.o: Knossos survived the fall of its Bronze Age palace as a town and grew again in the early Iron Age. By the 7th century BCE it was a Dorian-speaking polis and, with Gortyn, one of the two strongest cities of Crete. The Minoan past was remembered in myths of Minos and the Labyrinth.
knossos.r: Like other Cretan cities, Knossos was ruled by annual magistrates called kosmoi, with men's messes and citizen training. The seer Epimenides was said to come from Knossos. Its coins showed the Labyrinth and the Minotaur. In the Hellenistic period Knossos fought Gortyn and Lyttos, destroying Lyttos in 220 BCE, and took part in the Cretan Koinon.
knossos.e: Rome conquered Crete under Quintus Caecilius Metellus between 69 and 67 BCE. Gortyn became the provincial capital, while Knossos was refounded as a Roman colony under Augustus. The Palace State of Knossos is described separately.

kazakh-assr.t: The autonomous Soviet republic of the Kazakhs within Russia, whose collectivisation brought a famine that killed over a third of the Kazakh people.
kazakh-assr.o: In August 1920 the Soviet government created the Kirghiz ASSR, as Kazakhs were then called by Russians, within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, with Orenburg as capital, absorbing the territory of the Alash Autonomy. In 1925 it was renamed the Kazakh ASSR, the capital moved to Kyzylorda, and in 1929 to Alma-Ata.
kazakh-assr.r: The republic's leaders, such as First Secretary Filipp Goloshchekin from 1925, imposed Soviet rule on a mainly nomadic population. Collectivisation and forced settlement of nomads from 1929, combined with grain and livestock requisitioning, caused the famine of 1930 to 1933, the Asharshylyk, in which about 1.5 million people died and many fled to China and Central Asia.
kazakh-assr.e: Under the 1936 Soviet constitution the republic was raised to the status of a union republic, becoming the Kazakh SSR.

kingdom-of-loigis.t: Irish midland kingdom of the O'Mores, centred on the Rock of Dunamase, which fought the English until the plantation of Laois in 1556.
kingdom-of-loigis.o: The Loígis were a people of the Irish midlands in what is now County Laois, which takes its name from them. Tradition claimed they had won their lands as warriors serving the kings of the Kingdom of Leinster, and they formed a subject kingdom of Leinster from the early medieval period. From the 11th century their ruling family was the Uí Mórda, O'More.
kingdom-of-loigis.r: The kingdom was a land of bog, woodland and pasture, defended by its terrain. The Rock of Dunamase was a royal stronghold before the Anglo-Normans took it in the late 12th century and built a castle there. From the 14th century the O'Mores regained much of their territory, raiding the English Pale and living by cattle and the tribute of their followers.
kingdom-of-loigis.e: Under Mary I the English government confiscated Laois and Offaly and in 1556 created Queen's County, planted with English settlers around Maryborough, today Portlaoise. The O'Mores resisted for decades, notably under Rory Óg O'More, but their kingdom was ended.
kingdom-of-loigis.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-athamania.t: Small mountain kingdom on the borders of Epirus and Thessaly whose king Amynander played the Roman, Macedonian and Seleucid powers off against each other.
kingdom-of-athamania.o: The Athamanians were a people of the Pindus mountains around the upper Achelous, between Epirus, Thessaly and Aetolia. Little is known of their early history. Under Macedonian and Epirote dominance they had their own kings, and the kingdom became visible in the later 3rd century BCE, with its royal seat at Argithea.
kingdom-of-athamania.r: Athamania was a pastoral highland realm of villages and fortified hilltop towns. Its importance came from its position on routes between Thessaly and western Greece. King Amynander joined Rome against Philip V of Macedon in 200-197 BCE and acted as an intermediary, then sided with Antiochus III in 191 BCE.
kingdom-of-athamania.e: Philip V overran Athamania in 191 BCE and Amynander fled to Ambracia. With Aetolian help he recovered his kingdom in 189 BCE, but it disappears from the record soon after and was absorbed into its neighbours. Knowledge of it comes almost entirely from Polybius and Livy.

kingdom-of-fortriu.t: The leading Pictish kingdom, whose kings dominated northern Britain in the 7th to 9th centuries and whose heartland is now placed around Moray.
kingdom-of-fortriu.o: Fortriu takes its name from the Verturiones, listed by Ammianus Marcellinus in the 360s as one of the two main peoples of the Picts. In early Irish annals 'king of Fortriu' became the title of the most powerful Pictish rulers. Long located in Strathearn, it is now usually placed around Moray and Easter Ross, following work by Alex Woolf.
kingdom-of-fortriu.r: Kings of Fortriu built an over-kingship across Pictland. Bridei son of Beli destroyed the Northumbrian army at Dun Nechtain in 685, ending English dominance in the north. Óengus son of Fergus, from 729 to 761, defeated rivals and even campaigned against Dál Riata and Strathclyde. Major centres included the fortress of Burghead and the monastery of Portmahomack. Later kings such as Constantín son of Fergus also ruled Dál Riata.
kingdom-of-fortriu.e: In 839 a Viking army killed the king of Fortriu, Eóganán, with many nobles. In the aftermath Cináed mac Ailpín seized power, and Fortriu merged into the Gaelic kingdom of Alba around 900. The region later re-emerged as the province of Moray.

kingdom-of-holland.t: Napoleon's client kingdom for his brother Louis, who tried to rule as a Dutch king and was removed for defending his subjects.
kingdom-of-holland.o: In 1806 Napoleon replaced the Batavian Republic with a kingdom and installed his brother Louis Bonaparte as king. Louis learned Dutch, made Amsterdam the capital and turned its town hall into a royal palace.
kingdom-of-holland.r: Louis founded the Royal Institute and a national museum, introduced a civil code and took a sympathetic line toward Dutch interests. He resisted conscription and enforced the Continental System only loosely, which allowed smuggling with Britain. The economy suffered nonetheless, and the British landed on Walcheren in 1809.
kingdom-of-holland.e: Napoleon, angry at Louis's independence, forced him to abdicate in July 1810, and the kingdom was annexed to the French Empire. French rule ended in 1813, leading to the Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands.

kingdom-of-armenia-arsacid.t: Armenia under a branch of the Parthian Arsacid dynasty, which in the early 4th century made Christianity its state religion and later created the Armenian alphabet.
kingdom-of-armenia-arsacid.o: After the Artaxiad line ended, Armenia passed through years of rival kings installed by Rome and Parthia. The Arsacid branch took hold when Tiridates I, brother of the Parthian king, was crowned by Nero in Rome in 66 CE, a compromise that followed the Roman defeat at Rhandeia and let both empires claim a stake.
kingdom-of-armenia-arsacid.r: Kings ruled from Artaxata and later Vagharshapat over powerful hereditary noble houses such as the Mamikonians and Bagratunis. Tiridates III adopted Christianity around 301 through Gregory the Illuminator, and Etchmiadzin cathedral was founded. Around 405 Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet, launching a translation literature. Armenia was a battleground between the Roman Empire and the Sasanian Empire.
kingdom-of-armenia-arsacid.e: In 387 Rome and Persia partitioned Armenia, leaving most of it as a Sasanian client. In 428 Armenian nobles asked the Persian king to remove Artaxias IV, and the monarchy was abolished; the east became Persarmenia.

kingdom-of-wurttemberg.t: South German kingdom raised by Napoleon, which grew from a Protestant duchy into a constitutional monarchy of industry and engineering.
kingdom-of-wurttemberg.o: Elector Frederick of Württemberg allied with Napoleon and was rewarded with territory and the title of king, which he proclaimed on 1 January 1806. The new kingdom doubled in size with Catholic Upper Swabia, former imperial cities and church lands.
kingdom-of-wurttemberg.r: Frederick I ruled autocratically, but his son William I granted a constitution in 1819 and promoted agriculture, founding the Hohenheim academy and the Cannstatter Wasen festival. Württemberg had a strong tradition of skilled crafts, and by the late 19th century Stuttgart was a centre of engineering, with Gottlieb Daimler and Robert Bosch. It kept its own army and postal service in the German Empire.
kingdom-of-wurttemberg.e: Württemberg sided with Austria in 1866 but joined the German Empire in 1871. In November 1918 King William II abdicated, and the state became the Free People's State of Württemberg.

kingdom-of-arles.t: The united kingdom of Burgundy and Provence, stretching from Basel to the Mediterranean, that became the third crown of the Holy Roman emperors.
kingdom-of-arles.o: Around 933 Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy acquired the Kingdom of Lower Burgundy from Hugh of Arles, uniting the lands between the Jura and the Mediterranean. His son Conrad the Peaceful ruled from 937 to 993 under the protection of Otto I, who had taken the young king to his court.
kingdom-of-arles.r: Royal power was weak: counts, archbishops of Lyon, Vienne and Arles, and later lords such as the dauphins of Viennois and counts of Provence held real authority. When the childless Rudolf III died in 1032, the kingdom passed to Emperor Conrad II. Frederick Barbarossa was crowned at Arles in 1178 and Charles IV in 1365.
kingdom-of-arles.e: French influence grew steadily along the Rhône. In 1378 Charles IV made the French Dauphin, the future Charles VI, imperial vicar of the kingdom for life, effectively ending imperial rule there. Its lands were gradually absorbed by the Kingdom of France and Savoy.

kingdom-of-sardinia.t: An island kingdom created for Aragon in the 14th century that passed to Savoy in 1720 and became the core of the Kingdom of Italy.
kingdom-of-sardinia.o: In 1297 Pope Boniface VIII created a Kingdom of Sardinia and Corsica for James II of the Kingdom of Aragon. His son Alfonso conquered the Pisan parts of the island in 1323–1324, founding the kingdom in fact.
kingdom-of-sardinia.r: Aragonese rule met long resistance from the Judicate of Arborea, whose Eleonora issued the Carta de Logu law code; Arborea fell in 1420. Sardinia was then governed by viceroys at Cagliari, under Aragon and Habsburg Spain, with its own parliament. Austria took it in 1708, and in 1720 the Treaty of The Hague gave it to Victor Amadeus II of the Duchy of Savoy, who ruled from Turin.
kingdom-of-sardinia.e: The Savoy kingdom joined Piedmont, Savoy and Nice; the Perfect Fusion of 1847 unified it, and Charles Albert granted the Statuto in 1848. Under Victor Emmanuel II and Cavour it led Italian unification, becoming the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

kingdom-of-lysimachus.t: Short-lived Hellenistic kingdom of Alexander's general Lysimachus, ruling Thrace, Macedon and western Asia Minor before his death at Corupedium.
kingdom-of-lysimachus.o: After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Lysimachus received Thrace as his satrapy and spent years subduing the Odrysian Kingdom under Seuthes III. In 309 BCE he founded Lysimachia on the Gallipoli peninsula as his capital, and around 306 BCE he took the royal title with the other Successors.
kingdom-of-lysimachus.r: Lysimachus was a careful financier who built a large treasury and minted famous tetradrachms showing the deified Alexander. After the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE he gained most of western Asia Minor, refounding Ephesus. North of the Haemus he campaigned against the Getae, and around 292 BCE was captured by their king Dromichaetes. In 288 BCE he and Pyrrhus took Macedon, which he held alone from 285 BCE.
kingdom-of-lysimachus.e: Family murders, including the killing of his son Agathocles, alienated his supporters. Seleucus I defeated and killed him at Corupedium in 281 BCE. His realm broke up, and Thrace soon fell to the Celtic invasions and the Kingdom of Tylis.

kaitag-utsmiyate.t: A Dargin and Kumyk principality of Dagestan ruled by the utsmi, known today for its distinctive Kaitag embroideries.
kaitag-utsmiyate.o: Kaitag, in the foothills and mountains west of Derbent, was ruled by a dynasty bearing the title utsmi from at least the 15th century. Islam had become dominant there by then, after a long history of mixed beliefs; Arab geographers had earlier described the region as partly Christian and pagan.
kaitag-utsmiyate.r: The utsmi ruled through nobles over Dargin and Kumyk villages from Majalis and other seats, with free communities keeping their own customs. The economy combined farming, herding and slave raiding. Kaitag women produced silk embroideries with bold abstract designs. Utsmi Amir Hamza captured the German naturalist Samuel Gmelin, who died in captivity in 1774.
kaitag-utsmiyate.e: The utsmiyate was a vassal of the Safavid Empire for long periods and later allied with or resisted Russia. In 1820 the Russian Empire deposed the last utsmi and annexed Kaitag.

kingdom-of-bohemia.t: Central European kingdom centred on Prague, home of Charles IV's golden age and the Hussite revolution, and the crown at the heart of the Thirty Years War.
kingdom-of-bohemia.o: The Přemyslid dukes had ruled Bohemia since the 9th century, and some held a personal royal title. In 1198 Ottokar I was crowned king, and the Golden Bull of Sicily of 1212 made the title hereditary. The kingdom held a special place within the Holy Roman Empire, with its king among the electors.
kingdom-of-bohemia.r: Under Ottokar II and Charles IV of the Luxembourg dynasty, Prague became an imperial capital with a university founded in 1348. The Hussite movement after Jan Hus's execution in 1415 created a reformed church and defeated several crusades. The Lands of the Bohemian Crown included Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia. Silver from Kutná Hora funded the crown, and Czech and German speakers lived side by side.
kingdom-of-bohemia.e: The Habsburgs took the throne in 1526. The Defenestration of Prague in 1618 began the Thirty Years War, and defeat at the White Mountain in 1620 brought forced Catholicism and Habsburg absolutism. Bohemia stayed a Habsburg crown land until 1918, when it became the core of Czechoslovakia.

kingdom-of-the-isles.t: A Norse-Gaelic sea kingdom of Man and the Hebrides, ruled from the Isle of Man by the Crovan dynasty under Norwegian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-isles.o: Godred Crovan, a Norse-Gael who had fought at Stamford Bridge in 1066, seized the Isle of Man in 1079 after a battle at Sky Hill. His descendants ruled Man and the Hebrides, the Sudreys, as a kingdom under the nominal overlordship of Norway.
kingdom-of-the-isles.r: The kingdom was a maritime power of galleys and island fortresses, with Castle Rushen and the church at Rushen Abbey. Man's Tynwald assembly descends from its Norse institutions. Its kings intervened in Irish and Scottish affairs. Somerled's revolt in 1156 took the southern Hebrides, leaving the Crovan line with Man, Lewis and Skye.
kingdom-of-the-isles.e: After the Battle of Largs in 1263, Norway ceded Man and the Isles to the Kingdom of Scotland by the Treaty of Perth in 1266, the year after the last king, Magnus Olafsson, died. Man later came under English rule as the Lordship of Mann.

kingdom-of-jerusalem.t: The principal Crusader state, founded after the capture of Jerusalem in 1099 and ended with the fall of Acre in 1291.
kingdom-of-jerusalem.o: The First Crusade took Jerusalem in July 1099, massacring much of its population. Godfrey of Bouillon governed it as Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre, and on his death in 1100 his brother Baldwin I was crowned the first king. Over the next decades the Franks conquered the coastal cities with the help of Italian fleets.
kingdom-of-jerusalem.r: The king ruled with a High Court of barons, and great lordships such as Galilee, Jaffa and Oultrejordain held wide powers. The Templars and Hospitallers garrisoned castles, while Venetian, Genoese and Pisan communes controlled trade in Acre and Tyre. Most subjects were Muslims and Eastern Christians. Under Baldwin IV the kingdom held off Saladin, but in 1187 he destroyed its army at Hattin and took Jerusalem.
kingdom-of-jerusalem.e: The Third Crusade recovered the coast, and the kingdom continued from Acre. Frederick II regained Jerusalem by treaty in 1229, but it was lost for good in 1244. The Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil took Acre in May 1291, ending the kingdom; the title passed to the kings of Cyprus.

kingdom-of-kakheti.t: The eastern Georgian kingdom of Kakheti, a land of vineyards and silk routes that suffered terribly under Shah Abbas before uniting with Kartli in 1762.
kingdom-of-kakheti.o: In 1465, amid the disintegration of the Kingdom of Georgia, George I, a prince of the royal Bagratid house, made Kakheti a separate kingdom. Its independence was confirmed when Georgia split into three kingdoms in 1490. His line, a branch of the Bagratids, held the throne of Kakheti for almost three centuries.
kingdom-of-kakheti.r: Kakheti prospered on wine, silk and the caravan trade between Shirvan and Russia; King Levan built a royal residence at Gremi. The kings balanced between the Ottomans and the Safavid Empire. Teimuraz I's resistance provoked Shah Abbas I to devastate the country in 1616, deporting many thousands of Kakhetians to Iran; Teimuraz's mother Ketevan was martyred in 1624.
kingdom-of-kakheti.e: Kakheti endured Persian governors and Lezgin raids. Erekle II became king in 1744, and on his father Teimuraz II's death in 1762 he united Kakheti with Kartli as the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti.

karabakh-khanate.t: A khanate founded by Panah Ali Khan in Karabakh, whose fortress capital Shusha withstood Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar and became a cultural centre.
karabakh-khanate.o: After Nader Shah's death in 1747, Panah Ali Khan of the Javanshir tribe returned from exile and made himself khan of Karabakh. He built a series of fortresses and in the 1750s founded Shusha on a mountain plateau, while forcing the Armenian Melikdoms of Karabakh to accept his authority.
karabakh-khanate.r: The khanate ruled over Turkic tribal groups in the lowlands and Armenian villages in the highlands. Ibrahim Khalil Khan, from 1763, was a powerful ruler, and his vizier, the poet Molla Panah Vagif, shaped court culture. In 1795 Shusha withstood a siege by Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar, who in 1797 took the town but was murdered there.
karabakh-khanate.e: In 1805 Ibrahim Khalil Khan signed the Treaty of Kurekchay accepting Russian suzerainty. His son Mehdi Qoli Khan fled to Persia in 1822, and the Russian Empire abolished the khanate.

kingdom-of-salamis.t: The leading city-kingdom of ancient Cyprus, whose king Evagoras I united much of the island and defied the Persian Empire for a decade.
kingdom-of-salamis.o: Salamis was founded on the east coast of Cyprus in the 11th century BCE, succeeding nearby Enkomi as its harbour silted up. Greek tradition named Teucer, brother of Ajax, as its founder. Its royal tombs of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, with chariots and sacrificed horses, recall Homeric burial customs.
kingdom-of-salamis.r: The kings of Salamis were often the most powerful on Cyprus. Evelthon struck the island's first coins in the 6th century BCE, and Onesilus led the Cypriot revolt against Persia in 498 BCE. Evagoras I, who reigned from 411 to 374 BCE, promoted Greek culture, allied with Athens and fought the Achaemenid Empire until a negotiated peace in 380 BCE.
kingdom-of-salamis.e: The last king, Nicocreon, allied with Ptolemy I and died c. 310 BCE, and in 306 BCE Demetrius Poliorcetes won a great naval battle off Salamis. The kingdom then passed under the Ptolemaic Empire. Salamis remained a major city, renamed Constantia, until abandoned after the Arab raids of the 7th century CE.

komancza-republic.t: A tiny Ukrainian-oriented republic of Lemko villages in the Carpathians, which lasted from November 1918 to January 1919.
komancza-republic.o: When Austro-Hungarian rule collapsed in November 1918, Ukrainian-minded Lemkos in about thirty villages around Komancza, in the eastern Lemko region of Galicia, set up their own commissariat. Unlike the pro-Russian Lemko-Rusyn Republic further west, they aimed to join the West Ukrainian People's Republic.
komancza-republic.r: The republic was a local self-government led by a council and the Greek Catholic priest Pantaleimon Shpylka, with a small militia to keep order and guard against Polish units. It had little territory and no resources of its own, and it existed mainly to hold the area until it could be united with the Ukrainian state.
komancza-republic.e: In January 1919 Polish troops entered the area during the Polish-Ukrainian War and dissolved the republic. Its villages became part of the Second Polish Republic, and their Lemko inhabitants were deported in 1947.

kingdom-of-liaodong-206-bc.t: A remote north-eastern kingdom given to the deposed Yan king Han Guang in 206 BCE, who was killed within months for refusing to leave his old realm.
kingdom-of-liaodong-206-bc.o: Han Guang, once a commander sent north by Chen Sheng, had made himself king of Yan during the rising against the Qin dynasty. In Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE he was demoted to King of Liaodong, a distant territory beyond the Liao River with its capital at Wuzhong, while his general Zang Tu received Yan.
kingdom-of-liaodong-206-bc.r: Han Guang refused to give up Yan and move to Liaodong, so the kingdom hardly functioned as a separate state.
kingdom-of-liaodong-206-bc.e: Later in 206 BCE Zang Tu attacked and killed Han Guang at Wuzhong and annexed Liaodong to Yan (206 BC).

kingdom-of-isandra.t: A Betsileo kingdom of the southern Malagasy highlands, a strong regional power before its absorption by the Merina early in the 19th century.
kingdom-of-isandra.o: Isandra emerged in the 18th century as one of the four main Betsileo kingdoms of the southern highlands of Madagascar, west of the Kingdom of Lalangina. Its dynasty, like other Betsileo houses, claimed descent from noble immigrants, and much of its history survives only in oral tradition.
kingdom-of-isandra.r: Isandra's kings ruled through local lords over rice-farming communities in highland valleys and drew prestige from ancestral tombs and royal rituals. The kingdom was considered among the strongest of the Betsileo states and fought its neighbours for land, cattle and captives.
kingdom-of-isandra.e: Around 1811 the Merina Kingdom absorbed Isandra together with the other Betsileo kingdoms, partly through alliances with local nobles. Its territory became part of the Merina province of Betsileo.

kingdom-of-leinster.t: Province-kingdom of south-east Ireland, whose exiled king Diarmait Mac Murchada invited the Anglo-Normans in and so opened eight centuries of English involvement.
kingdom-of-leinster.o: The Laigin, the people of Leinster, appear in the earliest Irish traditions as a major power whose kings once held the midlands and Tara. From the 5th century the rising Uí Néill drove them south, and Leinster settled into an over-kingdom covering most of the south-east, contested between dynasties such as the Uí Dúnlainge in the north and the Ui Chennselaig in the south.
kingdom-of-leinster.r: Kings ruled through tribute and alliances with subject peoples, and great monasteries such as Kildare, Glendalough and Ferns flourished. Brandub mac Echach defeated the high king at Dún Bolg in 598. Viking Dublin lay within Leinster, and from the 11th century its kings sought to control it; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, who died in 1072, ruled Dublin and nearly became high king.
kingdom-of-leinster.e: In 1166 Diarmait Mac Murchada was expelled and sought help from Henry II. Anglo-Norman knights led by Strongbow, who married Diarmait's daughter Aoife, took Wexford, Waterford and Dublin. On Diarmait's death in 1171 Strongbow claimed Leinster, and Henry II's arrival brought it under the English crown.

kingdom-of-kanongesha.t: The Ndembu Lunda chiefdom of the upper Zambezi watershed, an outpost of Lunda kingship later made famous by anthropological studies of its rituals.
kingdom-of-kanongesha.o: The Kanongesha title was established in the 18th century by Lunda nobles who moved south-west from the court of the Lunda Empire into the headwaters of the Zambezi and Kabompo rivers. They settled among local peoples who became known as the Ndembu or Southern Lunda.
kingdom-of-kanongesha.r: The Kanongesha held senior rank over Ndembu sub-chiefs, but his power was limited and largely ritual, rooted in Lunda titles, perpetual kinship between offices, and ties to the Mwata Yamvo. Villages farmed cassava and hunted, and in the 19th century the area supplied slaves, ivory and beeswax to Ovimbundu and Chokwe traders.
kingdom-of-kanongesha.e: Colonial boundaries drawn in the early 20th century divided the Ndembu between Northern Rhodesia, Portuguese Angola and the Belgian Congo. The chieftaincy continues in Zambia, and Victor Turner's studies of Ndembu ritual in the 1950s made it well known.

kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.t: The kingdom of Provence founded by Boso in 879, the first realm in the Carolingian West to elect a king from outside the Carolingian family.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.o: In 879, after the death of Louis the Stammerer, bishops and nobles meeting at Mantaille elected Boso, a brother-in-law of Charles the Bald, as king of the lands around Vienne, Lyon and Provence. The Carolingian kings besieged Vienne in 880–882, but Boso's family kept control of the Rhône valley.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.r: The kingdom was a loose union of counties along the Rhône and in Provence, governed from Vienne with strong support from the bishops. Boso's son Louis the Blind was crowned emperor in Rome in 901 but was captured and blinded by Berengar of Italy in 905. Afterwards real power lay with his kinsman Hugh of Arles.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.e: Hugh of Arles, busy with his ambitions as king of Italy, gave up his claims to Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy around 933. The two Burgundian kingdoms were then united as the Kingdom of Arles, which later passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-awsan.t: A short-lived south Arabian kingdom in Wadi Markha whose power over the coast was broken by Saba in the 7th century BCE.
kingdom-of-awsan.o: Awsan lay in Wadi Markha, south-west of the incense valleys, with its capital at Hagar Yahirr. Known mainly from Sabaean inscriptions, it seems to have risen in the 8th century BCE and controlled territory towards the Gulf of Aden coast and its harbours.
kingdom-of-awsan.r: Very little is known of its internal life. Its wealth probably came from coastal trade and the routes linking the Arabian Sea with the inland incense kingdoms. Later Awsanite inscriptions show kings who were honoured as gods after death, an unusual practice in south Arabia.
kingdom-of-awsan.e: The Sabaean ruler Karib'il Watar destroyed Awsan in the 7th century BCE, according to his great inscription at Sirwah, killing thousands and handing its lands to the Kingdom of Saba and its allies. A smaller Awsan reappeared later, and the Greek name of the Ausanitic coast of East Africa recalls it.

kingdom-of-romania.t: Romanian monarchy that doubled its territory after the First World War as Greater Romania, then fell to dictatorship, war and a communist takeover.
kingdom-of-romania.o: Romania won independence at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and in 1881 Prince Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was crowned king. The kingdom inherited the constitution of 1866 and the territory of the United Principalities, with Northern Dobruja added in 1878. It gained Southern Dobruja from Bulgaria in the Second Balkan War of 1913.
kingdom-of-romania.r: Before 1914 Romania was a constitutional monarchy run by landowners, exporting grain and oil from Ploiești, and a great peasant revolt in 1907 was harshly put down. In 1918 Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transylvania joined, creating Greater Romania. Land reform and the 1923 constitution followed, but the interwar years saw the fascist Iron Guard and Carol II's royal dictatorship from 1938.
kingdom-of-romania.e: In 1940 Romania lost Bessarabia and northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union and northern Transylvania to Hungary. Ion Antonescu led it into war as an Axis ally until King Michael's coup of August 1944. Under Soviet pressure the communists took power, and Michael was forced to abdicate on 30 December 1947.

khamag-mongol.t: The 12th-century confederation of Mongol clans in the Onon and Kherlen valleys, out of which Temüjin built the Mongol Empire.
khamag-mongol.o: Mongol clans of the Onon and Kherlen river valleys in north-eastern Mongolia united in the early 12th century under Khabul Khan, an ancestor of Genghis Khan, who is said to have defied the Jin dynasty (1115-1234). The name means 'All the Mongols'.
khamag-mongol.r: The confederation was a loose alliance of Borjigin, Tayichiud and other clans, choosing khans at assemblies. Its second khan, Ambaghai, was handed over by the Tatars to the Jin and executed; his successor Hotula Khan fought the Tatars, but after him the khanship lapsed and clans feuded, as with Yesügei, father of Temüjin, and the Tayichiud.
khamag-mongol.e: Temüjin gathered followers in the 1180s and was acclaimed khan of the Mongols, then defeated the Tatars, Keraites and Naimans. In 1206 an assembly on the Onon proclaimed him Genghis Khan, turning the confederation into the Mongol Empire.

kuba-kingdom.t: A Bushong-led kingdom of the Kasai, famous for its royal portrait statues, raffia velvet textiles and long oral history of kings.
kuba-kingdom.o: Bushong tradition credits Shyaam a Mbul a Ngoong with founding the kingdom around 1625, uniting chiefdoms between the Kasai and Sankuru rivers. He is remembered as a culture hero who brought new crops, including maize, tobacco and cassava, from the west, together with new political institutions.
kuba-kingdom.r: The king (nyimi) ruled from the capital Nsheng with an elaborate council of titled officials, and the court sponsored an exceptional art tradition: wooden ndop statues commemorating each king, carved cups, masks and embroidered raffia cloth. Agriculture and trade in raffia and camwood supported dense villages. Kuba oral history was studied in detail by the historian Jan Vansina.
kuba-kingdom.e: In 1899 Zappo Zap raiders working for the Congo Free State sacked Nsheng, and Belgian administration followed, though the kingship continued under colonial rule. The Kuba remain known worldwide for their art, and the nyimi is still a traditional ruler in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

kingdom-of-spain.t: Spain's present parliamentary monarchy, built through the peaceful transition from Franco's dictatorship to democracy.
kingdom-of-spain.o: Two days after Franco's death, Juan Carlos I was proclaimed king on 22 November 1975, ending Francoist Spain. With Prime Minister Adolfo Suárez he dismantled the dictatorship: the Law for Political Reform of 1976, free elections in June 1977 and the Constitution of 1978, approved by referendum.
kingdom-of-spain.r: Spain became a parliamentary monarchy divided into 17 autonomous communities, recognising Catalan, Basque and Galician identities. The king's stand against the coup attempt of 23 February 1981 secured democracy. Felipe González's Socialists governed from 1982 to 1996, joining NATO and the European Economic Community in 1986. The 1992 Barcelona Olympics and Seville Expo marked modernisation.
kingdom-of-spain.e: Spain remains a parliamentary monarchy. ETA declared an end to violence in 2011, Felipe VI succeeded his father in 2014, and the Catalan independence crisis of 2017 tested the constitutional order.

kingdom-of-sicily.t: Southern Italy's Norman kingdom, famed for its Arab-Byzantine-Latin court culture, which after 1282 continued as the island realm of Sicily until 1816.
kingdom-of-sicily.o: Roger II, ruler of the County of Sicily and the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria, obtained a royal title from Antipope Anacletus II and was crowned in Palermo on Christmas Day 1130. The kingdom united Sicily and the Italian south, including the former principalities of Capua and Bari.
kingdom-of-sicily.r: The Norman kings ran a centralised state with Arabic, Greek and Latin chanceries, and built the Palatine Chapel, Cefalù and Monreale. Through marriage it passed to the Hohenstaufen: Frederick II issued the Constitutions of Melfi in 1231. Charles of Anjou took it in 1266, but the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 brought Peter III of Aragon to the island, leaving the mainland as the Kingdom of Naples.
kingdom-of-sicily.e: The island kingdom passed to Aragon and Habsburg Spain under viceroys, then briefly to Savoy in 1713, to Austria in 1720 and to the Bourbons in 1735. In 1816 Ferdinand merged it with Naples to form the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
