kirghiz-assr.t: The autonomous Soviet republic that gave the Kyrgyz their first modern territorial state, the forerunner of today's Kyrgyzstan.
kirghiz-assr.o: In the national delimitation of 1924 the Kyrgyz lands of the Turkestan ASSR were made the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. In 1925 it was renamed the Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast and in 1926 raised to an Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, with its capital at Pishpek, renamed Frunze.
kirghiz-assr.r: The republic introduced Soviet administration, schools and a written Kyrgyz language, first in Arabic and then Latin script. Collectivisation and settlement of nomadic herders from 1929 brought hardship and revolt, and many fled to China. Leading Kyrgyz communists such as Yusup Abdrakhmanov were purged in the 1930s.
kirghiz-assr.e: Under the 1936 Soviet constitution the republic became a union republic, the Kirghiz SSR.

kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.t: The realm created by Alfred the Great and his son Edward, joining Wessex and English Mercia into the direct ancestor of the Kingdom of England.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.o: In 886 Alfred occupied London and, according to the Chronicle, all the English not under the Danes submitted to him. His charters began to use the title king of the Anglo-Saxons, uniting the Kingdom of Wessex with western Mercia under Aethelred, Lord of the Mercians, who married Alfred's daughter Aethelflaed.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.r: The kingdom was defended by burhs and a reorganised army. Alfred issued a law code and sponsored translations of Latin works into English. Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed reconquered the southern Danelaw, including the Five Boroughs and Danish East Anglia, between 910 and 920.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.e: After Aethelflaed's death Edward absorbed Mercia in 918. In 927 his son Aethelstan took York and received the submission of northern rulers, becoming the first king of the Kingdom of England.

kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.t: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, held by the Zhao general Sima Ang until he surrendered to Liu Bang a year later.
kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.o: After the fall of the Qin dynasty, Xiang Yu divided the empire into eighteen kingdoms in 206 BCE. Sima Ang, a general of the revived state of Zhao who had captured the Henei region, was made King of Yin, ruling from Zhaoge in northern Henan, the old Shang capital area.
kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.r: The kingdom was a military holding with no time to develop institutions of its own. It covered the Henei commandery north of the Yellow River and served as a buffer between the kingdoms around Luoyang and those of Zhao.
kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.e: In 205 BCE, as Liu Bang advanced east from the Kingdom of Han (206 BC), Sima Ang was captured or surrendered, and his realm became the Henei commandery of Han. Sima Ang was later claimed as an ancestor of the Sima family who founded the Western Jin.

kingdom-of-prilep.t: Western Macedonian realm of King Vukašin and his son Marko, whose life as an Ottoman vassal inspired the hero of South Slav epic poetry.
kingdom-of-prilep.o: Vukašin Mrnjavčević, a Serbian noble, was crowned king in 1365 as co-ruler with Emperor Uroš V of the Serbian Empire, ruling lands in western Macedonia from Prilep. With his brother Jovan Uglješa of the Despotate of Serres he led the campaign against the Ottomans in 1371.
kingdom-of-prilep.r: After Vukašin was killed at the Maritsa in 1371, his son Marko inherited the royal title and a much smaller realm around Prilep, Ohrid and the Pelagonian plain. Marko became an Ottoman vassal, minted coins and founded the Marko's Monastery near Skopje. His neighbours took Ohrid and other lands.
kingdom-of-prilep.e: Marko died fighting for the Ottomans against Mircea the Elder of Wallachia at Rovine in 1395, and his lands were annexed by the Ottomans. As Kraljević Marko, he became the best-loved hero of Serbian, Macedonian and Bulgarian folk epic.

kos.t: Dorian island state off Anatolia, birthplace of Hippocrates and home of the famous healing sanctuary of Asclepius.
kos.o: Kos, an island off the Carian coast near Halicarnassus, was settled from the Bronze Age, with Mycenaean remains. Dorian Greeks occupied it in the early Iron Age, and it joined the Dorian Hexapolis with Knidos, Halicarnassus and the Rhodian cities. Its first chief town was Astypalaia in the south-west.
kos.r: Kos was known for wine and fine translucent silk cloth. Hippocrates was born there c. 460 BCE and the Coan school of medicine bears his name. After Persian rule the island joined the Delian League. In 366 BCE the Coans founded a new capital on the north-east tip, and the Asclepieion was later built nearby.
kos.e: Kos was a favoured base of the Ptolemaic Empire, where Ptolemy II was born and the poet Philitas taught. It later allied with Rome and became part of the province of Asia in 129 BCE, remaining a free city prized for its sanctuary.

kingdom-of-zimbabwe.t: The builders of Great Zimbabwe, whose dry-stone city controlled the gold trade of the southern African plateau for over two centuries.
kingdom-of-zimbabwe.o: After the decline of the Kingdom of Mapungubwe in the early 13th century, a Shona-speaking elite on the Zimbabwe plateau took over the routes carrying gold and ivory to the coast. Building at Great Zimbabwe began with walls on the Hill Complex and grew into the largest stone-built settlement in sub-Saharan Africa south of Ethiopia.
kingdom-of-zimbabwe.r: Kings ruled from the Hill Complex, while the Great Enclosure, with its conical tower and walls up to 11 metres high, probably served royal or ritual purposes. The economy rested on cattle, farming and gold mined across the plateau and sent via Sofala to Kilwa. Finds include soapstone bird carvings, Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery and a Kilwa copper coin. The city may have held 10,000 to 18,000 people.
kingdom-of-zimbabwe.e: Great Zimbabwe declined from the mid-15th century, perhaps through overgrazing, exhausted resources and a northward shift of the gold trade. Its heirs were the Mutapa state in the north and the Kingdom of Butua at Khami in the south-west. The ruins gave modern Zimbabwe its name and its national emblem, the Zimbabwe bird.

kimek-khanate.t: A confederation of Turkic tribes on the Irtysh whose western Kipchak wing became the Cumans, masters of the western steppe.
kimek-khanate.o: The Kimek confederation formed in the mid-8th century on the Irtysh River from tribes, including the Imek and Kipchaks, who left the Mongolian steppe as the Uyghur Khaganate rose. By the 9th century their ruler held the title khagan.
kimek-khanate.r: Arab and Persian geographers such as Gardizi and the Hudud al-Alam describe the Kimek as a confederation of seven tribes, pastoral but with towns along the Irtysh, with Imakiya as the ruler's seat. They traded furs and slaves south to the Samanid Empire and the Oghuz. Religion included Tengrism and Manichaean and Buddhist influences, and they burned their dead.
kimek-khanate.e: In the early 11th century the confederation broke up as the Kipchaks, its western component, moved west across the steppe. Pressure from the Qai and other peoples of the east also played a part. The Kipchaks became the Cumans, who dominated the Pontic steppe until the Mongol conquest.

kingdom-of-pontus.t: Pontus, a Hellenistic kingdom on the Black Sea whose king Mithridates VI fought Rome in three wars and nearly drove it from Asia.
kingdom-of-pontus.o: Mithridates I Ktistes, a noble of Persian descent, fled the wars of Alexander's successors and seized lands in north-eastern Anatolia. He took the title king in 281 BCE, with his capital at Amaseia, where royal tombs are cut into the cliffs. Pharnaces I captured Sinope in 183 BCE and made it the capital.
kingdom-of-pontus.r: The kings combined Persian court traditions with Greek city culture, ruling over Greek ports and rural temple estates. Pontus was rich in metals, timber and grain. Mithridates VI extended his rule around the Black Sea and in 88 BCE ordered the massacre of Romans and Italians in Asia.
kingdom-of-pontus.e: Mithridates VI fought Sulla, Lucullus and Pompey in three wars. Defeated, he died at Panticapaeum in 63 BCE, and Pompey divided Pontus between Roman provinces and client kings, later including Polemonid Pontus.

kingdom-of-hermopolis.t: A short-lived Middle Egyptian kingdom whose king Nimlot defied, then surrendered to, the Kushite conqueror Piye.
kingdom-of-hermopolis.o: As the Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt fragmented in the 8th century BCE, Hermopolis, the cult centre of the god Thoth, became the seat of an independent local king. Its ruler Nimlot (Namart), probably of Libyan descent, held the region of Middle Egypt around the city by about 750 BCE.
kingdom-of-hermopolis.r: Almost all that is known comes from the Victory Stela of Piye. Nimlot first acknowledged Kushite overlordship, then joined the coalition of Tefnakht of Sais, which brought on a Kushite siege. After months of siege his queen pleaded with Piye's women, and Nimlot surrendered his treasures and horses; Piye, a lover of horses, was angered to find them starving.
kingdom-of-hermopolis.e: Nimlot was allowed to keep his throne as a vassal of the Kushite Empire after about 728 BCE, but the kingdom vanishes from the record soon after.

kingdom-of-paris.t: Merovingian kingdom centred on Paris, created when Clovis' realm was divided among his sons in 511.
kingdom-of-paris.o: On the death of Clovis in 511 the Kingdom of the Franks was shared among his four sons. Childebert I received the lands around Paris, together with the Channel coast and later parts of Aquitaine and Burgundy.
kingdom-of-paris.r: Childebert ruled for nearly fifty years, campaigning against the Kingdom of the Burgundians and the Visigoths in Spain, from where he brought back relics of Saint Vincent. For them he founded the abbey later called Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He joined his brother Chlothar I in murdering their nephews, the sons of Chlodomer of Orléans.
kingdom-of-paris.e: Childebert died without sons in 558, and Chlothar I briefly reunited the Frankish lands. In 561 Paris passed to Chlothar's son Charibert I, and after Charibert's death in 567 his kingdom was divided among his brothers, with Paris shared between them.

kingdom-of-portugal.t: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, which fixed its borders by 1249, led the age of oceanic exploration and lasted until the revolution of 1910.
kingdom-of-portugal.o: The County of Portugal, a fief of León, passed to Afonso Henriques, who styled himself king after his victory at Ourique in 1139. León recognised him at Zamora in 1143 and the papacy in 1179. With crusader help he took Lisbon in 1147, and Afonso III completed the conquest of the Algarve in 1249.
kingdom-of-portugal.r: Portugal was a Catholic monarchy with Cortes, military orders and a strong maritime economy. After the victory of Aljubarrota in 1385, John I founded the Aviz dynasty, whose princes launched the voyages that created the Portuguese Empire. Pepper, Brazilian sugar and gold financed the crown. Manuel I ruled at the peak of the spice trade.
kingdom-of-portugal.e: The kingdom fell under Spanish kings in the Iberian Union from 1580 to 1640, then revived under the Braganzas. After the 1908 assassination of Carlos I, a revolution on 5 October 1910 ended the monarchy and created the First Portuguese Republic.

cr.a: Tonyjeff, based on ancient national symbol.

kingdom-of-judah.t: The southern Kingdom of Judah, ruled from Jerusalem by the House of David, whose fall and exile shaped the Hebrew Bible.
kingdom-of-judah.o: Judah emerged as a separate kingdom c. 930 BCE when Solomon's son Rehoboam kept only the southern tribes after the split of the United Kingdom of Israel. It remained smaller and poorer than the Kingdom of Israel, but its capital Jerusalem held the temple of Yahweh.
kingdom-of-judah.r: Kings of the line of David ruled throughout. Hezekiah dug the Siloam tunnel and survived Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BCE, though Lachish fell. Josiah centralised worship in Jerusalem. Prophets such as Isaiah and Jeremiah were active, and inscriptions such as the Lachish letters reveal daily administration.
kingdom-of-judah.e: Judah became a vassal of the Chaldean Empire. After revolts, Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 BCE and deported King Zedekiah and the elite to Babylon. The exile shaped Judaism, and later Yehud Medinata arose under Persian rule.

kingdom-of-ait-abbas.t: A Kabyle mountain kingdom in the Bibans, ruled from the fortress of Kalâa, that long resisted Ottoman Algiers and later led the 1871 Mokrani revolt.
kingdom-of-ait-abbas.o: After Spain took Bejaia in 1510, Hafsid-era notables of the region founded a principality in the Bibans mountains of Lesser Kabylia, with its stronghold at the Kalâa of the Ait Abbas. It controlled the Iron Gates pass on the route between Algiers and Constantine.
kingdom-of-ait-abbas.r: The kingdom's rulers drew on Kabyle tribal levies armed with firearms and on the craft workshops of the Kalâa. Abd al-Aziz, its most famous ruler, alternately allied with and fought the Regency of Algiers and the rival Kingdom of Kuku, and fell in battle against the Ottomans around 1559. Later the ruling family became known as the Mokrani.
kingdom-of-ait-abbas.e: The Mokrani accommodated Ottoman and then French rule as local lords. In 1871 Mohamed El Mokrani led a great uprising against French Algeria; its defeat in 1872 brought confiscations and the end of the family's power.

kingdom-of-ui-maine.t: Kingdom of the O'Kellys in east Galway and south Roscommon, one of the largest subject kingdoms of Connacht, which lasted until the Composition of 1585.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.o: The Uí Maine claimed descent from Maine Mór, said to have won lands west of the Shannon in the 5th century. By the early medieval period they held a large kingdom in what is now east County Galway and south Roscommon, within the over-kingdom of the Kingdom of Connacht, with privileges of their own.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.r: Their kings, from the 10th century the Ua Cellaig, O'Kelly, served the kings of Connacht in war and sometimes contested the kingship. Tadhg Mór Ua Cellaig fell fighting for Brian Bóruma at Clontarf in 1014. The O'Kellys were famous patrons of learning: Uilliam Buidhe Ó Ceallaigh held a great Christmas feast for the poets of Ireland in 1351, and the Book of Uí Maine was compiled for the family.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.e: Anglo-Norman lords, especially the de Burghs, took part of Uí Maine in the 13th century, but the O'Kellys kept much of it. Under the Composition of Connacht in 1585 their lordship was converted into crown tenure, ending the kingdom's independent status.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.t: The Piast kingdom of Poland, which fragmented into rival duchies, was reunited in 1320 and flourished under Casimir the Great.
kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.o: Boleslaw I the Brave was crowned king in 1025, turning the Duchy of Poland into a kingdom. His son Mieszko II faced invasion and revolt, and in the 1030s a pagan uprising and a Bohemian raid devastated Greater Poland. Casimir I the Restorer rebuilt the state and made Krakow its main seat.
kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.r: Under the testament of Boleslaw III in 1138 the realm was divided among his sons, with the senior duke ruling Krakow. For almost two centuries Poland was a patchwork of duchies, settled by German colonists and towns under German law and hit by the Mongols in 1241. The church, with the archbishopric of Gniezno, held it together.
kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.e: Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high reunited much of the country and was crowned in 1320. His son Casimir III the Great codified law, founded the University of Krakow in 1364 and added Red Ruthenia. After Louis of Hungary, his daughter Jadwiga married Jogaila of Lithuania under the Union of Krewo of 1385, beginning the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569).

kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.t: The breakaway Hellenistic kingdom of Magas, stepson of Ptolemy I, who ruled Cyrenaica independently of Egypt.
kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.o: Magas, son of Ptolemy I's queen Berenice I by an earlier marriage, became governor of Cyrene around 300 BCE after a revolt there was suppressed. On the death of his stepfather he grew restive and around 276 BCE proclaimed himself king, breaking away from the Ptolemaic Empire.
kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.r: Magas married Apama, daughter of the Seleucid king Antiochus I, and in alliance with the Seleucids marched on Egypt in the mid-270s BCE, but was forced back by a Libyan revolt. He ruled Cyrene and the Pentapolis for decades, minting his own coins. Later he made peace with his half-brother Ptolemy II and betrothed his daughter Berenice to the heir, the future Ptolemy III.
kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.e: After Magas died around 250 BCE, Apama invited Demetrius the Fair to marry Berenice and rule, but Berenice had him killed. She then married Ptolemy III in 246 BCE, reuniting Cyrene with Egypt, and became the queen Berenice II.

kholodny-yar-republic.t: A partisan self-governing district in the forests of central Ukraine, which held out against Whites and Bolsheviks from 1919 to 1922.
kholodny-yar-republic.o: Kholodny Yar is a forested ravine area near Chyhyryn, rich in memories of the Cossack Hetmanate and the 18th-century haidamaka rebels. In 1919 villagers around the Motronynskyi Monastery formed a self-defence force under Vasyl Chuchupak, which took control of some twenty villages and declared loyalty to the Ukrainian People's Republic.
kholodny-yar-republic.r: The district was governed by village councils and its partisan otamans, with the monastery as headquarters. The insurgents fought Denikin's Whites and then the Red Army, raiding railways and Soviet detachments, and kept contact with the exiled government of the Ukrainian People's Republic. Its forces numbered from a few hundred to several thousand fighters.
kholodny-yar-republic.e: Vasyl Chuchupak was killed in 1920, and Soviet campaigns slowly broke the resistance. In 1922 the Cheka lured several leading otamans to a fake meeting and arrested them, ending organised resistance. The story was later told in Yuri Horlis-Horsky's memoir Kholodny Yar.

kingdom-of-dalmatia.t: Austrian crown land along the Adriatic coast, where Croatian and Italian national movements competed for a century before it joined Yugoslavia.
kingdom-of-dalmatia.o: Austria had taken Venetian Dalmatia in 1797 but lost it to Napoleon. After the Congress of Vienna it recovered the coast, now including the former Republic of Ragusa and the Bay of Kotor, and organised it in 1815 as the Kingdom of Dalmatia, a crown land of the Austrian Empire governed from Zara.
kingdom-of-dalmatia.r: Dalmatia was poor and rural, living from wine, olive oil, fishing and seafaring, and many emigrated to the Americas. Its diet, created in 1861, was at first dominated by the Italian-speaking Autonomist Party, but the Croatian People's Party won control in 1870. Croats sought union with Croatia-Slavonia, which Vienna refused. The Austrian navy defeated Italy off Lissa in 1866.
kingdom-of-dalmatia.e: In October 1918 Dalmatia joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, and then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Zara and some islands passed to Italy under the Treaty of Rapallo in 1920, returning to Yugoslavia after 1945.

kingdom-of-khwarazm.t: The ancient oasis kingdom of the lower Amu Darya, a land of canals and fortified towns that kept its own kings and Iranian culture for eight centuries.
kingdom-of-khwarazm.o: Khwarazm, or Chorasmia, grew from irrigation farming on the Amu Darya delta south of the Aral Sea. It appears as a province of the Achaemenid Empire under Darius I and seems to have regained independence by the 4th century BCE, when its king Pharasmanes offered alliance to Alexander the Great in 328 BCE.
kingdom-of-khwarazm.r: Its economy rested on a dense canal network feeding wheat, cotton, vines and orchards, protected by walled settlements and fortresses such as Toprak-Kala, Koy-Krylgan-Kala and Ayaz-Kala. Kings issued their own silver coinage, and later Khwarazmian tradition traced their line to the hero Siyavush. Zoroastrian practice included bone burial in ossuaries, and the Khwarazmian language had its own Aramaic-derived script.
kingdom-of-khwarazm.e: In the early 4th century CE the ancient royal house gave way to the Afrighid Khwarazm dynasty, which al-Biruni dates to 305. The Kushan Empire and Sasanians may have held loose overlordship at times. Khwarazm's distinct language and calendar survived until the Mongol era.

kingdom-of-paphos.t: Ancient Cypriot kingdom centred on the great sanctuary of Aphrodite, whose kings served as the goddess's high priests for some eight centuries.
kingdom-of-paphos.o: Paphos grew at Palaepaphos, modern Kouklia, a Late Bronze Age town in south-west Cyprus. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE Aegean settlers arrived, and Greek legend credited Agapenor of Tegea with founding the city after the Trojan War. An inscription of the 11th century BCE shows Greek already written there.
kingdom-of-paphos.r: Its kings combined royal power with the priesthood of the Paphian goddess, later identified with Aphrodite, whose open-air sanctuary with a conical stone drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean. Paphos used the Cypriot syllabary for Greek and struck its own coins. It paid tribute to Assyria and later to the Achaemenid Empire, and joined the revolt against Persia in 498 BCE.
kingdom-of-paphos.e: The last king, Nicocles, founded the harbour city of Nea Paphos, which became the capital of Ptolemaic and Roman Cyprus. The kingdom was abolished when Ptolemy I took the island, by c. 306 BCE, but the sanctuary of Aphrodite flourished into late antiquity.

kingdom-of-alashiya.t: Late Bronze Age kingdom on Cyprus whose rulers traded copper with Egypt, the Hittites and Ugarit, as revealed by the Amarna letters.
kingdom-of-alashiya.o: Alashiya appears in Near Eastern texts from the 18th century BCE as a source of copper, and most scholars identify it with Cyprus or part of it. Cyprus developed urban centres in the Late Cypriot period from c. 1650 BCE, including Enkomi on the east coast, Kalavasos and Alassa, though which was the royal seat is uncertain.
kingdom-of-alashiya.r: The king of Alashiya corresponded with Pharaoh Akhenaten as a 'brother' in the Amarna letters, sending copper ingots in return for silver, oil and luxury goods. Clay analysis shows these letters were made on Cyprus. Enkomi had copper workshops and ashlar buildings, and the island used the Cypro-Minoan script. The Hittite Empire claimed overlordship in the 13th century BCE.
kingdom-of-alashiya.e: Letters from Ugarit describe enemy ships threatening Alashiya c. 1200 BCE, and Suppiluliuma II fought naval battles off its coast. In the following century Cypriot towns declined or moved, Aegean settlers arrived, and the island reorganised into the Iron Age kingdoms such as Salamis, Paphos and Kition.

kangju.t: A long-lived nomad kingdom of the middle Syr Darya, a rival of the Wusun and Dayuan that dominated the steppe north of Sogdiana for six centuries.
kangju.o: Kangju first appears in the account of the Han envoy Zhang Qian, who passed through around 128 BCE and reported a nomadic state north-west of Dayuan with perhaps 120,000 archers. Its people were Iranian-speaking pastoralists on the middle Syr Darya and the Talas and Chu valleys, part of the wider Saka world.
kangju.r: The king ruled from a winter seat called Beitian and summered in the steppe, with five lesser kings beneath him, according to the Han histories. Kangju controlled routes between the steppe, Sogdiana and the Kingdom of Dayuan, and at times held Sogdian towns as dependencies. In 36 BCE it sheltered the Xiongnu chanyu Zhizhi, whom a Han army killed there.
kangju.e: Kangju is linked by archaeologists to the Kaunchi and Otrar-Karatau cultures. It weakened under pressure from the Kidarite Kingdom, Hephthalites and Rouran, and by the 5th century its name passed to Sogdiana itself, 'Kang' being the later Chinese name for Samarkand.

kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.t: A northern kingdom of the Chu-Han war, first the place of exile for the Zhao king Zhao Xie and then the fief of Chen Yu, overrun by Han Xin.
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.o: In 206 BCE Xiang Yu moved Zhao Xie, the restored king of Zhao, north to the frontier region of Dai, with its capital at Dai near modern Yuxian, Hebei, so that Zhang Er could rule the Zhao heartland as the Kingdom of Changshan.
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.r: In 205 BCE Chen Yu drove out Zhang Er and brought Zhao Xie back to Zhao; in thanks, Zhao Xie made Chen Yu King of Dai. Chen Yu stayed in Zhao as chief minister and governed Dai through his deputy Xia Yue. The kingdom was a frontier zone of herding and farming facing the Xiongnu.
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.e: In 205 BCE Han Xin defeated and captured Xia Yue, and in 204 BCE he destroyed the Zhao army at Jingxing, where Chen Yu was killed. Dai passed to the Han Dynasty and later became a Han kingdom held by Liu Bang's son, the future Emperor Wen.

kingdom-of-hazor.t: Hazor, the largest Canaanite city, which traded with Mari and Babylon and which the Bible calls the head of all those kingdoms.
kingdom-of-hazor.o: Hazor grew north of the Sea of Galilee on the road from Egypt to Syria. In the 18th century BCE a huge lower city was added to the old mound, creating a city of some 80 hectares. It is the only Canaanite city named in the Mari letters, which mention tin sent to its king.
kingdom-of-hazor.r: Its kings ruled from a palace on the upper city with basalt orthostats and temples in Syrian style, and controlled much of northern Canaan. In the Amarna age King Abdi-Tirshi was a vassal of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, though neighbours accused him of disloyalty. Excavations by Yigael Yadin and Amnon Ben-Tor uncovered statues and cuneiform tablets.
kingdom-of-hazor.e: In the 13th century BCE the Canaanite city was destroyed by fire, and its statues deliberately defaced. The Book of Joshua credits its destruction to the Israelites; scholars still debate who was responsible. A smaller fortified town later belonged to the Kingdom of Israel.

kingdom-of-desmond.t: The MacCarthy kingdom of South Munster, created when Munster was split in 1118 and surviving in parts until the end of the 16th century.
kingdom-of-desmond.o: The Treaty of Glanmire in 1118 divided Munster, giving the south, Deasmumu, to the MacCarthys, heirs of the Eoganacht kings of Cashel. Cormac MacCarthy ruled from Cork and built Cormac's Chapel on the Rock of Cashel, consecrated in 1134.
kingdom-of-desmond.r: Desmond's kings lost much of Cork to the Normans after 1177, but Finghin MacCarthy's victory at Callann in 1261 halted the colonists. The MacCarthy Mor branch then ruled from Pallis in Kerry, with cadet lines in Carbery and Muskerry. The kingdom was an overlordship of Gaelic lords such as the O'Sullivans and O'Donoghues.
kingdom-of-desmond.e: Donal MacCarthy Mor became Earl of Clancare in 1565 under the Kingdom of Ireland. His death without a legitimate male heir in 1596 ended the senior line, and its lands passed into English plantations.

kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.t: Croatian kingdom in personal union with Hungary, governed by bans and a noble diet, until the disaster of Mohács led it to the Habsburgs.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.o: After the Trpimirović line ended and the last king fell at Gvozd in 1097, Coloman of Hungary was crowned king of Croatia and Dalmatia at Biograd in 1102. Later tradition held that a pact (Pacta conventa) with Croatian nobles guaranteed their rights, though its authenticity is disputed.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.r: The kingdom kept its own institutions: a ban governed for the king, and the Sabor (diet) of nobles met separately. Great families such as the Šubići of Bribir and the Frankopans held vast lands; Ban Paul I Šubić was almost independent around 1300. Venice and Hungary fought over Dalmatia for centuries, and in 1409 Ladislaus of Naples sold his Dalmatian claims to Venice. Ottoman raids grew after 1463, with a heavy defeat at Krbava Field in 1493.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.e: After Louis II died at Mohács in 1526, the Croatian nobles meeting at Cetin in 1527 elected Ferdinand of Habsburg as king, beginning centuries of Habsburg rule.

kingdom-of-urartu.t: Urartu, a mountain kingdom around Lake Van, Assyria's great northern rival, famed for its fortresses, canals and bronze work.
kingdom-of-urartu.o: Urartu formed in the 9th century BCE when the chiefdoms of Nairi united under pressure from the Assyrian Empire. Sarduri I built the fortress of Van, called Tushpa, on a rock above Lake Van c. 840 BCE, and his successors pushed the kingdom into Transcaucasia and north-western Iran.
kingdom-of-urartu.r: Kings governed through fortified centres with storerooms for grain and wine, linked by roads. Menua built a canal over 50 km long that still waters Van, and Argishti I founded Erebuni in 782 BCE, origin of Yerevan. The god Haldi headed the pantheon; his temple at Musasir was famous for its treasures.
kingdom-of-urartu.e: Sargon II of the Assyrian Empire defeated Rusa I and sacked Musasir in 714 BCE. Urartu recovered under Rusa II but collapsed in the early 6th century BCE, probably under attacks by the Median Empire and Scythians. Armenians later occupied its lands.

kahat.t: Kahat, a small kingdom of the upper Khabur plains in the age of Mari, one of many rival city-states of the region known as Ida-Maras.
kahat.o: Kahat grew at Tell Barri on the Jaghjagh river in north-eastern Syria, a site inhabited since the 4th millennium BCE. By the 18th century BCE it was one of the minor kingdoms of the Ida-Maras district, between the larger powers of Mari, Ashnakkum and Shubat-Enlil.
kahat.r: Known mainly from the Mari letters, its kings swore alliances with Zimri-Lim and switched sides as the balance of power shifted. Kahat was also a religious centre of the storm god, honoured in later Hurrian and Assyrian sources. Italian excavations since 1980 have explored the town.
kahat.e: The kingdom lost its independence when Hammurabi's Babylonian Empire and later the Mitanni Empire reshaped northern Mesopotamia. Kahat survived as a town under Mitanni and the Assyrian Empire.

kingdom-of-kasanje.t: An Imbangala kingdom on the Kwango whose fair channelled captives from the Lunda interior to Portuguese Luanda for two centuries.
kingdom-of-kasanje.o: Kasanje was founded around 1620 by an Imbangala warband, formerly allied with Portuguese Angola, which settled in the Baixa de Kasanje, the fertile Kwango valley. Its leader, Kasanje, and his successors combined Imbangala military traditions with Mbundu lineage institutions to build a stable kingdom.
kingdom-of-kasanje.r: The king, titled the Jaga Kasanje, ruled through officials drawn from different lineages, and Imbangala rituals shaped kingship. The kingdom's wealth came from its position as middleman: captives and ivory from the Lunda Empire passed through the Kasanje market to Portuguese traders, who kept a resident agent there. Kasanje jealously blocked direct contact between the coast and the interior.
kingdom-of-kasanje.e: The end of the slave trade undermined Kasanje's economy, and wars with the Portuguese in the 1850s weakened it. Portuguese forces finally occupied the region in 1912, absorbing it into Portuguese Angola.

kingdom-of-eile.t: Irish kingdom of the O'Carrolls around Birr, on the border of Munster and Leinster, which survived as Ely O'Carroll until the 16th century.
kingdom-of-eile.o: Éile was the territory of an early medieval people of the Irish midlands, in what is now south Offaly and north Tipperary, counted as part of the Kingdom of Munster. Its ruling family claimed descent from the Eóganachta's kin, and from the 11th century the Ua Cerbaill, O'Carroll, became the dominant line, giving the region its later name of Ely O'Carroll.
kingdom-of-eile.r: The kingdom lay on the boundary between Munster and Leinster, which gave it strategic value and exposed it to raids. The monastery of Birr, founded by St Brendan of Birr in the 6th century, produced the Book of MacRegol, an illuminated gospel book of about 800. The O'Carrolls ruled from strongholds such as Leap Castle and Birr.
kingdom-of-eile.e: Anglo-Norman settlers took part of the territory in the 13th century, but the O'Carrolls recovered much of it. In 1552 their chief Tadhg O'Carroll surrendered his lands to the crown and was created Baron of Ely, and the region was later divided between King's County and Tipperary.
kingdom-of-eile.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-cusco.t: The small highland kingdom around Cusco from which the Incas rose to build the largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas.
kingdom-of-cusco.o: Inca tradition says the founder Manco Capac emerged from Lake Titicaca or the cave of Pacaritambo and led his people to the valley of Cusco, founding the city around 1200. Archaeology shows the Killke culture in the valley from about 1000, which developed into the early Inca polity.
kingdom-of-cusco.r: The early Inca kingdom was one of several competing lordships in the region, led by a ruler called the Sapa Inca and by royal lineages called panacas. Cusco was organised in two halves, Hanan and Hurin. Successive rulers such as Sinchi Roca, Mayta Capac and Viracocha Inca fought and allied with neighbours such as the Ayarmaca. The economy depended on maize terraces and herding.
kingdom-of-cusco.e: According to Inca tradition, around 1438 Cusi Yupanqui repelled the Chanka Confederation, deposed his father Viracocha Inca and took the name Pachacuti. He rebuilt Cusco and began the conquests that created the Inca Empire.

kingdom-of-the-regni.t: Client kingdom of Togidubnus in Sussex and Hampshire, a loyal ally of Rome after the conquest whose seat may have been the palace at Fishbourne.
kingdom-of-the-regni.o: After the Roman invasion of 43, much of the former realm of the Atrebates (Britain) was entrusted to Togidubnus, a British noble loyal to Rome. Tacitus says that certain states were given to him and that he remained faithful down to his own day, and the region became a base for Roman operations along the south coast.
kingdom-of-the-regni.r: An inscription from Chichester dedicating a temple to Neptune and Minerva names Tiberius Claudius Togidubnus as great king in Britain, showing that he held Roman citizenship and royal status. His capital, Noviomagus Reginorum, grew into a Roman-style town, and the lavish villa at Fishbourne, with mosaics and formal gardens, has often been linked to him. The kingdom provided Rome with a stable and Romanised territory.
kingdom-of-the-regni.e: When Togidubnus died, probably around 80, the client kingdom was absorbed into the province of Roman Britain. Its lands were divided into civitates, the Regni around Chichester and probably the Belgae (Britain) around Winchester. Chichester remains the main town of the region.

kingdom-of-the-heruli.t: A short-lived East Germanic kingdom on the middle Danube, briefly dominant over the Lombards before a crushing defeat around 508.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.o: The Heruli had been in the Black Sea region and under Hunnic rule; after the Huns' collapse following the Battle of Nedao in 454, one group settled near the middle Danube, probably in southern Moravia, western Slovakia and Lower Austria. By about 490 they had a strong kingdom that took tribute from the Lombards.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.r: Procopius describes the Heruli as fierce warriors who kept old pagan customs, including the sacrifice of elderly people and the suicide of widows. Their king Rodulf allied with Theodoric the Great, who adopted him as a 'son in arms' around 507. The kingdom rested on warrior power and tribute rather than settled institutions.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.e: Around 508 Rodulf attacked the Lombards under Tato and was killed in a heavy defeat. The Heruli scattered: some moved into Roman territory and became federates in Illyricum, others went to Scandinavia according to Procopius. Herul soldiers later fought for Justinian in Italy and Persia.

kingdom-of-bavaria.t: Wittelsbach kingdom created by Napoleon, the largest German state after Prussia and home of the fairy-tale castles of Ludwig II.
kingdom-of-bavaria.o: Elector Maximilian IV Joseph, allied with Napoleon, was proclaimed King Maximilian I of Bavaria on 1 January 1806. Napoleon's settlements added Franconia, Swabian lands and imperial cities, creating a state of mixed religion and identity.
kingdom-of-bavaria.r: Minister Montgelas modernised the administration, and the constitution of 1818 established a parliament. Ludwig I turned Munich into a city of classical architecture and museums before abdicating in 1848 over the Lola Montez affair. Ludwig II, patron of Wagner, built Neuschwanstein and Linderhof and was deposed in 1886; his uncle Luitpold ruled as regent. Bavaria kept its own army and railway in the German Empire.
kingdom-of-bavaria.e: Bavaria sided with Austria in 1866 but joined the German Empire in 1871. In November 1918 Kurt Eisner proclaimed a republic in Munich and Ludwig III fled, ending the monarchy; the state became the Free State of Bavaria.

kingdom-of-cottius.t: Alpine client kingdom around Susa whose ruler Cottius allied with Augustus and gave his name to the Cottian Alps.
kingdom-of-cottius.o: In the 1st century BCE the Segusini and neighbouring Alpine peoples around the Mont Genèvre pass were ruled by a king named Donnus, who appears in Caesar's time. His son, Marcus Julius Cottius, chose to make peace with Augustus rather than resist the Roman conquest of the Alps.
kingdom-of-cottius.r: Cottius governed fourteen Alpine communities as a Roman prefect while keeping royal status locally. He built and maintained the road over the Mont Genèvre pass, a key route between Italy and Gaul. In 9–8 BCE he erected the Arch of Augustus at Segusio (Susa), whose inscription lists his peoples. The kingdom combined Celtic traditions with Roman administration.
kingdom-of-cottius.e: Claudius restored the royal title to Cottius's son, Marcus Julius Cottius II, in 44 CE. When he died without an heir around 63 CE, Nero annexed the kingdom as the province of the Alpes Cottiae. The name survives in the Cottian Alps.

kingdom-of-moylurg.t: A Gaelic lordship of north Roscommon ruled by the MacDermots from their island fortress on Lough Key.
kingdom-of-moylurg.o: Magh Luirg was the territory of a branch of the Sil Muiredaig, the ruling kindred of Connacht. In the 12th century the MacDermot family, descended from Diarmait mac Taidg, emerged as its rulers and as marshals of the O'Connor kings of Connacht.
kingdom-of-moylurg.r: The MacDermots ruled from the Rock of Lough Ce, an island fortress on Lough Key, and patronised the abbey of Boyle and the learned families who compiled the Annals of Loch Ce. Their lordship was based on cattle, clients and armed retainers, and they served as kingmakers in Connacht politics.
kingdom-of-moylurg.e: The Composition of Connacht in 1585 brought the lordship under English land law. The MacDermots kept part of their lands and their title, the MacDermot, Prince of Coolavin, has been recognised into modern times.

kievan-rus.t: The first great East Slavic state, ruled by the Rurikid princes from Kiev, which brought Orthodox Christianity to the lands of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.
kievan-rus.o: In 882, according to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg of Novgorod seized Kiev and joined the northern and southern ends of the river route from the Varangians to the Greeks. His successors Igor, Olga and Sviatoslav I forced the East Slavic tribes into tribute, destroyed the Khazar Khaganate and raided Byzantium.
kievan-rus.r: The state was a family enterprise of the Rurikid princes, who shared out towns among themselves, with Kiev as the senior seat. Vladimir the Great accepted Christianity from Byzantium in 988, bringing churches, Church Slavonic writing and Byzantine art. Yaroslav the Wise issued the law code known as the Russkaya Pravda and built the Cathedral of Saint Sophia.
kievan-rus.e: After Vladimir Monomakh and his son Mstislav, who died in 1132, Rus' broke into rival principalities such as Chernigov, Vladimir-Suzdal and the Novgorod Republic. The Mongol invasion ended it, sacking Kiev in 1240. Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all trace their history to Rus'.

kingdom-of-lapethos.t: North Cypriot kingdom where Phoenician kings ruled a Greek population in the Classical age, until Ptolemy I deposed the last king in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-lapethos.o: Lapethos lay on the north coast of Cyprus near modern Lambousa, facing Anatolia. Greek tradition said it was founded by Praxandros from Laconia after the Trojan War. A city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE, it had close ties with the Phoenician coast.
kingdom-of-lapethos.r: In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE Lapethos was ruled by a dynasty with Phoenician names, such as Sidqmelek, who issued coins with Phoenician legends; Phoenician inscriptions from the town honour Melqart and other gods. The economy rested on farming, fishing and trade, and the city had a good harbour.
kingdom-of-lapethos.e: Its last king, Praxippos, supported Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who removed him in 312 BCE and annexed the kingdom. Lapethos continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman town, later called Lambousa, abandoned after Arab raids in the 7th century CE.

kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.t: Self-governing Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary, a time of rapid growth and Budapest's rise, and of tension with the kingdom's many nationalities.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.o: Austria's defeat by Prussia in 1866 forced Franz Joseph to settle with the Hungarian leaders Ferenc Deák and Gyula Andrássy. The Compromise of 1867 restored Hungary's constitution and parliament, with the emperor crowned king, and created Austria-Hungary, sharing only the monarch, foreign policy, the army and common finances. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868 gave Croatia-Slavonia autonomy within it.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.r: Parliament was dominated by the landed nobility and gentry under a narrow franchise, led by premiers such as Kálmán Tisza and István Tisza. Pest, Buda and Óbuda merged into Budapest in 1873, which grew into a major industrial city, celebrated in the Millennium of 1896. Policies of Magyarisation, such as the Apponyi school laws of 1907, angered Slovaks, Romanians and Serbs.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.e: Defeat in the First World War brought the Aster Revolution of October 1918, and the Hungarian Democratic Republic was proclaimed in November. The Treaty of Trianon in 1920 transferred two-thirds of the former kingdom to its neighbours.

kingdom-of-pylos.t: Mycenaean kingdom of Messenia whose burnt palace preserved more than a thousand Linear B tablets, the fullest record of a Bronze Age Greek state.
kingdom-of-pylos.o: Pylos grew on the Englianos ridge in western Messenia, where rich shaft and tholos tombs show an emerging elite by c. 1650 BCE, including the Griffin Warrior burial found in 2015. By the 14th and 13th centuries BCE its rulers had unified Messenia into a single kingdom divided into two provinces.
kingdom-of-pylos.r: The palace, linked by Homer with King Nestor, was headed by a wanax with a lawagetas below him. Its Linear B archive records taxation of some 16 districts, landholding, bronze-smiths, flax and perfumed oil production, rowers for the fleet and offerings to Poseidon, Zeus, Hera and the Potnia. Frescoes and a well-preserved throne room survive.
kingdom-of-pylos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire c. 1180 BCE, apparently while preparing coastal defences, and the region largely depopulated. Its tablets, baked by the fire, were found by Carl Blegen in 1939 and helped Michael Ventris show in 1952 that Linear B was Greek.

kingdom-of-circinn.t: A Pictish kingdom or province in the area of Angus and the Mearns, named in early Irish annals and in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
kingdom-of-circinn.o: Circinn appears as one of the seven Pictish provinces in the origin legend that named them after the sons of Cruithne, and in Irish annals, which record a battle of Circinn in 598. It is usually placed in Angus and the Mearns, south of the Mounth.
kingdom-of-circinn.r: Almost nothing is known of its government. It was probably one of the regional lordships within the Pictish kingdom, and the fertile lowlands of Angus held important church sites such as Aberlemno and later Brechin, with their carved Pictish stones.
kingdom-of-circinn.e: Circinn's identity merged into the Kingdom of Scotland when Pictland became Alba in the 9th and 10th centuries. The later earldoms of Angus and the Mearns may continue its territory.

kingdom-of-mycenae.t: The leading Bronze Age Greek kingdom in the Argolid, whose shaft graves, Lion Gate and tholos tombs gave its name to the Mycenaean civilisation.
kingdom-of-mycenae.o: Mycenae occupies a hill in the north-east Argolid controlling routes to Corinth. Its rise is shown by Grave Circles A and B, used c. 1650 to 1500 BCE, with gold masks and weapons. In the 14th and 13th centuries BCE a palace, Cyclopean walls and great tholos tombs such as the Treasury of Atreus were built.
kingdom-of-mycenae.r: Mycenae was ruled by a wanax from a palace with a central megaron and frescoes, and was probably the most powerful of several Argolid centres including Tiryns. Linear B tablets record perfumed oil and other goods. Its pottery spread across the Mediterranean, and some scholars link it to the Ahhiyawa known from Hittite texts. The Lion Gate dates to c. 1250 BCE.
kingdom-of-mycenae.e: The citadel suffered destructions c. 1200 BCE and the palace system collapsed, though occupation continued until c. 1100 BCE. Later the small town was destroyed by Argos c. 468 BCE. Homer made it the seat of Agamemnon, and Schliemann's excavations from 1876 made it famous.

kingdom-of-norway.t: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, forged by Harald Fairhair in the Viking Age and, after five centuries of union with its neighbours, independent again since 1905.
kingdom-of-norway.o: Norway grew out of the petty kingdoms of the Viking Age. Harald Fairhair of Vestfold united much of the coast, traditionally after the Battle of Hafrsfjord around 872. Olaf Tryggvason and Olaf Haraldsson imposed Christianity; Olaf fell at Stiklestad in 1030 and, as Saint Olaf, became the kingdom's patron and eternal king.
kingdom-of-norway.r: After a century of civil wars, Haakon IV restored strong monarchy, and Magnus the Lawmender issued a national law code in 1274. Medieval Norway ruled Iceland, Greenland, the Faroes and the Northern Isles, and lived from fishing, especially the stockfish trade through Bergen, dominated by the Hanseatic League. The Black Death of 1349 severely weakened it.
kingdom-of-norway.e: From 1380 Norway shared its kings with Denmark, in the Kalmar Union and then Denmark-Norway until 1814, when it adopted a constitution at Eidsvoll but was joined to Sweden as Sweden-Norway. Full independence came in 1905 under Haakon VII. Occupied by Germany in 1940-1945, it became a wealthy oil-producing constitutional monarchy.

kingdom-of-cologne.t: Kingdom of the Rhineland Franks at Cologne, absorbed by Clovis through murder around 509.
kingdom-of-cologne.o: The Franks of the middle Rhine, later called Ripuarian Franks, took over Cologne in the mid 5th century as Roman power collapsed. By the late 5th century they had their own king, Sigibert, who ruled from the former Roman capital of Germania Inferior.
kingdom-of-cologne.r: Sigibert, called the Lame from a wound received fighting the Alemanni at Zülpich, was an ally of Clovis and sent his son Chloderic to fight the Visigoths at Vouillé in 507. The Ripuarian Franks kept their own law, the Lex Ripuaria, written down in the 7th century.
kingdom-of-cologne.e: Gregory of Tours relates that Clovis incited Chloderic to murder his father, then had Chloderic killed and was raised on a shield as king by the people of Cologne, around 509. The realm became part of the Kingdom of the Franks and later of Austrasia.

kingdom-of-kent.t: The first English kingdom to accept Christianity, under Æthelberht in 597, and the home of the earliest laws written in English.
kingdom-of-kent.o: Bede says Kent was settled by Jutes led by Hengest and Horsa, who came as mercenaries of Vortigern around 449 and then turned against the Britons. The story is legendary, but archaeology shows strong links with Jutland and Frankish Gaul by the 6th century. The kingdom took its name from the British Cantiaci, and its centre was Canterbury.
kingdom-of-kent.r: Æthelberht, king from about 589 to 616, married the Frankish Christian princess Bertha and in 597 received Augustine's mission from Pope Gregory, making Canterbury the seat of the English Church. His law code is the earliest document in English. Kent was rich from trade with Francia, producing fine garnet jewellery and gold coinage, and later kings such as Wihtred issued further laws.
kingdom-of-kent.e: From the 760s Kent fell under Offa of Mercia; a revolt by Eadberht Præn was crushed in 798. In 825 Egbert of Wessex took Kent, which was ruled as a sub-kingdom by West Saxon princes until it was merged into Wessex in the 860s, later becoming an English shire.

kingdom-of-deheubarth.t: The kingdom of south-west Wales, founded by Hywel Dda and later led by the Lord Rhys, a centre of Welsh law, poetry and resistance to Norman conquest.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.o: Deheubarth, 'the southern part', was formed around 920 when Hywel Dda united his inheritance of the Kingdom of Seisyllwg with Dyfed. Hywel later also ruled Gwynedd and Powys, and became the only Welsh king to issue coins.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.r: Hywel was credited with codifying Welsh law, the Cyfraith Hywel, which governed inheritance, compensation and status. The kingdom's centre was Dinefwr in the Tywi valley. Norman lords overran much of it after 1093, but Rhys ap Gruffydd, the Lord Rhys, rebuilt its power, held the first recorded eisteddfod at Cardigan in 1176 and patronised Strata Florida Abbey.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.e: After the Lord Rhys died in 1197, his sons divided Deheubarth in bitter feuds. Its remnants came under Gwynedd's Principality of Wales, and its lands were absorbed by the English crown after 1283.

kingdom-of-kars.t: A small Armenian kingdom centred on the fortress city of Kars, ruled by a junior Bagratid line until it was handed to Byzantium.
kingdom-of-kars.o: In 963 Ashot III of Bagratid Armenia gave the district of Vanand, with the fortress of Kars, to his brother Mushegh, who took the title king. The kingdom remained linked to the senior line at Ani while governing its own affairs.
kingdom-of-kars.r: Kars was a strong fortress town on the route from Anatolia to the Caucasus, and its Cathedral of the Holy Apostles, built by King Abas in the 930s-40s when Kars was still the Bagratid capital, dominated the city. The kings ruled local nobles and peasants and acted as allies and rivals of the kings at Ani.
kingdom-of-kars.e: After Byzantium annexed Ani in 1045 and the Seljuks sacked it in 1064, King Gagik-Abas surrendered Kars to the Byzantine Empire in 1065 for lands in Cappadocia. The Seljuks took the city soon after.

kingdom-of-lori.t: An Armenian Bagratid kingdom in the gorges of northern Armenia, known for the monasteries of Haghpat and Sanahin.
kingdom-of-lori.o: Around 979 Gurgen, son of Ashot III of Bagratid Armenia, was given the northern provinces of Tashir and Dzoraget and took the title king, founding the Kyurikian line, named after his Georgian-style name Kyurike. The kingdom straddled the borderlands between Armenia and Georgia.
kingdom-of-lori.r: Kings ruled from fortresses such as Samshvilde and later Lori, controlling routes between Armenia and Georgia. The royal family endowed the monasteries of Sanahin and Haghpat, founded by Queen Khosrovanuysh in the 960s and 970s, which became major centres of learning and manuscript copying. The kingdom survived the fall of Ani in 1045 by allying with neighbours.
kingdom-of-lori.e: Seljuk attacks reduced the kingdom to Lori and its gorges, and it paid tribute to the Seljuk Empire. In 1118 David IV of the Kingdom of Georgia took Lori; the Kyurikians later held Tavush and Matsnaberd in the north-east.

kingdom-of-sweden.t: Scandinavian kingdom formed by uniting the Svear and Geats, which became a 17th-century great power and later a model of neutrality and welfare.
kingdom-of-sweden.o: The medieval kingdom emerged when Eric the Victorious and his son Olof Skötkonung, the first Christian king, ruled both the Svear around Uppsala and the Geats of Götaland, around 1000. Christianity and royal power spread slowly, and in the 13th century Birger Jarl strengthened the crown, founded Stockholm and conquered Tavastia.
kingdom-of-sweden.r: Sweden joined the Kalmar Union in 1397 but broke away when Gustav Vasa was elected king in 1523 and introduced the Lutheran Reformation. Gustav II Adolf made Sweden a great power in the Thirty Years' War, and its empire ringed the Baltic, from Finland and Livonia to Pomerania. Copper and iron mining at Falun and Bergslagen funded the state, and the Riksdag shared power with the crown.
kingdom-of-sweden.e: Defeat by Russia under Charles XII in the Great Northern War ended the empire in 1721, and Finland was lost in 1809. The Bernadotte dynasty took the throne in 1818, and Sweden ruled Norway in union until 1905. It stayed neutral in both world wars, built an extensive welfare state, joined the EU in 1995 and NATO in 2024.

kingdom-of-the-burgundians.t: East Germanic kingdom of the Rhône and Saône valleys, whose destruction on the Rhine inspired the Nibelungenlied and whose laws shaped Burgundy.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.o: The Burgundians crossed the Rhine in the early 5th century, and in 411 their king Gundahar set up a realm around Worms as Roman allies. In 436 the general Aetius had them crushed by Hunnic troops, a disaster remembered in the Nibelungenlied. In 443 the survivors were resettled in Sapaudia, around Geneva.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.r: From there they spread across the Rhône and Saône valleys, ruling from Lyon and Geneva. King Gundobad issued a law code for his Burgundian subjects and another for Romans, and Burgundians and Gallo-Romans shared land. The kings were Arians, but Sigismund converted to Catholic Christianity.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.e: Clovis' sons attacked them in 523, killing Sigismund. After a final defeat in 534 King Godomar disappeared and the land became part of the Kingdom of the Franks, later the Frankish Kingdom of Burgundy. The name Burgundy has endured for fifteen centuries.

kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.t: The Austrian-ruled kingdom of Lombardy and Venetia, centre of Habsburg power in Italy and target of the wars of Italian independence.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.o: In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave Lombardy and the former Republic of Venice to the Austrian Empire, which joined them as a kingdom with the emperor as king, governed by a viceroy, at first Archduke Rainer.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.r: Lombardy-Venetia had an efficient administration, good schools and a prosperous economy, but censorship and police repression made Austria unpopular; the patriot Silvio Pellico described his imprisonment in the Spielberg fortress. In 1848 the Five Days of Milan and the Republic of San Marco drove out the Austrians, but Marshal Radetzky reconquered both. Archduke Maximilian tried liberal reforms as governor-general in 1857–1859.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.e: Defeat by France and the Kingdom of Sardinia at Solferino in 1859 cost Austria Lombardy. After the war of 1866, Venetia passed to the Kingdom of Italy.

kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.t: Christian kingdom of the Árpád dynasty in the Carpathian basin, founded by Stephen I, which survived the Mongol invasion and united with Croatia.
kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.o: Stephen I, son of Grand Prince Géza of the Principality of Hungary, was crowned in 1000 or 1001. He defeated rival chiefs, annexed the Realm of the Gyulas and the Duchy of Ahtum, and built a Latin church with archbishoprics at Esztergom and Kalocsa.
kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.r: Royal counties centred on castles organised the realm, and the king owned vast estates. Ladislaus I and Coloman extended rule to Croatia, crowned in 1102. Germans settled in Transylvania and the towns, and the Golden Bull of 1222 under Andrew II limited royal power. The Mongols devastated the country in 1241–1242; Béla IV rebuilt it with stone castles and new towns.
kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.e: Royal power weakened as barons such as Matthew Csák built regional domains. With the death of Andrew III in 1301 the Árpád male line ended, and the throne was contested, leading to the Angevin Kingdom of Hungary (1301-1526).

kingdom-of-linjiang.t: The middle Yangtze kingdom of Gong Ao and his son, the last ally of Xiang Yu to hold out, conquered by Han forces in 202 BCE.
kingdom-of-linjiang.o: Gong Ao had served as Pillar of State to King Huai of Chu, the figurehead of the rebellion against the Qin dynasty, and led an army into the Nanjun region. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Linjiang, with his capital at Jiangling in Hubei, the former heartland of the State of Chu.
kingdom-of-linjiang.r: Linjiang controlled the rich Jianghan plain and the river routes to the south. Gong Ao died in 204 BCE and was succeeded by his son Gong Wei, who remained loyal to Xiang Yu when other kings defected.
kingdom-of-linjiang.e: After Xiang Yu's death in 202 BCE, Liu Bang sent Lu Wan and Liu Jia to attack Linjiang. Gong Wei was captured and executed, and his lands became part of the Han Dynasty.

kuban-peoples-republic.t: A Cossack republic on the Kuban, proclaimed in 1918, that sought union with Ukraine and fought the Bolsheviks while quarrelling with the Whites.
kuban-peoples-republic.o: After the Russian Revolution the Kuban Cossack Host, descended partly from the Black Sea Cossack Host, set up its own Rada in Yekaterinodar. In January 1918 the Rada proclaimed an independent Kuban People's Republic, with a population split between Ukrainian-speaking Black Sea Cossacks, Russian line Cossacks and non-Cossack settlers.
kuban-peoples-republic.r: The Bolsheviks took Yekaterinodar in March 1918, and the government retreated with the Volunteer Army, which recaptured the city in August. The republic had its own ataman, Alexander Filimonov, and a Rada in which a Ukrainian-minded faction under Mykola Ryabovol and Luka Bych pushed for federation with Ukraine. This brought conflict with General Denikin, who wanted a united Russia.
kuban-peoples-republic.e: Ryabovol was assassinated in 1919, and in November Denikin had the Rada member Kulabukhov hanged and the Rada purged. Demoralised Kuban units deserted, and the Red Army took Yekaterinodar in March 1920, ending the republic.

kingdom-of-dedan.t: An oasis kingdom at al-Ula in the Hejaz, a key stop on the incense road and precursor of the Lihyanite kings.
kingdom-of-dedan.o: Dedan, the ancient name of the oasis at al-Ula, is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible as a trading people. A local monarchy is attested in Dadanitic inscriptions from around the 7th century BCE. The oasis grew rich supplying water and provisions to caravans moving between south Arabia and the Levant.
kingdom-of-dedan.r: Kings of Dedan are known by name from short inscriptions, and the town had sanctuaries of the god Dhu Ghabat. In the mid-6th century BCE the Babylonian king Nabonidus campaigned in the Hejaz and listed Dedan among the oases he took while residing at Tayma. A colony of Minaean merchants from the Kingdom of Ma'in was later based there.
kingdom-of-dedan.e: After the Babylonian interlude the oasis came under the Lihyanite dynasty, and the Kingdom of Lihyan ruled from the same site. The ruins at al-Khuraybah near al-Ula, with their temple and lion tombs, are now excavated.

kingdom-of-syrmia.t: Realm of the former Serbian king Stefan Dragutin on the Sava and Danube, held as a Hungarian fief and rival to his brother's Serbia.
kingdom-of-syrmia.o: In 1282 Stefan Dragutin, king of Serbia, gave up the throne to his brother Milutin after a riding accident, keeping some Serbian lands. Through his wife Catherine, daughter of Stephen V of Hungary, he received from Ladislaus IV in 1284 the Banate of Macsó, Belgrade, Usora and Soli.
kingdom-of-syrmia.r: Dragutin, styled king, ruled from Debrc near Belgrade, supporting the Catholic Church in his lands as well as Orthodox monasteries. He joined Milutin against the Bulgarian lords of Braničevo, but from about 1301 the brothers fought for years over the Serbian succession.
kingdom-of-syrmia.e: After Dragutin's death in 1316 Milutin seized most of his lands, imprisoning Dragutin's son Vladislav II. Hungary soon retook Mačva and Belgrade, restoring the Banate of Macsó.

kingdom-of-dunoding.t: Small early kingdom of north-west Wales, named in legend after a son of Cunedda, which became the cantrefi of Eifionydd and Ardudwy in Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dunoding.o: According to Welsh genealogical tradition, Dunoding was named after Dunod, a son of Cunedda, who received the land as his share when Cunedda's family settled north Wales in the 5th century. Historians treat the Cunedda story as a later origin legend, but Dunoding existed as a distinct territory on the coast south of Snowdonia.
kingdom-of-dunoding.r: Little is recorded of its rulers or government. The kingdom comprised two districts, Eifionydd around Criccieth and Ardudwy around Harlech, a land of coastal farmland backed by mountains, rich in prehistoric monuments. It seems to have been ruled by a local branch of the dynasty of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dunoding.e: Dunoding was absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd as two cantrefi, probably by the 10th century. Eifionydd and Ardudwy remained administrative districts, later guarded by the castles of Criccieth and Harlech after the English conquest of 1283.

kingdom-of-cyprus.t: Crusader kingdom of the Lusignan dynasty that ruled Cyprus for three centuries, the last Latin outpost in the Levant after the fall of Acre.
kingdom-of-cyprus.o: In 1192 Richard I sold Cyprus, recently taken from Isaac Komnenos and returned by the Templars, to Guy of Lusignan, the deposed king of Jerusalem. Guy settled Frankish knights on the island. His brother Aimery obtained a crown from the Emperor Henry VI and was crowned king in 1197.
kingdom-of-cyprus.r: A French-speaking Catholic nobility ruled a mostly Greek Orthodox population, using the laws of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and a High Court of barons. The Orthodox church was subordinated to Latin bishops. After the fall of Acre in 1291 Famagusta became a great entrepot for Italian merchants. Gothic cathedrals in Nicosia and Famagusta and the abbey of Bellapais survive. Peter I led a crusade that sacked Alexandria in 1365.
kingdom-of-cyprus.e: Genoa seized Famagusta in 1373, and a Mamluk invasion in 1426 captured King Janus and made the kingdom tributary to Egypt. James II married the Venetian Catherine Cornaro; after his death she ruled as queen until Venice forced her to abdicate in 1489, creating Venetian Cyprus.

kokand-autonomy.t: A short-lived Muslim autonomous government in Turkestan, set up by Jadid reformers in 1917 and crushed by Soviet forces months later.
kokand-autonomy.o: After the October Revolution, the Tashkent Soviet, dominated by Russian settlers, excluded Muslims from power. In November 1917 the Fourth Extraordinary Regional Muslim Congress met in Kokand and proclaimed the Turkestan Autonomy within a future democratic Russian federation.
kokand-autonomy.r: The government, led first by Muhammadjan Tynyshbaev and then by Mustafa Chokay, included Jadid reformers and some Russian members. It planned a constituent assembly and a militia, but lacked money and troops and depended on the support of the Kokand population and local strongmen.
kokand-autonomy.e: In February 1918 Red Guards and Armenian Dashnak units from Tashkent stormed Kokand, killing thousands and burning much of the city. The government collapsed, and Chokay fled into exile. Its destruction helped spark the Basmachi resistance against Soviet rule.

kingdom-of-alania.t: The medieval Christian kingdom of the Alans in the North Caucasus, a Byzantine ally and Georgian partner until the Mongols destroyed it in 1239.
kingdom-of-alania.o: The Alans who stayed in the North Caucasus after the Hunnic invasions came under the Khazar Khaganate. As Khazar power declined in the 10th century, Alanian rulers formed a kingdom along the upper Kuban and Terek rivers, and around 916 they accepted Christianity from a Byzantine mission sent by Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos.
kingdom-of-alania.r: Kings ruled a land of fortified towns and hill forts, controlling the Darial Pass and trade with the Black Sea and the steppe. The Alanian church had its own metropolitan, and stone churches survive in the Zelenchuk valley. Royal marriages linked the Alans to the Kingdom of Georgia and Byzantium; Queen Tamar's husband David Soslan was an Alanian prince.
kingdom-of-alania.e: The Mongols defeated the Alans in 1222, and in 1239 they stormed the capital Maghas. Survivors withdrew into the mountains, where their descendants became the Ossetians. Others fled to Hungary, the Crimea and Mongol service in China, and the name of Alania survives in the official title of North Ossetia.

kingdom-of-idalion.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom famous for the Idalion Tablet, a bronze contract recording how the city paid a doctor to treat the wounded during a siege.
kingdom-of-idalion.o: Idalion grew on the hills of central Cyprus, near the copper-bearing foothills of Troodos, in the early Iron Age. By the 7th century BCE it was a city-kingdom listed among Cypriot states paying tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon. Its acropolis held sanctuaries of the goddesses later called Athena and Aphrodite.
kingdom-of-idalion.r: Idalion controlled copper production and fertile land. The Idalion Tablet, a bronze plaque of the early 5th century BCE written in the Cypriot syllabary, records that King Stasicypros and the city granted land to the physician Onasilos and his brothers for treating those wounded when 'the Medes and the Kitians' besieged the town.
kingdom-of-idalion.e: Idalion was conquered by the Phoenician Kingdom of Kition c. 450 BCE and lost its independence, Kition then ruling it with Phoenician administration. The town continued under Ptolemaic and Roman rule but declined.

kingdom-of-macedon.t: The Argead kingdom of northern Greece that Philip II turned into the dominant power of the Greek world, launching the conquests of his son Alexander.
kingdom-of-macedon.o: The Argead kings, who claimed descent from Temenos of Argos, built a kingdom in the plains of Lower Macedonia around Aigai, modern Vergina. Herodotus names Perdiccas I as founder in the 7th century BCE; later writers added an earlier Caranus, traditionally dated 808 BCE. The kingdom expanded over the Haliacmon and Axios plains.
kingdom-of-macedon.r: Macedon was a monarchy whose king ruled with a warrior aristocracy of Companions. It was a vassal of the Achaemenid Empire c. 512 to 479 BCE; Alexander I then courted Greek opinion. Archelaus I moved the capital to Pella c. 400 BCE and hosted Euripides. Timber, silver and horses supported it. Philip II, from 359 BCE, built a professional army with the long sarissa pike.
kingdom-of-macedon.e: Philip II took Amphipolis and the Chalcidice, defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and founded the League of Corinth. His murder at Aigai in 336 BCE brought Alexander to the throne, opening the age of the Macedonian Empire.

kingdom-of-montenegro.t: Montenegro's brief kingdom under Nikola I, which fought in the Balkan Wars and the First World War before being merged into Yugoslavia.
kingdom-of-montenegro.o: On the fiftieth anniversary of his reign, on 28 August 1910, Prince Nikola I of the Principality of Montenegro proclaimed himself king, with the agreement of the Great Powers. The new kingdom kept its capital at Cetinje and its constitution of 1905.
kingdom-of-montenegro.r: Nikola continued to rule as a patriarchal monarch, clashing with opponents who favoured union with Serbia. In the First Balkan War Montenegro besieged and took Scutari in 1913, but the powers forced it to hand the town to the new Albania; it did gain much of the Sandžak and Metohija, including Peć and Đakovica.
kingdom-of-montenegro.e: Montenegro joined Serbia in the First World War but was occupied by Austria-Hungary in January 1916, and Nikola went into exile. In November 1918 the Podgorica Assembly deposed him and voted for union with Serbia, provoking the Christmas Uprising of 1919. Montenegro became part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

kingdom-of-dacia.t: Kingdom of the Dacians in the Carpathian basin, united by Burebista and defended by Decebalus against Trajan, whose conquest created Roman Dacia.
kingdom-of-dacia.o: About 82 BCE Burebista united the Getae and Dacian tribes, aided by the high priest Deceneus. He built a realm from the middle Danube to the Black Sea, defeating the Boii and Scordisci and taking Greek coastal cities such as Olbia and Apollonia.
kingdom-of-dacia.r: The heart of the kingdom lay in the Orăștie Mountains, where fortresses and sanctuaries ringed the capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia. Kings ruled with a priestly elite devoted to Zalmoxis. Gold and silver mining, iron working and trade with Rome supported the state. After Burebista's murder in 44 BCE the realm split, but Decebalus reunited it and defeated a Roman army at Tapae.
kingdom-of-dacia.e: Trajan's two Dacian Wars (101–102 and 105–106 CE) destroyed the kingdom; Sarmizegetusa fell and Decebalus killed himself in 106 CE. Most of the land became the province of Dacia, commemorated on Trajan's Column, and Dacian identity later became central to Romanian national history.

kroraina.t: The kingdom of Loulan, later Shanshan, on the shores of Lop Nur, whose desert-preserved documents give an unusually detailed view of Silk Road life.
kroraina.o: Kroraina, called Loulan in Chinese, was an oasis state on the north-western shore of Lop Nur in the eastern Tarim Basin, the first stop for travellers leaving China westward. It appears in a Xiongnu letter to the Han of 176 BCE. In 77 BCE the Han envoy Fu Jiezi assassinated its pro-Xiongnu king, and the Han installed Weituqi, renaming the kingdom Shanshan and moving its centre south to Yuni.
kroraina.r: In the 3rd and 4th centuries Shanshan used Gandhari Prakrit in Kharoshthi script for government; hundreds of wooden tablets found at Niya record taxes, lawsuits, camels and slaves. Buddhism flourished, and its monasteries and paintings show Indian and Hellenistic influence. Chinese garrisons were stationed at Loulan, and its kings balanced between China and the steppe.
kroraina.e: Weakened by the drying of Lop Nur and wars with its neighbours, Shanshan was conquered by the Northern Wei in 445. The ruins of Loulan and Niya were rediscovered by Sven Hedin and Aurel Stein around 1900.

kingdom-of-viguera.t: A short-lived sub-kingdom in La Rioja, carved out of Pamplona for a royal younger son and soon folded back into the realm of Navarre.
kingdom-of-viguera.o: Around 970 King Sancho II Garcés of Pamplona, following the will of his father García Sánchez I, granted the Rioja lands around Viguera to his younger brother Ramiro Garcés with the title of king. The territory, recently won from the Muslims, guarded the upper Ebro and the approaches to Nájera.
kingdom-of-viguera.r: Viguera was an appanage rather than a fully independent state: its kings acknowledged the senior line in Pamplona and fought alongside it against the Caliphate of Córdoba. Ramiro is said to have died at the Battle of Torrevicente in 981. Charters show his sons Sancho Ramírez and García Ramírez styled as kings, though little else is recorded.
kingdom-of-viguera.e: After the line of Ramiro faded out in the early 11th century, Viguera was reabsorbed into the Kingdom of Navarre, by then under Sancho III the Great. It survives chiefly as a case study in how Iberian kings provided for younger sons with subordinate royal titles.
