kingdom-of-ondonga.t: An Ovambo kingdom of northern Namibia and the first to welcome Finnish Lutheran missionaries, whose influence reshaped its society.
kingdom-of-ondonga.o: Ondonga was one of the Ovambo kingdoms on the floodplains south of the Kunene river, formed by the 17th century under rulers drawn from a royal matriclan. Its people farmed millet, kept cattle and traded salt from the Etosha pan and copper with neighbours.
kingdom-of-ondonga.r: The king held wide powers over land and justice and governed through district headmen. Finnish Lutheran missionaries arrived in 1870, and Martti Rautanen worked at Olukonda, translating the Bible into Oshindonga. In 1904 Nehale lyaMpingana, ruler of eastern Ondonga, attacked the German fort at Namutoni. King Martin Elifas, baptised in 1912, made Ondonga largely Christian.
kingdom-of-ondonga.e: German colonial claims reached Ovamboland but had little effect until South Africa occupied South West Africa in 1915, after which the kingdom came under South African administration. Ondonga's kingship survives as a traditional authority in independent Namibia.

kingdom-of-amurru.t: Amurru, a kingdom on the Syrian-Lebanese coast built by adventurers in the Amarna age, which changed sides between Egypt and the Hittites.
kingdom-of-amurru.o: Amurru was the mountainous land behind the coast between Byblos and Ugarit, home to fugitives and landless groups. In the 14th century BCE Abdi-Ashirta united them into a kingdom at the expense of Egyptian vassals, and his son Aziru captured Simyra and made it his capital, despite angry letters from Rib-Hadda of Byblos.
kingdom-of-amurru.r: Aziru defected from the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom to the Hittite Empire and signed a treaty with Suppiluliuma I. His successors ruled as Hittite vassals with family ties to the Hittite court; a treaty with Shaushgamuwa ordered him to stop Ahhiyawan ships from trading with Assyria.
kingdom-of-amurru.e: Bentesina was deposed for siding with Egypt after Kadesh but restored by Hattusili III. Around 1190 BCE Amurru was overrun in the attacks by the Sea Peoples recorded at Medinet Habu, and the kingdom disappeared.

kart-dynasty.t: A Tajik dynasty of maliks who rebuilt Herat after the Mongol destruction and ruled it for more than a century.
kart-dynasty.o: Shams al-Din Muhammad Kart, of a family linked to the Ghurid Sultanate, was appointed ruler of Herat by the Mongols around 1245. The Mongol khan Möngke confirmed him, and he and his successors became vassals of the Ilkhanate.
kart-dynasty.r: The Karts rebuilt Herat, which had been devastated by the Mongols in 1221, restoring its walls, mosques and irrigation. They ruled over Herat, Ghor and parts of Khurasan as maliks, balancing Ilkhanid and Chagatai pressures. After the Ilkhanate collapsed in 1335, Mu'izz al-Din Husayn Kart ruled as an independent sovereign, patronising Persian scholarship and Sunni learning.
kart-dynasty.e: In 1381 Timur took Herat and deposed Ghiyath al-Din Pir Ali. After a revolt in 1383 the dynasty was exterminated. Herat later became the brilliant Timurid capital.

kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.t: Late medieval Hungary under the Angevins, Sigismund and Matthias Corvinus, a gold-rich central European power that fell at Mohács in 1526.
kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.o: When the Árpád line ended in 1301, rival claimants fought for the crown. Charles Robert of Anjou, grandson of a Hungarian princess, won out, was crowned in 1310 and broke the power of oligarchs such as Matthew Csák by 1321.
kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.r: Charles I reformed finances, and gold from Kremnica and Transylvania made the Hungarian florin a standard coin. Louis I also became king of Poland in 1370. Sigismund, later Holy Roman Emperor, led the crusade crushed at Nicopolis in 1396. John Hunyadi held off the Ottomans, saving Belgrade in 1456, and his son Matthias Corvinus built the Black Army, a famous Renaissance library, and took Vienna in 1485.
kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.e: Under the Jagiellonian kings royal power weakened, and the Dózsa peasant revolt of 1514 was brutally suppressed. In 1526 Suleiman the Magnificent destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács, killing Louis II; the kingdom was then divided between the Habsburgs, John Zápolya and the Ottomans.

kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.t: A Soviet republic formed in May 1918 by merging the Kuban and Black Sea soviets during the Russian Civil War.
kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.o: On 28 May 1918 the Bolsheviks united the Kuban Soviet Republic, centred on Yekaterinodar, and the Black Sea Soviet Republic, based in Novorossiysk, into a single Kuban-Black Sea Soviet Republic, as an autonomous part of the Russian SFSR. The merger reflected the threat posed by the Volunteer Army and by German forces advancing from Ukraine.
kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.r: The republic was governed by a council of commissars and fought both the Volunteer Army and the Kuban Cossack government. In June 1918, on Lenin's orders, much of the Black Sea Fleet was scuttled in the bay of Novorossiysk to prevent its capture by Germany. The republic struggled with grain requisitions and Cossack resistance.
kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.e: In July 1918 it was merged with the Terek and Stavropol soviet republics into the North Caucasian Soviet Republic, which the White armies overran by the end of the year.

kingdom-of-georgia.t: The united medieval Georgian monarchy, which under David the Builder and Queen Tamar became the leading power of the Caucasus and the setting of a golden age.
kingdom-of-georgia.o: Bagrat III, heir to both the Kingdom of Abkhazia and the Bagratid lands of the Kingdom of the Iberians, united western and eastern Georgia in 1008. The young kingdom first faced Byzantine pressure and then the Seljuk invasions, paying tribute to the Seljuk Empire from the 1080s.
kingdom-of-georgia.r: David IV the Builder reformed the army, settled Kipchak warriors, won the Battle of Didgori in 1121 and took Tbilisi. Under Queen Tamar, who ruled from 1184, Georgia dominated Shirvan and Armenia, the Zakarids governed Ani, and culture flourished: Rustaveli's poem The Knight in the Panther's Skin, the cave monastery of Vardzia and the Gelati academy. The church and great nobles balanced royal power.
kingdom-of-georgia.e: Mongol conquest in the 1230s made Georgia a vassal of the Ilkhanate; George V the Brilliant restored unity after 1327, but Timur's invasions devastated the country. After 1490 it split into the Kingdom of Kartli, the Kingdom of Kakheti, the Kingdom of Imereti and the Principality of Samtskhe.

kingdom-of-brazil.t: The kingdom created when Brazil was raised to equal status with Portugal, with Rio de Janeiro as the capital of the whole Portuguese monarchy.
kingdom-of-brazil.o: The Portuguese royal court had moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1808 to escape Napoleon. On 16 December 1815 the Prince Regent John raised Brazil to a kingdom within the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves, ending colonial status for the State of Brazil. He was acclaimed King John VI in Rio in 1818.
kingdom-of-brazil.r: Rio grew into a royal capital with the Bank of Brazil, a royal library, a botanical garden and a French artistic mission. Brazil's ports had been open to friendly nations since 1808. The crown crushed the Republic of Pernambuco in 1817 and annexed the Banda Oriental as Cisplatina. Slavery and the slave trade continued to expand.
kingdom-of-brazil.e: The liberal revolution in Porto in 1820 forced John VI to return to Lisbon in 1821, leaving his son Pedro as regent. When the Portuguese Cortes sought to reduce Brazil's status, Pedro declared independence on 7 September 1822 and founded the Empire of Brazil.

kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.t: The Habsburg crown land carved from partitioned Poland, a poor but politically lively province that shaped modern Polish and Ukrainian identity.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.o: In the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the Habsburg Monarchy took the lands around Lviv and south of the Vistula. It justified the annexation through old Hungarian claims to the medieval principalities of Halych and Volodymyr, hence the name Galicia and Lodomeria. Krakow was added in 1846.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.r: Lviv, called Lemberg, was the capital. After 1867 the province gained wide autonomy within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, run by Polish nobles through a Diet, with Polish schools and universities in Krakow and Lviv. It was a land of Poles, Ukrainians and a large Jewish population, known for rural poverty and mass emigration, but also for oil wells at Boryslav and a flourishing Ukrainian national movement.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.e: Galicia was a major battlefield in the First World War. When the empire collapsed in 1918, Ukrainians in Lviv proclaimed the West Ukrainian People's Republic, and the Second Polish Republic won the war that followed, taking all of Galicia by 1919.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.re: Catholic and Greek Catholic Christianity, Judaism

kamarina.t: Syracusan colony on Sicily's south coast, destroyed and refounded several times, whose restless history became a Greek proverb.
kamarina.o: Syracuse founded Kamarina around 598 BCE near the mouth of the Hipparis river, on the south-east coast of Sicily, to extend its reach towards the territory of Gela. The settlers laid out a regular town on a coastal hill beside a marsh.
kamarina.r: Kamarina repeatedly defied its mother city: it revolted around 553 BCE and was destroyed, was refounded by Hippocrates of Gela around 492 BCE, emptied again by Gelon in 484 BCE and refounded from Gela in 461 BCE. Pindar wrote odes for its Olympic victor Psaumis. The Greek proverb 'do not move Camarina', said to come from a disastrous draining of the marsh, warned against stirring up trouble.
kamarina.e: Its people evacuated before the Carthaginians in 405 BCE, and Timoleon resettled it in the 4th century. In 258 BCE, during the First Punic War, the Romans captured it and sold most inhabitants into slavery. The site, near Santa Croce Camerina, was excavated from the 19th century.

kingdom-of-gwynedd.t: The most enduring Welsh kingdom, ruled from Aberffraw on Anglesey, whose princes led Welsh resistance until Edward I's conquest in 1283.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.o: Gwynedd arose in north-west Wales after Roman rule ended. Its dynasty traced descent from Cunedda, said to have come from Manaw Gododdin in the 5th century. By the 6th century it was a leading power under Maelgwn Gwynedd, whom Gildas denounced as Maglocunus, the dragon of the island, and its core lay in Snowdonia and the grain lands of Anglesey.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.r: Kings ruled from llysoedd, royal courts, with Aberffraw as the chief seat, governing through cantrefi and kin-based Welsh law. Cadwallon ap Cadfan killed Edwin of Northumbria in 633. Rhodri the Great, who died in 878, joined the Kingdom of Powys and Seisyllwg to Gwynedd. Later princes such as Owain Gwynedd and Llywelyn the Great built castles and charters, and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd won recognition as Prince of Wales by the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.e: Edward I invaded in 1277 and again in 1282. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed at Cilmeri in 1282, and his brother Dafydd was executed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 turned Gwynedd into English shires, guarded by castles such as Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech.

kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.t: The O'Neill kingdom of mid-Ulster, the most powerful Gaelic lordship of late medieval Ireland, whose last ruler led the Nine Years' War.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.o: Tir Eoghain, 'Eogan's land', descends from the Cenel nEogain, the northern Ui Neill kindred traced to Eogan, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. After the decline of the Mac Lochlainn line in the late 12th century, the O'Neills emerged as kings, ruling from Dungannon with inaugurations at Tullyhogue.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.r: The O'Neills dominated Ulster, taking tribute from lesser lords such as the O'Cahans and Maguires. Their power rested on cattle, a large army including Scottish gallowglasses, and a court of poets and lawyers. Conn Bacach O'Neill became Earl of Tyrone in 1542, but conflict with the crown continued under Shane O'Neill.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.e: Hugh O'Neill led the Nine Years' War against England, but defeat at Kinsale in 1601 forced his submission. He left in the Flight of the Earls in 1607, and Tyrone was confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster in the Kingdom of Ireland.

kingdom-of-scotland.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom of the Scots, forged from Pictland and Dal Riata, which kept its independence until the Union with England in 1707.
kingdom-of-scotland.o: Tradition dates the kingdom to Kenneth MacAlpin, who ruled the Picts from about 843. The Pictish and Gaelic realms merged into the kingdom of Alba by around 900, centred on Scone and Dunkeld. It expanded over Lothian, Strathclyde, and in 1266 the Western Isles from Norway.
kingdom-of-scotland.r: Scotland developed royal burghs, feudal lordship and a church of its own under David I. The Wars of Independence, with William Wallace and Robert the Bruce's victory at Bannockburn in 1314, secured independence. The Stewart monarchy followed in 1371, Edinburgh became the capital, and the Reformation of 1560 created a Presbyterian church.
kingdom-of-scotland.e: In 1603 James VI inherited England, joining the crowns. The Acts of Union of 1707 merged the Scottish and English parliaments into the Kingdom of Great Britain, though Scotland kept its own law, church and education.

kingdom-of-kition.t: Phoenician kingdom on Cyprus, founded by Tyre, that conquered its Greek neighbours Idalion and Tamassos and was the birthplace of Zeno the Stoic.
kingdom-of-kition.o: Kition, at modern Larnaca, was a Late Bronze Age copper-working town. In the 9th century BCE Phoenicians from Tyre settled there and built a great temple of Astarte on the ruins of an earlier sanctuary. Kition probably began as a Tyrian dependency, and in 707 BCE Sargon II of Assyria set up a stele there recording Cypriot submission.
kingdom-of-kition.r: From the early 5th century BCE an independent Phoenician dynasty ruled Kition, beginning with Baalmelek I, and it was loyal to the Achaemenid Empire. Kition conquered Idalion c. 450 BCE, its kings then styling themselves rulers of both, and Pumiyaton later bought Tamassos. Its harbour served Persian fleets, and its kings issued coins showing Heracles-Melqart.
kingdom-of-kition.e: Ptolemy I executed Pumiyaton and annexed the kingdom in 312 BCE. Kition continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman city; its most famous son, Zeno, founded Stoic philosophy at Athens.
kingdom-of-kition.re: Phoenician religion; cults of Astarte and Melqart

kingdom-of-osraige.t: Irish kingdom between Leinster and Munster, centred on Kilkenny, whose Mac Giolla Phádraig rulers survived as lords until the Tudor surrender of 1541.
kingdom-of-osraige.o: Osraige emerged in early medieval Ireland as the kingdom of a people living in the valleys of the Nore and its tributaries, in modern County Kilkenny and south Laois. Its kings traced descent from ancestors distinct from both the Laigin and the Eóganachta, and the kingdom stood between the Kingdom of Leinster and the Kingdom of Munster, usually as a tributary of Munster.
kingdom-of-osraige.r: The monasteries of Saighir, linked with St Ciarán, and later Aghaboe and Kilkenny, where St Canice is honoured, were centres of learning and gave their names to the diocese of Ossory. Cerball mac Dúnlainge, who died in 888, made Osraige a major power by fighting and allying with Viking leaders. His descendants, the Mac Giolla Phádraig, briefly held the kingship of Leinster under Donnchad mac Gilla Pátraic in the 1030s.
kingdom-of-osraige.e: After the Anglo-Norman invasion of 1169, Kilkenny became the seat of English lords, and the Mac Giolla Phádraig held only Upper Ossory. In 1541 their chief, Brian, surrendered his lands to Henry VIII and received them back as Baron of Upper Ossory, ending the kingdom.

kingdom-of-france.t: The monarchy that grew from the Capetians' small domain around Paris into Europe's most populous and centralised state, ending with the Revolution.
kingdom-of-france.o: In 987 the magnates elected Hugh Capet, duke of the Franks, as king after the last Carolingian died. The early Capetians directly controlled only the Île-de-France and Orléans, while dukes and counts of Normandy, Aquitaine, Burgundy and Flanders were in practice independent.
kingdom-of-france.r: Kings slowly extended the royal domain by war, marriage and law: Philip II took Normandy in 1204, Louis IX became a model of Christian kingship, and the Valois survived the Hundred Years' War. After the Wars of Religion, Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. Louis XIV built absolute rule at Versailles, and French language and culture dominated Europe.
kingdom-of-france.e: Debt and political crisis led Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789, beginning the Revolution. The monarchy became constitutional in 1791 and was abolished in September 1792, replaced by the French First Republic; Louis XVI was executed in 1793.

kaska.t: The Kaska, tribal peoples of the Pontic mountains who for three centuries raided the Hittite heartland and once burned Hattusa.
kaska.o: The Kaska lived in the wooded mountains between the Hittite heartland and the Black Sea. They appear in Hittite texts from the 15th century BCE, when they overran the holy city of Nerik and pushed into central Anatolia.
kaska.r: They were not a state but groups of villages under local chiefs, living from herding and farming and raiding Hittite lands. Hittite kings made short-lived treaties with individual groups. Mursili II wrote that one chief, Pihhuniya, ruled not in the Kaska way but like a king.
kaska.e: Kaska raiders sacked Hattusa in the 14th century BCE, and Hattusili III only recovered Nerik in the 13th. After the Hittite collapse they moved south-east, where Tiglath-Pileser I of the Assyrian Empire fought them c. 1100 BCE; then they vanish.

kingdom-of-dublin.t: The Norse kingdom founded around Dublin's harbour, a hub of the Viking trade network that linked Ireland to Scandinavia, Britain and the slave markets.
kingdom-of-dublin.o: Vikings built a fortified base, the longphort, at Dublin in 841. From 853 the annals record Amlaib and later Imar, ancestors of a dynasty of kings who ruled both Dublin and, at times, the Kingdom of York. Expelled by the Irish in 902, they returned in 917.
kingdom-of-dublin.r: Dublin was a trading town of streets, houses and workshops, revealed by excavations at Wood Quay, dealing in slaves, silver, furs and craft goods. It minted coins from about 997. Its rulers converted to Christianity in the 10th century and Sitric Silkbeard founded Christ Church Cathedral around 1030. Irish kings often controlled it as a valuable prize.
kingdom-of-dublin.e: After defeat at Clontarf in 1014, Dublin was dominated by Irish overkings. In 1170 Strongbow and Diarmait Mac Murchada captured it, and in 1171 Henry II made it the capital of the Lordship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-dublin.re: Norse paganism; Christianity from the 10th century

kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.t: The Alpine kingdom of the Welf dynasty, founded at Saint-Maurice in 888, which later absorbed Provence to form the Kingdom of Arles.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.o: After the deposition of Emperor Charles the Fat in 888, the Welf noble Rudolf, margrave of Transjurane Burgundy, had himself crowned king at the abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune. His kingdom covered western Switzerland, the Jura and parts of Franche-Comté, and he held it against the East Frankish king Arnulf.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.r: The kings controlled the Great St Bernard pass and relied on rich abbeys such as Saint-Maurice and on alliances with local bishops at Lausanne, Geneva and Sion. Rudolf II was defeated by Swabia at Winterthur in 919, then reached for the Italian crown in the 920s before trading those claims for Provence.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.e: Around 933 Rudolf II obtained Lower Burgundy from Hugh of Arles, merging the two realms into the Kingdom of Arles. His son Conrad the Peaceful ruled the united kingdom under strong Ottonian influence, and in 1032 it passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-leon.t: The Christian kingdom that succeeded Asturias in 910, claimed Visigothic heritage and held the first European parliament with townsmen in 1188.
kingdom-of-leon.o: In 910 the sons of Alfonso III of Asturias divided his realm, García I taking León. In 914 Ordoño II made the city of León the royal seat, and the kingdom took its name from it, incorporating Asturias and Galicia and the newly resettled lands of the Douro plain.
kingdom-of-leon.r: The Leonese kings claimed to restore the Visigothic monarchy, some styling themselves emperor. Ramiro II beat Abd al-Rahman III at Simancas in 939, though Almanzor later sacked León and Santiago. Alfonso V's fuero of 1017 regulated the city, and Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085. Alfonso IX summoned the Cortes of León in 1188, with representatives of towns alongside nobles and clergy.
kingdom-of-leon.e: León was united with Castile under Ferdinand I and his successors, separated again from 1157, and definitively joined with Castile in 1230 under Ferdinand III, forming the Crown of Castile.

kidarite-kingdom.t: The first of the Hunnic dynasties to rule Bactria and Gandhara, named after its founder Kidara and long locked in war with Sasanian Persia.
kidarite-kingdom.o: The Kidarites emerged in Bactria in the 4th century, probably from among the Chionites who invaded the lands of the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom. Their eponymous leader Kidara issued coins in the Kushan style and claimed the old Kushan title, ruling from Balkh and later spreading into Gandhara.
kidarite-kingdom.r: They governed a mixed population of Bactrians and Indians, issuing gold coins modelled on Kushan and Sasanian types, some with Brahmi legends naming Kidara. They fought repeated wars with Sasanian kings such as Yazdegerd II and Peroz I, and probably clashed with the Gupta Empire in northern India.
kidarite-kingdom.e: Around 467 the Sasanians under Peroz I drove them from Bactria, and the Hephthalite Empire soon took over their northern lands. Remnant Kidarite principalities held out in Gandhara and Kashmir until the Alchon Huns absorbed them in the late 5th century.

kingdom-of-ugarit.t: Ugarit, a rich Late Bronze Age port-kingdom on the Syrian coast whose scribes invented an alphabetic cuneiform and recorded the myths of Baal.
kingdom-of-ugarit.o: Ugarit, at Ras Shamra north of Latakia, was settled from the Neolithic. In the early 2nd millennium BCE it became the capital of a coastal kingdom with an outlet at Minet el-Beida, and it appears in the Mari letters when Zimri-Lim travelled there. A farmer's discovery of a tomb in 1928 led to excavations by Claude Schaeffer.
kingdom-of-ugarit.r: Its kings ruled a cosmopolitan trading state linking Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean and Mesopotamia. Scribes wrote in Akkadian, Hurrian, Hittite, Egyptian and the local Ugaritic, using a 30-sign cuneiform alphabet. Temple libraries preserved the Baal cycle and the epics of Kirta and Aqhat, close relatives of later Hebrew poetry.
kingdom-of-ugarit.e: Ugarit was a vassal first of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom and then, from Niqmaddu II, of the Hittite Empire. Around 1185 BCE seaborne raiders destroyed it; letters of its last king Ammurapi describe enemy ships. The city was never rebuilt.

kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.t: The largest pre-unification Italian state, the Bourbon kingdom of Naples and Sicily, overthrown by Garibaldi's Thousand in 1860.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.o: After the Congress of Vienna restored him, Ferdinand IV of Naples and III of Sicily merged the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily in December 1816, becoming Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies, with Naples as capital.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.r: The kingdom was an absolute monarchy that put down revolts in 1820 and 1848; Sicilians resented losing their autonomy. Ferdinand II opened Italy's first railway, from Naples to Portici, in 1839 and built a strong navy, but his harsh repression earned him the nickname King Bomba. The south remained largely rural, with powerful landowners and widespread poverty.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.e: In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand conquered Sicily and Naples. Francis II held out at Gaeta until February 1861, and the kingdom was annexed to the new Kingdom of Italy.

kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.t: Croatian kingdom under the Habsburgs, reduced by Ottoman conquest to the 'remnants of the remnants' and later a centre of the Croatian national revival.
kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.o: On 1 January 1527 the Croatian nobles assembled at Cetin elected Ferdinand of Habsburg as king, in return for his help against the Ottomans. By the late 16th century Ottoman conquests had reduced Croatia to a narrow band around Zagreb, Karlovac and the coast, the reliquiae reliquiarum of the old kingdom.
kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.r: Croatia was governed by a ban and its own Sabor, within the Lands of the Hungarian Crown, while much of its territory was detached into the Military Frontier under Vienna. The victory at Sisak in 1593 halted the Ottoman advance. Nobility, Catholic Church and Latin dominated public life until the Illyrian movement of Ljudevit Gaj revived Croatian in the 1830s.
kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.e: In 1848 Ban Josip Jelačić led Croatian forces against the Hungarian revolution. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868 joined the kingdom with Slavonia as the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia, an autonomous part of the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary.

kingdom-of-iceland.t: Sovereign Iceland in personal union with Denmark from 1918, until Icelanders voted to become a republic in 1944.
kingdom-of-iceland.o: After a century of national struggle led by figures such as Jón Sigurðsson, Iceland won home rule in 1904. The Danish-Icelandic Act of Union, effective 1 December 1918, recognised Iceland as a sovereign kingdom sharing a king, Christian X, with Denmark, with the right to end the union after 25 years.
kingdom-of-iceland.r: Iceland governed itself through the Althing and its own cabinet, while Denmark handled foreign affairs and fisheries protection on its behalf. A Supreme Court was set up in 1920, and in 1930 the Althing celebrated its millennium at Þingvellir. The economy depended on fishing, and the Depression hit hard.
kingdom-of-iceland.e: When Germany occupied Denmark in 1940, Iceland took over its own foreign affairs and Britain, then the United States, occupied the island. Sveinn Björnsson became regent in 1941. In a 1944 referendum Icelanders voted overwhelmingly to end the union, and the Republic of Iceland was proclaimed on 17 June 1944.

kingdom-of-the-picts.t: Early medieval kingdom of northern and eastern Scotland, known for its carved symbol stones, which merged with the Gaels to form the kingdom of Alba.
kingdom-of-the-picts.o: The Picts are first named in a Roman panegyric of 297 as enemies of Britain alongside the Irish. The name, Latin for 'painted people', was applied to the peoples north of the Forth, descendants of the Caledonii, Maeatae and other Iron Age groups. Over the following centuries their many districts were drawn together under powerful over-kings.
kingdom-of-the-picts.r: The Picts left few written records but carved distinctive symbol stones with combs, mirrors, crescents and animals, later combined with Christian crosses. Kings such as Bridei son of Maelchon, visited by Columba in the 560s, ruled through regional lords. Bridei son of Beli defeated the Northumbrians at Dun Nechtain in 685, and Óengus son of Fergus dominated northern Britain in the 8th century. Christianity spread from Iona and Northumbria.
kingdom-of-the-picts.e: Viking attacks in the 9th century devastated the Pictish elite, notably in a great defeat in 839. Cináed mac Ailpín, a king of Gaelic descent, took power around 843, and by about 900 Pictland had become the Gaelic-speaking kingdom of Alba, the core of medieval Scotland.
kingdom-of-the-picts.re: Celtic polytheism; Christianity from the 6th century

kingdom-of-maroboduus.t: The first large Germanic kingdom known by name, built in Bohemia by Maroboduus, who drilled an army on Roman lines and alarmed Augustus.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.o: Maroboduus, a Marcomannic noble who had spent his youth in Rome, led his people from the Main region into Bohemia around 9 BCE to escape Roman offensives. There he subjected neighbouring peoples, including the Quadi, Lugii, Semnones and Langobardi, building a realm that stretched from the Danube to the Elbe and beyond.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.r: Velleius Paterculus describes a centralised monarchy with a standing army of about 70,000 foot and 4,000 horse trained in Roman fashion, and a royal seat called Marobudum. Roman merchants lived there. Augustus planned to crush him in 6 CE with twelve legions, but the Pannonian revolt forced a treaty recognising Maroboduus as a friend of Rome.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.e: Maroboduus stayed neutral when Arminius destroyed Varus' legions in 9, and in 17 Arminius defeated him; the Semnones and Langobardi deserted. In 19 the Gothic exile Catualda seized his capital, and Maroboduus fled to Roman territory, dying in Ravenna in 37. Rome then created the client Kingdom of Vannius.

kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.t: An eastern Georgian kingdom that resisted absorption into the united Georgian monarchy for nearly a century before David the Builder conquered it.
kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.o: Around 1010 Kvirike III, chorepiscopus of the Principality of Kakheti, which had already absorbed the Principality of Hereti, took the title king of the Kakhs and Rans. His realm, centred on Telavi, emerged just as Bagrat III was uniting the rest of Georgia and fought off his attempts to take it.
kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.r: Kvirike III, called the Great, was a strong ruler and builder who allied with neighbours against the Georgian kings. The kingdom lived from the vineyards and pastures of the Alazani valley and controlled routes towards Shirvan. Aghsartan I submitted to the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan in 1068 and outwardly converted to Islam to keep his throne.
kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.e: Seljuk overlordship weakened the kingdom, and in 1104 nobles of Hereti handed King Aghsartan II to David IV, who annexed it to the Kingdom of Georgia. Kakheti re-emerged as a separate kingdom in 1465.

kingdom-of-essex.t: The kingdom of the East Saxons north of the Thames, which controlled London for long periods and had a dynasty with unusual 'S' names.
kingdom-of-essex.o: The East Saxons settled Essex, Middlesex and parts of Hertfordshire. Their royal genealogy traces kings to Aescwine, traditionally placed in 527, and later kings bore names beginning with S, such as Saeberht, Sigeberht and Swithred.
kingdom-of-essex.r: Essex held London, which Bede called a market of many peoples. Saeberht accepted Christianity around 604 and Mellitus became bishop of London, but the kingdom reverted to paganism after his death until Cedd's mission in the 650s. Several kings often ruled jointly. Essex usually stood under the overlordship of Kent or Mercia.
kingdom-of-essex.e: After 825 Essex submitted to Ecgberht of the Kingdom of Wessex, and later fell within the Danelaw. In the 10th century it was absorbed into the Kingdom of England as a shire, which survives as the county of Essex.

khanate-of-bukhara.t: The Uzbek khanate of Transoxiana under the Shaybanid and Janid dynasties, whose capital Bukhara was a leading centre of Islamic learning.
khanate-of-bukhara.o: In 1500 Muhammad Shaybani, grandson of Abu'l-Khayr of the Uzbek Khanate, took Samarkand from the Timurids and soon conquered Transoxiana and Khurasan. After he was killed by the Safavid Shah Ismail at Merv in 1510, his kinsmen restored Shaybanid rule in Transoxiana, with Bukhara becoming the capital in the mid-16th century.
khanate-of-bukhara.r: The Shaybanids ruled through appanages held by members of the dynasty and Uzbek tribal chiefs. Abdullah Khan II reunited the realm in the late 16th century, building caravanserais, bridges and madrasas. In 1599 the Janids, or Ashtarkhanids, a branch of the Astrakhan Khanate's Jochid line, took over. Trade with India, Russia and Persia continued, and Naqshbandi Sufi orders were influential.
khanate-of-bukhara.e: Janid power declined, and in 1740 Nader Shah of Persia made Bukhara a vassal. The Manghit atalik Muhammad Rahim took effective power, and in 1785 his relative Shah Murad formally founded the Emirate of Bukhara.

kingdom-of-dyfed.t: South-west Welsh kingdom ruled by a dynasty of Irish descent, home of St Davids, which became the core of Deheubarth under Hywel Dda.
kingdom-of-dyfed.o: Dyfed grew from the Roman civitas of the Demetae after Roman rule ended around 410. Irish settlers crossed to the region in the 4th and 5th centuries, and its royal line traced descent from the Déisi of Ireland, a link supported by the many ogham-inscribed stones of the area.
kingdom-of-dyfed.r: In the 6th century Gildas denounced its king Vortiporius as tyrant of the Demetae, and a memorial stone at Castell Dwyran bearing his name in Latin and ogham may be his. The monastery of St Davids, founded by Dewi Sant, became the leading church of Wales. Asser records that its king Hyfaidd ap Bleddri submitted to Alfred of Wessex in the 880s to escape pressure from Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dyfed.e: After Llywarch ap Hyfaidd died around 904, his daughter Elen married Hywel Dda of Seisyllwg, who took over Dyfed. Hywel joined the two realms to form the kingdom of Deheubarth, and Dyfed survived as a region and, much later, as a county name.

kussara.t: Kussara, the Anatolian kingdom of Pithana and Anitta, who forged the first large state of central Anatolia and paved the way for the Hittites.
kussara.o: Kussara was a city in central or eastern Anatolia whose site is still unknown. In the 18th century BCE its king Pithana seized Nesa, the city of Kanesh, and made it a second capital, launching the kingdom's rise.
kussara.r: His son Anitta conquered Zalpa, Hattus and the great kingdom of Purushanda, and took the title great king. His deeds are told in the Anitta text, the oldest known text in the Hittite language. Anitta built temples to the storm god and his own god Siusummi and celebrated victories with hunts of wild animals.
kussara.e: The kingdom of Anitta did not last long, but the Hittite royal line traced its origins to Kussara; Hattusili I called himself a man of Kussara. His move to Hattusa c. 1650 BCE marks the start of the Hittite Empire.

kingdom-of-naples.t: The southern Italian kingdom ruled from Naples for five centuries by Angevins, Aragonese, Spanish viceroys and Bourbons.
kingdom-of-naples.o: The Sicilian Vespers of 1282 drove Charles of Anjou from Sicily, leaving him only the mainland part of the Kingdom of Sicily. He and his heirs kept calling themselves kings of Sicily but ruled from Naples, which became the capital of a separate kingdom.
kingdom-of-naples.r: Robert the Wise made Naples a cultural centre, hosting Petrarch and Giotto. Alfonso V of Aragon conquered the kingdom in 1442. After French invasions, Spain ruled it from 1504 through viceroys, making Naples one of Europe's largest cities. A powerful baronage, heavy taxes and the Masaniello revolt of 1647 marked this period. Austria took the kingdom in 1707, and in 1734 Charles of Bourbon made it independent again.
kingdom-of-naples.e: Napoleon's armies drove out the Bourbons in 1806, creating the Kingdom of Naples (1806–1815). Ferdinand IV returned in 1815 and in 1816 united Naples and Sicily as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

karluk-yabgu.t: A Turkic confederation that fought beside the Arabs at Talas and seized Suyab, preparing the ground for the Kara-Khanid Khanate.
karluk-yabgu.o: The Karluks lived in the Altai and joined the Uyghurs and Basmyls in overthrowing the Second Turkic Khaganate in 744. Driven west by the Uyghur Khaganate, they moved to the Zhetysu region, and in 751 their defection to the Abbasid side helped decide the Battle of Talas against Tang China.
karluk-yabgu.r: Led by a yabghu, the Karluks took Suyab and the lands of the Turgesh Khaganate by 766, ruling a mix of nomadic tribes and the Sogdian towns of the Chu valley. They controlled Silk Road routes between Transoxiana and the Tarim, and Muslim geographers describe them as rich in livestock and towns. Some groups converted to Islam early.
karluk-yabgu.e: After the Uyghur Khaganate fell in 840, the Karluk leader Bilge Kul Qadir Khan proclaimed himself khagan, an event many historians take as the founding of the Kara-Khanid Khanate, which absorbed the Karluk lands.

khanate-of-sibir.t: The Tatar khanate of western Siberia whose defeat by Yermak's Cossacks in 1582 began Russia's conquest of Siberia.
khanate-of-sibir.o: The khanate emerged from the Tyumen Khanate when the local Taibugid dynasty seized power around 1495 and moved the capital to Qashliq (Isker) on the Irtysh. The Shibanid descendants of Jochi later contested the throne with the Taibugids.
khanate-of-sibir.r: Sibir ruled Siberian Tatars and tribute-paying forest peoples such as the Khanty and Mansi, whose fur tribute was its main wealth. The Taibugid ruler Yadegar paid tribute to Ivan IV from 1555, but in 1563 the Shibanid Kuchum seized power, stopped payments and promoted Islam among his subjects with missionaries from Bukhara.
khanate-of-sibir.e: In 1582 the Cossack leader Yermak, employed by the Stroganov merchants, took Qashliq. Kuchum fought on from the steppe until his final defeat on the Ob in 1598, after which the khanate's lands became part of Russia.

kingdom-of-aquitaine.t: Carolingian sub-kingdom of south-western Francia, created by Charlemagne for his son Louis the Pious.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.o: After crushing the last independent dukes of the Early Duchy of Aquitaine, Charlemagne made Aquitaine a kingdom for his three-year-old son Louis, crowned by the pope in Rome in 781. It reached from the Loire to the Pyrenees and was meant to secure the frontier against Al-Andalus.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.r: Louis governed with Frankish counts and advisers, reformed monasteries with Benedict of Aniane and led campaigns into Spain, taking Barcelona in 801. Royal residences included Toulouse, Poitiers and Chasseneuil. After he became emperor in 814 the kingdom passed to his son Pepin I.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.e: After Pepin I died in 838, his son Pepin II fought a long war against his uncle Charles the Bald of West Francia. Charles installed his own sons, Charles the Child and Louis the Stammerer, and when Louis succeeded to West Francia in 877 the kingdom merged into it.

kingdom-of-denmark.t: The world's oldest continuing monarchy, founded by Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth, which once ruled England, Norway and much of the Baltic.
kingdom-of-denmark.o: Danish kings are mentioned from the 8th century, but the continuous kingdom is traced to Gorm the Old, who ruled from Jelling around 936. His son Harald Bluetooth raised the Jelling stone, which claims that he won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian, and built ring fortresses such as Trelleborg.
kingdom-of-denmark.r: Sweyn Forkbeard and Cnut the Great ruled England, and the Valdemar kings of the 12th and 13th centuries expanded into the Baltic. Margaret I united Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union in 1397. The Lutheran Reformation came in 1536, and Frederick III made the monarchy absolute in 1660. Copenhagen grew rich from the Sound Toll on Baltic shipping.
kingdom-of-denmark.e: Denmark lost Scania to Sweden in 1658, Norway in 1814 and Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864. A liberal constitution was adopted in 1849. Occupied by Germany in 1940-1945, Denmark became a welfare state and joined the European Community in 1973; the Faroe Islands and Greenland remain self-governing parts of the realm.

kingdom-of-livonia.t: Puppet kingdom created by Ivan the Terrible for the Danish prince Magnus during the Livonian War, which collapsed within eight years.
kingdom-of-livonia.o: Ivan IV of Russia, seeking to win the Baltic Germans to his side in the Livonian War, proclaimed Magnus of Holstein, brother of Frederick II of Denmark and ruler of Danish Ösel, king of Livonia in 1570. Magnus was to rule all Livonia as the tsar's vassal, and he married Ivan's relative Maria Staritskaya.
kingdom-of-livonia.r: Magnus resided at Oberpahlen (Põltsamaa) in central Estonia. His kingdom depended entirely on Russian troops and never controlled the major towns. A 30-week siege of Reval in 1570-1571 failed, and the Estonian and Livonian nobility largely refused to accept him.
kingdom-of-livonia.e: In 1577 Magnus tried to act independently and was punished by Ivan, who seized his towns. Magnus fled to Polish protection in 1578, renounced his royal title and died at Pilten in 1583. The kingdom disappeared, and its lands were divided among Poland-Lithuania, Sweden and Russia.

kingdom-of-england.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom unified by Aethelstan, transformed by the Norman Conquest and joined with Scotland in 1707.
kingdom-of-england.o: In 927 Aethelstan took York and received the submission of the northern rulers, completing the work of the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons. Viking kings briefly regained York until 954, and Danish kings Cnut and his sons ruled England from 1016 to 1042.
kingdom-of-england.r: Late Anglo-Saxon England had shires, a strong coinage and royal writs. After William the Conqueror's victory at Hastings in 1066, Norman lords, Domesday Book and a French-speaking elite reshaped society. Magna Carta in 1215, the growth of Parliament and common law, the wool trade and the Reformation under Henry VIII defined later centuries.
kingdom-of-england.e: England annexed Wales between 1283 and 1543 and ruled the Lordship of Ireland. James VI of Scotland inherited the crown in 1603, and after the Civil War and the Commonwealth of England, the Acts of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain.

kingdom-of-the-geats.t: The kingdom or kingdoms of the Geats in southern Sweden's Götaland, the people of Beowulf, later merged with the Svear to form Sweden.
kingdom-of-the-geats.o: Ptolemy and Jordanes mention Gautoi and Gautigoths in southern Scandinavia, and the Old English poem Beowulf makes the Geats and their king Hygelac its heroes. Hygelac's raid on Frisia, recorded by Gregory of Tours around 520, is one of the few datable events. Their heartland lay in Västergötland and Östergötland, around lakes Vänern and Vättern.
kingdom-of-the-geats.r: Whether the Geats formed one kingdom or several regional lordships is uncertain. Each land kept its own assembly and laws, later written down as the Västgötalagen. Society was based on farming, ironworking and a warrior aristocracy, and the region kept close ties with Denmark across the Kattegat.
kingdom-of-the-geats.e: Around 1000 the Geats came under the kings of the Svear, and Olof Skötkonung, traditionally baptised at Husaby in Västergötland, ruled both peoples. Götaland remained a distinct part of the Kingdom of Sweden, with its own lawmen, and its people sometimes elected rival kings into the 12th century.

klein-venedig.t: A short-lived German colony in Venezuela, leased by Emperor Charles V to the Welser banking house of Augsburg to pay off his debts.
klein-venedig.o: In 1528 Charles V granted the Welser family of Augsburg the right to colonise and govern the province of Venezuela in return for loans. The Welsers took over Coro, founded the year before by Juan de Ampíes, and sent the first German governor, Ambrosius Ehinger, in 1529.
klein-venedig.r: The Welser governors used the colony mainly as a base for expeditions into the interior in search of gold and the legendary El Dorado. Ehinger, Nikolaus Federmann, Georg Hohermuth von Speyer and Philipp von Hutten led long marches into the Andes and llanos, often with great brutality towards indigenous peoples. Little permanent settlement or farming developed, and German miners brought to the colony achieved little. Indigenous people were enslaved and sold.
klein-venedig.e: In 1546 the Spaniard Juan de Carvajal killed Philipp von Hutten and Bartholomäus Welser the younger. The Council of the Indies withdrew the Welser lease, confirmed in 1556, and the territory reverted to the Spanish Province of Venezuela.

kingdom-of-vaspurakan.t: An Armenian kingdom around Lake Van ruled by the Artsruni dynasty, best known for the sculpted Church of the Holy Cross on Aghtamar island.
kingdom-of-vaspurakan.o: The Artsruni family had long held the lands south and east of Lake Van. In 908 the Sajid emir Yusuf crowned Gagik Artsruni king as a rival to Smbat I of Bagratid Armenia, creating a separate kingdom under Sajid Emirate overlordship.
kingdom-of-vaspurakan.r: Gagik I built a palace and the Church of the Holy Cross on Aghtamar island between 915 and 921, its walls carved with biblical scenes, vines and royal portraits. The kingdom was rich in farmland, fish and trade, and kept a lively literary culture; the History of the House of Artsruni was written there. Its kings alternated between rivalry and alliance with the Bagratids.
kingdom-of-vaspurakan.e: Facing Seljuk raids, King Senekerim-Hovhannes ceded Vaspurakan to the Byzantine Empire in 1021 in exchange for estates around Sebasteia, and many Armenians followed him west. The Aghtamar church survives, restored in 2007, as the kingdom's most celebrated monument.

kingdom-of-al-abwab.t: A Christian Nubian kingdom on the Nile south of Makuria, once a province of Alodia, known mainly from Mamluk-era Arabic sources.
kingdom-of-al-abwab.o: Al-Abwab, Arabic for 'the gates', was originally the northern province of Alodia, centred near Kabushiya close to the junction of the Nile and the Atbara. By 1276 it appears as an independent kingdom, apparently having broken away as Alodian power declined.
kingdom-of-al-abwab.r: Almost nothing is known of its internal government. In 1276 its king Adur captured the fugitive Makurian king David, who had fled the Mamluk Sultanate's invasion, and handed him over to Sultan Baybars. Adur later corresponded with Sultan Qalawun, offering alliance against Makuria. Its people were Christian Nubians.
kingdom-of-al-abwab.e: The kingdom fades from the record in the late 14th century, probably absorbed by advancing Arab tribes and the general collapse of Christian Nubia. The area later fell within the sphere of the Abdallab Sheikhdom and the Funj Sultanate.

kingdom-of-jiaodong.t: A short-lived kingdom on the eastern Shandong peninsula, given to the young Qi king Tian Shi in 206 BCE, whose ruler was killed within months.
kingdom-of-jiaodong.o: Tian Shi had been installed as king of Qi by his uncle Tian Rong during the war against the Qin dynasty. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu demoted him to King of Jiaodong, with his capital at Jimo, giving Linzi to Tian Du.
kingdom-of-jiaodong.r: Tian Rong ordered his nephew to stay in Linzi, but Tian Shi, fearing Xiang Yu, slipped away to Jiaodong. The kingdom existed for only a few months and left no trace of separate government.
kingdom-of-jiaodong.e: Enraged, Tian Rong pursued Tian Shi and killed him at Jimo in 206 BCE, absorbing Jiaodong into Qi (206 BC).

kingdom-of-cornwall.t: The last surviving British kingdom of the south-west peninsula, which held out against Wessex until the 9th and 10th centuries.
kingdom-of-cornwall.o: Cornwall emerged as a separate British kingdom as the larger kingdom of Dumnonia shrank under West Saxon pressure. By the early 8th century Wessex had taken Devon, and the British realm beyond the Tamar became known as Kernow or Cornwall. Its kings are poorly recorded; Geraint fought Ine of Wessex around 710.
kingdom-of-cornwall.r: Cornwall kept its Brittonic language, saints' cults and links with Wales and Brittany. Tin mining and sea trade continued from Roman times. A defeat of a combined Cornish and Viking army at Hingston Down in 838 shows its kings still resisting the Kingdom of Wessex. The Annales Cambriae record the drowning of King Dungarth in 875.
kingdom-of-cornwall.e: Cornwall was brought under English control by the 9th century, and Aethelstan fixed the Tamar as the boundary around 936. It became part of the Kingdom of England, while the Cornish language survived into the 18th century.

kingdom-of-bulgaria.t: Bulgarian tsardom that fought on the losing side of three wars in search of Macedonia and Thrace, before its monarchy was abolished under Soviet influence.
kingdom-of-bulgaria.o: On 5 October 1908 Prince Ferdinand of the Principality of Bulgaria proclaimed independence from the Ottoman Empire and took the title of tsar. Bulgaria joined the Balkan League and won the First Balkan War in 1912, but its attack on Serbia and Greece in 1913 led to defeat in the Second Balkan War and loss of most of its gains.
kingdom-of-bulgaria.r: Hoping to win Macedonia, Bulgaria joined the Central Powers in 1915; defeat in 1918 brought Ferdinand's abdication in favour of Boris III and the harsh Treaty of Neuilly. Aleksandar Stamboliyski's agrarian government was overthrown in 1923, and Boris ruled personally from 1935. As an Axis ally from 1941 Bulgaria occupied Yugoslav Macedonia and Thrace; Jews of the old kingdom were saved from deportation in 1943.
kingdom-of-bulgaria.e: After Boris died in 1943, the Soviet army entered Bulgaria in September 1944 and the communist-led Fatherland Front seized power. A referendum in 1946 abolished the monarchy, and the boy king Simeon II went into exile, leading to the People's Republic of Bulgaria.

karamanids.t: The most powerful Turkish beylik of Anatolia after the Ottomans, centred on Karaman and Konya and their chief rival for two centuries.
karamanids.o: The Karamanids took their name from Karaman Bey, son of Nure Sufi, a Turkmen leader in the Taurus mountains. Around 1250 they rose against the weakened Sultanate of Rum, and Karaman's son Mehmed Bey briefly occupied Konya in 1277, where he reportedly decreed that Turkish alone be used in government.
karamanids.r: The Karamanids held the old Seljuk heartland, including Larende (Karaman) and later Konya, and saw themselves as heirs of the Seljuks. They allied with Venice, the Mamluks and the Aq Qoyunlu against the Ottomans. Alaeddin Bey was defeated and executed by Bayezid I in 1397, but Timur restored the dynasty in 1402. They built mosques and madrasas, such as the Ak Tekke and Hatuniye in Karaman.
karamanids.e: Mehmed II conquered most of the beylik in 1468, and the last Karamanid claimants were defeated by the 1480s; the region became the Ottoman province of Karaman.

kingdom-of-fermanagh.t: The Maguire lordship around Lough Erne, a Gaelic lordship of islands and churches whose last chief joined the Flight of the Earls.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.o: The Maguires rose in Fermanagh in the 13th century, with Donn Mor Maguire recognised as king in 1264. They displaced earlier rulers and became vassals of the O'Neills of the Kingdom of Tir Eoghain.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.r: Fermanagh was organised around Lough Erne, with islands, crannogs and monasteries such as Devenish. The Maguires built Enniskillen Castle in the 15th century. Their learned families compiled the Annals of Ulster on Belle Isle under Cathal Mac Maghnusa. Their economy rested on cattle and fishing.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.e: Hugh Maguire fought with Hugh O'Neill in the Nine Years' War and died in 1600. His brother Cuchonnacht left with the Flight of the Earls in 1607. Fermanagh was then planted with English and Scottish settlers, and Enniskillen became a Protestant garrison town.

kingdom-of-butua.t: The Torwa kingdom centred on Khami, heir to Great Zimbabwe in the south-west of the plateau and builder of richly decorated stone platforms.
kingdom-of-butua.o: Butua arose in the mid-15th century as the Kingdom of Zimbabwe declined, when the Torwa dynasty took control of the south-western plateau around modern Bulawayo. Its capital at Khami continued the Great Zimbabwe building tradition, and the kingdom controlled gold-bearing lands and rich cattle pastures.
kingdom-of-butua.r: Khami was built on terraced stone platforms faced with chequered and herringbone patterns, a style later seen at Danangombe and Naletale. Kings drew wealth from cattle and gold, trading with the Portuguese and Swahili through the Mutapa lands and the coast. Portuguese sources describe Butua as a rich gold country but give few details of its rulers or government.
kingdom-of-butua.e: In the mid-17th century a succession dispute brought in Portuguese allies and Khami was burnt. In the 1680s Changamire Dombo, a former Mutapa herder-general, overthrew the Torwa and founded the Rozvi state on the same lands.

kingdom-of-lotharingia.t: Northern share of Middle Francia, named after its king Lothair II, whose name survives in Lorraine.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.o: At the Treaty of Prüm in 855 Lothair I left the northern part of Middle Francia, from Frisia through the Low Countries and the Rhineland to the Vosges, to his son Lothair II. The kingdom took its name from him as the realm of Lothair.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.r: It held the old Carolingian heartland around Aachen, Metz, Trier and Cologne, with wealthy abbeys and episcopal cities. Lothair II's reign was dominated by his attempt to divorce his childless wife Teutberga and marry Waldrada, which Pope Nicholas I blocked, leaving him without a legitimate heir.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.e: After Lothair II died in 869 his uncles divided the kingdom at Meerssen in 870, and in 880 all of it passed to East Francia. Arnulf of Carinthia made his son Zwentibold king in 895, but he was killed in 900, and the land became the Duchy of Lotharingia.

kingdom-of-jiujiang.t: The Huai River kingdom of Ying Bu, the tattooed convict turned general, whose defection from Xiang Yu to Liu Bang in 204 BCE helped decide the Chu-Han war.
kingdom-of-jiujiang.o: Ying Bu, also called Qing Bu after the tattoo that marked him as a convict, led a band of escaped labourers in the rising against the Qin dynasty and became one of Xiang Yu's fiercest generals. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Jiujiang, with his capital at Lu (near Lu'an, Anhui).
kingdom-of-jiujiang.r: Jiujiang was Ying Bu's personal military domain on the Huai River, covering the old Jiujiang commandery. When Xiang Yu demanded troops, Ying Bu sent only token forces and became estranged from his overlord.
kingdom-of-jiujiang.e: Persuaded by Liu Bang's envoy Sui He, Ying Bu defected in 204 BCE; Chu troops overran Jiujiang and he fled to Liu Bang. In 203 BCE he was made King of Huainan over much the same land, but he rebelled against the Han Dynasty in 196 BCE and was killed.

kingdom-of-chimor.t: The largest kingdom of the Andean coast before the Incas, ruled from the vast adobe city of Chan Chan and stretching some 1,000 km along northern Peru.
kingdom-of-chimor.o: Chimor arose around 900 in the Moche valley, where the Moche had once ruled. According to a legend recorded by the Spanish, its founder Tacaynamo came by sea and established a dynasty at Chan Chan. Later rulers expanded by conquest, and Ñancen Pinco extended the kingdom over neighbouring valleys.
kingdom-of-chimor.r: The Chimú kings ruled from Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas, with walled palace compounds called ciudadelas that each served a ruler in life and as his tomb after death. The state managed extensive irrigation canals, including one linking the Chicama and Moche valleys. Chimú craftsmen excelled in gold and silver work and black burnished pottery. Around 1375 Chimor conquered the lands of the Sicán, and under Minchancaman it reached as far as Tumbes.
kingdom-of-chimor.e: Around 1470 the Incas under Túpac Inca Yupanqui conquered Chimor, captured Minchancaman and moved its craftsmen to Cusco. Chan Chan was later looted for gold by the Spanish. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

kingdom-of-brega.t: A kingdom of the southern Ui Neill on the fertile plain north of Dublin, home to Tara, Knowth and Newgrange and rival of Mide.
kingdom-of-brega.o: Brega emerged in the 7th century when the Sil nAedo Slaine, descendants of Aed Slaine of the southern Ui Neill, established themselves in the plain between the Liffey and the Boyne. Their rulers made the ancient passage tomb at Knowth into a royal residence.
kingdom-of-brega.r: Brega's kings shared the kingship of Tara with Clann Cholmain of Mide until the 8th century, but later lost out. The kingdom split into northern and southern parts. It contained monasteries such as Slane, Duleek and Monasterboice, and from the 9th century suffered heavy pressure from the Norse of the Kingdom of Dublin.
kingdom-of-brega.e: By the 11th century Brega was fragmented and dominated by Mide, Dublin and Leinster. Its lands passed into the Lordship of Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy in 1172, and its name survives in Irish place-names.

kingdom-of-belgium.t: The kingdom born of the 1830 revolution, an early industrial power and colonial ruler of the Congo, now a federal state and home of the EU's institutions.
kingdom-of-belgium.o: In August 1830 a revolt in Brussels against the United Kingdom of the Netherlands spread across the south. A provisional government declared independence in October, a congress adopted a liberal constitution in 1831, and Leopold of Saxe-Coburg became king. The Netherlands recognised Belgium in the Treaty of London of 1839, which also guaranteed its neutrality.
kingdom-of-belgium.r: Belgium became continental Europe's first industrial nation, with coal, iron and railways in Wallonia. Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State as a personal possession, notorious for forced labour, until Belgium annexed it in 1908. Germany invaded in 1914 and 1940; King Albert I led resistance in the First World War. Tension between French and Dutch speakers grew steadily.
kingdom-of-belgium.e: After 1945 Belgium co-founded Benelux, NATO and the European Communities, and Brussels hosts the EU and NATO headquarters. The Congo became independent in 1960. Language conflicts led to reforms that made Belgium a federal state of regions and communities in 1993.

kingdom-of-tylis.t: Celtic kingdom in eastern Thrace that extorted heavy tribute from Byzantium after the great Celtic invasion of 279 BCE.
kingdom-of-tylis.o: Celts who had invaded the Balkans in 279 BCE, defeating Macedon, settled in eastern Thrace under their leader Comontorius around 277 BCE. They founded a kingdom with its capital at Tylis, whose exact location near the Haemus or Strandzha mountains is still debated.
kingdom-of-tylis.r: The kingdom lived largely from tribute. According to Polybius, Byzantium paid it ever larger sums, rising to 80 talents a year. Celtic warriors ruled over a Thracian population, and coins of the last king, Cavarus, are known. Cavarus was praised as a statesman and mediated in the war between Byzantium and Rhodes in 220 BCE.
kingdom-of-tylis.e: Around 212 BCE the local Thracians rose against Celtic rule and destroyed the kingdom. Thracian dynasts reasserted themselves in the region, which later came under Macedonian and Roman influence.

kingdom-of-northumbria.t: The kingdom of the Angles north of the Humber, home of Bede, Lindisfarne and the Northumbrian Renaissance, later carved up by the Vikings.
kingdom-of-northumbria.o: Northumbria grew out of the union of the Kingdom of Bernicia and the Kingdom of Deira, which became lasting under Oswiu after his victory over Penda at the Winwaed in 655. At its height it stretched from the Humber to the Firth of Forth and west to the Irish Sea.
kingdom-of-northumbria.r: Northumbrian kings were Christian patrons of monasteries such as Lindisfarne, Wearmouth-Jarrow and Whitby, where the Synod of 664 chose Roman over Irish church practice. This produced the Lindisfarne Gospels, the Codex Amiatinus and the works of Bede and Alcuin. The 8th century was marked by frequent royal murders and depositions.
kingdom-of-northumbria.e: Defeat by the Picts at Nechtansmere in 685 checked its northward growth, and Vikings sacked Lindisfarne in 793. In 867 the Great Heathen Army took York, creating the Kingdom of York, while English rulers held out at Bamburgh. The last Viking king, Eric Bloodaxe, was expelled in 954.

kingdom-of-thomond.t: The O'Brien kingdom of North Munster, descendant of Brian Boru's power base, which kept its independence until 1543.
kingdom-of-thomond.o: Thomond arose from the Dal Cais lands in Clare and Limerick. In 1118 the Treaty of Glanmire, imposed by Turlough O'Connor, split Munster, leaving the O'Briens with the north, Tuadmumu. Their capital was Limerick, the former Kingdom of Limerick.
kingdom-of-thomond.r: The O'Brien kings were patrons of churches such as Holy Cross, Killaloe and Limerick's cathedral, founded by Domnall Mor O'Brien. After losing Limerick to the Normans in the 1190s, they ruled from Clonroad near Ennis. In 1318 Muirchertach O'Brien defeated the Normans at Dysert O'Dea, preserving Gaelic rule west of the Shannon.
kingdom-of-thomond.e: In 1543 Murrough O'Brien surrendered his kingship to Henry VIII and became Earl of Thomond under the Kingdom of Ireland. His lands became County Clare in the 1570s.

kasadi-sultanate.t: A dynasty of Yafa'i origin that ruled the Hadrami port of Mukalla until the Qu'aiti sultans took it in 1881.
kasadi-sultanate.o: The Kasadi were a family of the Yafa tribal confederation, whose men served as soldiers across Hadramawt. In the 18th century they established themselves as naqibs, or governors, of the port of Mukalla on the coast of Hadramawt and ruled it as a small independent state.
kasadi-sultanate.r: Mukalla was the main outlet of Hadramawt to the sea, and the Kasadi lived from customs on trade with India, East Africa and the Red Sea, including slaves and dates. Their rule was contested by Kathiri and other Yafa'i rivals and depended on armed retainers. Little is recorded about their internal administration.
kasadi-sultanate.e: In the 19th century the Kasadi came into conflict with the rising Qu'aiti Sultanate. With British support the Qu'aiti took Mukalla in 1881, and the Kasadi naqib went into exile in Zanzibar. Mukalla became the Qu'aiti capital.

kingdom-of-kakongo.t: A small Kongo coastal kingdom between Loango and Ngoyo whose port of Malemba was a busy Atlantic slave-trading harbour.
kingdom-of-kakongo.o: Kakongo was one of the Kikongo-speaking kingdoms north of the Congo estuary that recognised the senior Kingdom of Loango in early times. By the mid-16th century it had its own king, ruling from Kinguele, with lands between the coast and the Mayombe forest.
kingdom-of-kakongo.r: Its sacred king was elected by senior lineages and surrounded by ritual restrictions, and regional chiefs controlled much of the land. In the 18th century the port of Malemba became a major market for French and English slavers, and the Abbe Proyart's history of Loango and Kakongo (1776), based on French missionaries' reports, described the court and customs.
kingdom-of-kakongo.e: With the end of the slave trade Kakongo declined into a cluster of chiefdoms. In 1885 its lands were divided between Portuguese Angola, where they formed part of Cabinda, and the Congo Free State.

kingdom-of-italy.t: The united Italian monarchy of the House of Savoy, which completed unification, fought two world wars and fell to a referendum in 1946.
kingdom-of-italy.o: On 17 March 1861 the parliament in Turin proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II of the Kingdom of Sardinia king of Italy, after the annexation of Lombardy, central Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Venetia was added in 1866 and Rome taken from the Papal States in 1870.
kingdom-of-italy.r: The capital moved from Turin to Florence in 1865 and to Rome in 1871. Under the Statuto Albertino, liberal governments led by Agostino Depretis, Francesco Crispi and Giovanni Giolitti industrialised the north while millions emigrated. Italy entered the First World War in 1915. Benito Mussolini took power in 1922, built a Fascist dictatorship, signed the Lateran Treaty in 1929, conquered Ethiopia in 1936 and allied with Nazi Germany.
kingdom-of-italy.e: Defeat led the king to dismiss Mussolini in 1943 and sign an armistice with the Allies. On 2 June 1946 a referendum abolished the monarchy, creating the Italian Republic.

kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.t: Habsburg-ruled Kingdom of Hungary, from the narrow frontier strip of Royal Hungary to the reconquered kingdom that won self-government in 1867.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.o: After the death of Louis II at Mohács in 1526, a diet at Pozsony elected Ferdinand of Habsburg king, against the rival John Zápolya. The Ottoman capture of Buda in 1541 left the Habsburgs with only a western and northern strip, Royal Hungary, governed from Pressburg, where diets met and kings were crowned.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.r: Hungary kept its own diet, counties and noble privileges while the Habsburgs controlled war and foreign affairs from Vienna. Latin was the official language until 1844. Ottoman wars dominated until the reconquest of Buda in 1686 and the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699. Revolts by Bocskai, Thököly and Rákóczi defended Protestant and noble rights; the Reform Era brought Széchenyi's modernisation.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.e: The revolution of 1848 and the war of independence were crushed in 1849 with Russian help, followed by direct rule from Vienna. Defeat by Prussia in 1866 forced the Compromise of 1867, which created Austria-Hungary and the self-governing Kingdom of Hungary (1867-1918).

kaulonia.t: Achaean Greek city on the Calabrian coast, a dependency of Croton, destroyed by Dionysius I of Syracuse in 389 BCE.
kaulonia.o: Kaulonia was founded in the 7th century BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, near modern Monasterace Marina, by Achaean settlers, probably sent out by Croton, to secure its southern border against Locri.
kaulonia.r: Kaulonia remained closely tied to Croton. Its silver coins, showing Apollo carrying a small running figure and a deer, are among the finest of Magna Graecia. Excavations have uncovered a Doric temple, walls and houses, and a large floor mosaic with a dragon of the 3rd century BCE. Little is known of its government.
kaulonia.e: After defeating the Italiote League at the Elleporus river in 389 BCE, Dionysius I took Kaulonia, moved its people to Syracuse and gave its land to Locri. A smaller town revived later but was destroyed during the wars with Pyrrhus and Hannibal, and by the Roman period the site was deserted.

kingdom-of-illyria.t: Austrian crown land formed from the former French Illyrian Provinces, uniting Slovene and Adriatic lands under one title for three decades.
kingdom-of-illyria.o: When Austria recovered Napoleon's Illyrian Provinces, it kept the name and in 1816 created the Kingdom of Illyria as a crown land of the Austrian Empire. It comprised Carniola, Carinthia, Gorizia and Gradisca, Istria and Trieste, and for a few years Civil Croatia south of the Sava, which returned to Hungary in 1822.
kingdom-of-illyria.r: The kingdom was mainly an administrative label: it was divided into two governorates, at Laibach and Trieste, each run by Austrian officials under the system of Metternich, with provincial estates of little power. Laibach hosted the congress of 1821 on revolutions in Italy. Slovene cultural life grew, with the poet France Prešeren writing in Laibach in the 1830s and 1840s.
kingdom-of-illyria.e: After the revolutions of 1848, the 1849 constitution dissolved the kingdom into separate crown lands: Carniola, Carinthia and the Austrian Littoral. The emperor kept the title King of Illyria until 1918.

kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.t: Jagiellonian Poland, which with Lithuania defeated the Teutonic Knights, built a powerful noble democracy and enjoyed a Renaissance golden age.
kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.o: In 1385 the Union of Krewo arranged the marriage of Queen Jadwiga to Jogaila, grand duke of Lithuania, who was baptised and crowned in 1386 as Wladyslaw II Jagiello. His dynasty linked the Polish Crown to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and for a time also ruled Bohemia and Hungary.
kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.r: Together, Poland and Lithuania crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410, and the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 brought Royal Prussia and the port of Gdansk under the Crown. The nobility won growing privileges, and the 1505 statute Nihil novi required the consent of the Sejm for new laws. Krakow became a Renaissance centre, home to Copernicus and to Italian builders at Wawel castle.
kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.e: Sigismund II Augustus, last of the male Jagiellons, had no heir. To preserve the union, the Union of Lublin in 1569 merged the kingdom with Lithuania into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, with a common elected king and Sejm.
