kingdom-of-rheged.t: A British kingdom of the 'Old North' around the Solway, celebrated in Welsh poetry for King Urien and his battles against the Angles.
kingdom-of-rheged.o: Rheged emerged in the 6th century among the Brittonic kingdoms of northern Britain. Its location is uncertain, but scholars usually place it around Carlisle, Cumbria and Galloway. Its fame rests on poems attributed to Taliesin praising Urien Rheged, and on the Historia Brittonum.
kingdom-of-rheged.r: Urien is remembered as a leader of a coalition of British kings that besieged the Angles of Bernicia on Lindisfarne in the late 6th century, before he was murdered by a rival. Welsh tradition remembers the court as a centre of bardic patronage. Its society and economy are otherwise almost unknown.
kingdom-of-rheged.e: Rheged seems to have passed peacefully to Northumbria, perhaps through the marriage of Oswiu to Rhiainfellt, a descendant of Urien, around 638. Its memory lived on in Welsh poetry and Arthurian romance, where Urien and his son Owain became famous figures.

kingdom-of-iberia.t: The eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli, centred on Mtskheta, which adopted Christianity in the 4th century and laid the foundations of Georgian statehood and letters.
kingdom-of-iberia.o: Georgian chronicles credit Pharnavaz I with uniting Kartli around 302 BCE after the collapse of Achaemenid power, establishing his seat at Mtskheta and organising the land into duchies. Classical authors knew the kingdom as Iberia, a well-organised state on the Mtkvari river guarding key passes across the Caucasus.
kingdom-of-iberia.r: Kings ruled through regional eristavis, with a priestly and military aristocracy above a farming population. Iberia balanced between Rome and Persia, hosting Pompey's army in 65 BCE and later serving as a Roman client. King Mirian III adopted Christianity in the 330s through the mission of St Nino, and the Georgian alphabet appeared by the 5th century.
kingdom-of-iberia.e: Vakhtang I Gorgasali fought the Persians and founded Tbilisi as a new capital, but Sasanian pressure grew. In 580 the Sasanian Empire abolished the monarchy, and the land passed to local aristocrats who formed the Principality of Iberia.

kingdom-of-valencia.t: A realm of the Crown of Aragon created by James I's conquest, famed for its rice and silk, its 15th-century golden age and its own laws.
kingdom-of-valencia.o: James I of Aragon conquered the Third Taifa of Valencia between 1232 and 1245, taking the city in 1238. He made it a separate kingdom with its own legal code, the Furs of Valencia, rather than attaching it to Aragon or Catalonia.
kingdom-of-valencia.r: Catalan and Aragonese settlers lived alongside a large Muslim population that farmed the irrigated huertas, producing rice, sugar and silk. In the 15th century Valencia was the Crown's largest city, building the Silk Exchange and producing writers such as Ausiàs March and Joanot Martorell. The Germanies revolt of 1519-1523 and the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609 brought upheaval.
kingdom-of-valencia.e: Valencia backed the Habsburg claimant in the War of the Spanish Succession. After the Bourbon victory at Almansa in 1707, Philip V abolished its Furs by the Nueva Planta decrees, absorbing it into Bourbon Spain.

kingdom-of-mide.t: The midland kingdom around the sacred hill of Uisnech, ruled by the Clann Cholmain kings who often held the kingship of Tara.
kingdom-of-mide.o: Mide formed in the 6th century as the southern Ui Neill dynasties established themselves in the Irish midlands. The Clann Cholmain branch, descended from Colman Mor, emerged as its dominant line by the 8th century, ruling in what is now Westmeath with Uisnech as its symbolic centre.
kingdom-of-mide.r: Clann Cholmain kings alternated the kingship of Tara with the northern Ui Neill. Mael Sechnaill mac Maele Ruanaid and Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill were among the most powerful kings in Ireland. The kingdom contained great monasteries such as Durrow and Clonard, and royal sites at Lough Ennell.
kingdom-of-mide.e: After Brian Boru's rise, Mide was repeatedly partitioned by rival provincial kings. In 1172 Henry II granted it to Hugh de Lacy, creating the Lordship of Meath, and the native line survived only as minor lords.

kizzuwatna.t: Kizzuwatna, a Hurrian-Luwian kingdom of the Cilician plain, through whose priests Hurrian gods and rituals entered Hittite religion.
kizzuwatna.o: Kizzuwatna arose in the plain of Cilicia and the Taurus mountains after the Hittite Old Kingdom weakened in the 16th century BCE. Its kings ruled from Kummanni and other centres such as Adaniya and Lawazantiya, and balanced between the Hittites and the Mitanni Empire.
kizzuwatna.r: Its kings, such as Isputahsu, Pilliya and Sunassura, concluded treaties with Hittite rulers and with Idrimi of Mukish. The population mixed Luwian and Hurrian elements, and its temples of Teshub and Hebat and its priests specialised in purification rituals.
kizzuwatna.e: Around 1400 BCE Sunassura accepted Hittite overlordship, and Kizzuwatna was soon absorbed into the Hittite Empire. Its cults passed to the Hittite court; Queen Puduhepa was a priest's daughter from Lawazantiya. The region later became Que.

kingdom-of-elmet.t: Small British kingdom around Leeds that held out against the Angles until Edwin of Northumbria expelled its king Ceretic around 617.
kingdom-of-elmet.o: Elmet emerged after Roman rule ended as a British kingdom in the area of modern West Yorkshire, between the Pennines and the Vale of York. It is remembered in place names such as Sherburn-in-Elmet and Barwick-in-Elmet, and a 6th-century memorial stone at Llanaelhaearn in Gwynedd names a man of Elmet.
kingdom-of-elmet.r: Very little is known of its government. Welsh poetry praises a king Gwallawg, possibly of Elmet, who fought alongside Urien of Rheged against the Angles. The kingdom survived surrounded by the growing Anglian powers of Deira and Mercia, perhaps protected by its wooded and marshy terrain and by dyke systems such as those near Barwick.
kingdom-of-elmet.e: The Historia Brittonum records that Edwin of Northumbria seized Elmet and expelled its king Ceretic, usually dated around 617. The district appears in the Tribal Hidage as the Elmetsæte, and its people were absorbed into Northumbria.

kingdom-of-dumnonia.t: Post-Roman British kingdom of Devon and Cornwall, with its high-status site at Tintagel, which slowly gave way to the West Saxons.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.o: Dumnonia grew from the Roman civitas of the Dumnonii after Roman rule ended around 410, covering Cornwall, Devon and parts of Somerset. In the 6th century Gildas denounced its king Constantine for murder and sacrilege. Many Britons from the region emigrated to Armorica, where the district of Domnonée in Brittany carries the same name.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.r: Little is recorded of its government. Imported Mediterranean pottery and glass at Tintagel, and at sites such as Bantham, show trade with the Byzantine world, probably for tin, in the 5th and 6th centuries. Christianity was organised around local saints and monasteries, and inscribed memorial stones in Latin and ogham mark the burials of its elite.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.e: The West Saxons pushed westward through Somerset and Devon in the 7th century, and around 705 Aldhelm wrote to King Geraint urging Roman practice on Easter. In 710 Ine of Wessex fought Geraint, and Devon was gradually absorbed. A smaller British kingdom of Cornwall survived until the 9th century.

kingdom-of-breifne.t: A Gaelic kingdom of the drumlin country of Leitrim and Cavan, ruled by the O'Rourkes, whose king Tigernan Ua Ruairc helped bring about the Norman invasion of 1169.
kingdom-of-breifne.o: Breifne emerged in the 8th century among the Ui Briuin of Connacht, whose branch, the Ui Briuin Breifne, settled the lakes and hills of later Leitrim and Cavan. The O'Rourke family became its leading dynasty by the 10th century.
kingdom-of-breifne.r: Breifne was an upland kingdom of cattle, lakes and crannog dwellings. Its kings occasionally claimed the kingship of Connacht. Tigernan Ua Ruairc, ruler from about 1124 to 1172, fought Diarmait Mac Murchada of Leinster, who had abducted his wife Derbforgaill; their feud helped bring the Normans to Ireland. Tigernan was killed at Tlachtga in 1172.
kingdom-of-breifne.e: After the death of its king in 1256, Breifne split between the O'Rourkes of West Breifne and the O'Reillys of East Breifne. Both survived until the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

kingdom-of-africa.t: The Norman Kingdom of Sicily's string of coastal conquests in Ifriqiya, a short-lived Christian dominion over Muslim ports from Tripoli to Mahdia.
kingdom-of-africa.o: Under Roger II, the Kingdom of Sicily exploited famine and the collapse of the Zirid emirate to seize the North African coast. His admiral George of Antioch took Tripoli in 1146, and in 1148 Mahdia, Sousse and Sfax fell as the Zirid ruler al-Hasan fled. Gabès and other towns accepted Sicilian overlordship, forming what Roger styled his realm of Africa.
kingdom-of-africa.r: The Normans ruled indirectly, as they did with the Muslims of Sicily. Local qadis and governors stayed in place, Islamic law and worship continued, and the towns paid tribute to Palermo. Garrisons held the ports, and the aim was control of grain and the sea lanes between Sicily and Africa rather than settlement or conversion.
kingdom-of-africa.e: After Roger's death in 1154 the towns revolted, starting with Sfax in 1156. The Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min marched east, besieged Mahdia and took it in January 1160, ending Christian rule. The episode foreshadowed later European footholds on the Maghreb coast.

kingdom-of-lundu.t: A Manganja kingdom of the lower Shire valley, a southern offshoot of the Maravi confederacy linked to the feared Zimba warriors.
kingdom-of-lundu.o: The Lundu title was held by a branch of the Phiri ruling clan of the Kingdom of Maravi, which settled in the lower Shire valley among the Manganja. By the late 16th century the Lundu was a powerful independent ruler, and Portuguese writers associated him with the Zimba, warrior bands that attacked Portuguese posts on the Zambezi and coastal towns.
kingdom-of-lundu.r: The Lundu controlled routes carrying ivory from the interior to the coast near Quelimane and Mozambique Island and drew tribute from Manganja chiefs. Religious authority was closely tied to the Mbona rain shrine at Khulubvi, a cult the Lundu dynasty is said to have taken over and reshaped.
kingdom-of-lundu.e: The kingdom was brought back under Maravi overlordship by Kalonga Masula in the early 17th century and gradually lost power to chiefs and Afro-Portuguese prazo holders. By around 1800 it had broken up, and 19th-century Kololo and Yao incursions completed its decline.

kingdom-of-tiryns.t: Mycenaean citadel near the Argolic Gulf whose Cyclopean walls, among the most massive of the Bronze Age, so impressed later Greeks that they credited them to giants.
kingdom-of-tiryns.o: Tiryns stands on a low rock near the coast of the Argolid, settled from the Early Bronze Age, when a large circular building was erected on its summit. Mycenaean rulers built a fortified palace from c. 1600 BCE, and in the 14th and 13th centuries BCE the citadel was enclosed by walls up to 8 metres thick, with vaulted galleries.
kingdom-of-tiryns.r: The palace had a megaron with painted floors and frescoes of women in procession and boar hunts. Tiryns probably served as the harbour and partner, or subordinate, of nearby Mycenae. A few Linear B tablets and inscribed jars show palace administration. Greek myth tied it to Perseus and to Heracles, who served King Eurystheus.
kingdom-of-tiryns.e: The palace was destroyed c. 1200 BCE, but unlike most centres Tiryns continued, with a large lower town and a rebuilt hall into the 12th century BCE. It later became a small city absorbed by Argos c. 470 BCE. Its walls are a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with Mycenae.

kingdom-of-bosnia.t: Medieval Bosnian kingdom of the Kotromanić dynasty, briefly the strongest Balkan state, until the Ottomans conquered it in 1463.
kingdom-of-bosnia.o: Ban Tvrtko I of the Banate of Bosnia, having won lands in western Serbia, was crowned king of the Serbs and Bosnia in 1377 at Mile near Visoko, claiming descent from the Nemanjić dynasty.
kingdom-of-bosnia.r: Tvrtko expanded to the Adriatic, taking Kotor and much of Dalmatia and Croatia by his death in 1391. Royal power then weakened as great nobles such as Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić and Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, whose lands became Herzegovina, made and unmade kings. Silver from Srebrenica supported the state, and the Bosnian Church, Catholicism and Orthodoxy coexisted. Carved tombstones called stećci mark the burials of the period.
kingdom-of-bosnia.e: The Ottomans took parts of the kingdom from the 1430s. In 1463 Mehmed II invaded, captured Bobovac and executed the last king, Stephen Tomašević, at Jajce. Most of Bosnia became an Ottoman province, while Hungary briefly held a northern banate.

kingdom-of-carchemish.t: Neo-Hittite Carchemish, the leading Iron Age kingdom on the Euphrates, heir to Hittite royal tradition and famed for its sculpted walls.
kingdom-of-carchemish.o: When the Hittite Empire fell c. 1180 BCE, the Viceroyalty of Carchemish survived, and King Kuzi-Teshub took the title great king. His descendants and their successors ruled a kingdom astride the Euphrates crossing, in what is now the Turkish-Syrian border.
kingdom-of-carchemish.r: Kings of the house of Suhi, and later Astiru and the regent Yariri, recorded their deeds in Luwian hieroglyphs on basalt reliefs lining processional ways, the Long Wall of Sculpture. Carchemish grew rich on river trade and textiles. British Museum excavations from 1911, with Leonard Woolley and T. E. Lawrence, uncovered much of the city.
kingdom-of-carchemish.e: The kingdom paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire from the 9th century BCE. In 717 BCE Sargon II deposed King Pisiri for plotting with Phrygia and turned Carchemish into a province. In 605 BCE the city saw Nebuchadnezzar's victory over Egypt.

kingdom-of-hanover.t: North German kingdom tied to the British crown until 1837, then ruled by its own kings until Prussia annexed it in 1866.
kingdom-of-hanover.o: The Congress of Vienna raised the Electorate of Hanover to a kingdom in 1814, with George III as king, and enlarged it with East Frisia, Hildesheim and Osnabrück. It continued in personal union with Great Britain under George III, George IV and William IV, governed by a viceroy.
kingdom-of-hanover.r: When Victoria became British queen in 1837, Salic law excluded her and her uncle Ernest Augustus became King of Hanover. He revoked the liberal constitution of 1833, and seven Göttingen professors who protested, including the Grimm brothers, were dismissed. The kingdom was largely agrarian, though railways and the port of Harburg developed. George V, blind from youth, became king in 1851.
kingdom-of-hanover.e: George V sided with Austria in 1866. His army won at Langensalza but surrendered two days later. Prussia annexed Hanover as a province, and the Guelph party long campaigned for restoration.

kingdom-of-thessalonica.t: Crusader kingdom created for Boniface of Montferrat after the Fourth Crusade, which lasted only twenty years before falling to Epirus.
kingdom-of-thessalonica.o: Boniface of Montferrat, leader of the Fourth Crusade, lost the election for Latin emperor in 1204 but received Thessalonica and much of Macedonia and Thessaly. He married Margaret of Hungary, widow of Isaac II, and invaded central and southern Greece, granting fiefs such as the Duchy of Athens and the Marquisate of Bodonitsa to his followers.
kingdom-of-thessalonica.r: The kingdom was ruled by Lombard nobles from northern Italy over a Greek population, under nominal homage to the Latin Empire. A Latin archbishop replaced the Orthodox metropolitan. Boniface was killed by the Bulgarians of Kaloyan in 1207, leaving his infant son Demetrius under a regency; the Lombard barons' revolt of 1208-1209 was suppressed by Emperor Henry.
kingdom-of-thessalonica.e: Weakened by internal divisions and Bulgarian attacks, the kingdom was gradually conquered by Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus, who took Thessalonica itself in 1224 and founded the Empire of Thessalonica. The title survived among Western claimants.

kingdom-of-soloi.t: Cypriot kingdom on Morphou Bay, said to have taken its name from the Athenian lawgiver Solon, who advised its king.
kingdom-of-soloi.o: Soloi lay on the bay of Morphou in north-western Cyprus, near the copper mines of Skouriotissa. Founded in the early Iron Age, it was a city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE. Plutarch tells that King Philocyprus moved the city to a better site on Solon's advice and named it after him.
kingdom-of-soloi.r: Soloi grew rich on copper and farmland. Its king Aristocyprus fell fighting the Persians at Salamis in 497 BCE, after which Soloi endured a five-month siege. The palace of Vouni on a nearby hill, built in the 5th century BCE, may have been used to watch over Soloi. King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre in 332 BCE.
kingdom-of-soloi.e: Its last king, Eunostos, married Eirene, daughter of Ptolemy I, and the kingdom was absorbed into Ptolemaic Cyprus c. 312 BCE. Soloi remained a city into Roman and early Christian times.

kingdom-of-deira.t: The Anglian kingdom of the Yorkshire Wolds and York, whose boys in a Roman slave market are said to have inspired Pope Gregory's mission to the English.
kingdom-of-deira.o: Deira developed from Anglian settlement in east Yorkshire, perhaps taking over a British territory whose name it kept. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle names Aelle as its first king from 560. Bede tells how Gregory the Great, seeing Deiran slave boys in Rome, punned that they were not Angles but angels.
kingdom-of-deira.r: Deira's centre lay around York and the Wolds. Edwin, son of Aelle, ruled all Northumbria from 616, accepted baptism from Paulinus at York in 627 and built the first church on the site of York Minster. After his death in 633 Deira had its own kings again, including Oswine, killed on the orders of Oswiu in 651.
kingdom-of-deira.e: Bernician kings repeatedly dominated Deira. Its last sub-king, Oethelwald, supported Penda against Oswiu and disappeared after the Winwaed in 655. Deira became the southern half of the Kingdom of Northumbria, its name surviving in later sources.

kingdom-of-the-iberians.t: The kingdom of the Georgian Bagratids in Tao-Klarjeti, a land of great monasteries whose rulers prepared the unification of Georgia.
kingdom-of-the-iberians.o: Early in the 9th century the Bagratid prince Ashot I moved from Kartli to the south-western borderland of Klarjeti, where he rebuilt Artanuji and the family won Byzantine titles. In 888 his grandson Adarnase IV took the title king of the Iberians, restoring the royal title in Georgia after three centuries.
kingdom-of-the-iberians.r: Several Bagratid branches shared rule over Tao, Klarjeti and Shavsheti, with titles granted by the Byzantine Empire. Monks led by Grigol of Khandzta founded monasteries, and great churches rose at Oshki, Ishkhani and Khakhuli, centres of Georgian learning. David III Kouropalates of Tao made the region powerful and helped Byzantium against the rebel Bardas Skleros.
kingdom-of-the-iberians.e: When David III died in 1000, Basil II annexed his lands of Tao to Byzantium. The remaining Bagratid holdings passed to Bagrat III, who in 1008 united them with Abkhazia and Kartli in the Kingdom of Georgia.

kingdom-of-the-lombards.t: Germanic kingdom that ruled most of Italy from 568 until Charlemagne's conquest in 774, shaping its regions and its law.
kingdom-of-the-lombards.o: The Lombards, a Germanic people settled in Pannonia, crossed into Italy under King Alboin in 568, just after the Gothic Wars had exhausted the peninsula. They overran the north and much of the centre and south, took Pavia in 572 after a long siege and made it their capital, leaving the Byzantines with Ravenna, Rome and the coasts.
kingdom-of-the-lombards.r: The king ruled with powerful dukes, some nearly independent, such as those of Spoleto and Benevento. Under Queen Theodelinda the Lombards began to move from Arian to Catholic Christianity. Rothari issued a written law code, the Edict of Rothari, in 643. Liutprand strengthened royal power and in 728 gave Sutri to the Pope, a step towards the Papal States. Lombard art survives at Cividale.
kingdom-of-the-lombards.e: When Aistulf took Ravenna in 751 and threatened Rome, the popes turned to the Franks. Pepin the Short defeated Aistulf, and Charlemagne besieged Pavia and captured King Desiderius in 774, taking the title King of the Lombards. The region of Lombardy keeps their name.

kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.t: A short-lived monarchy declared by the Council of Lithuania in 1918, which elected a German prince as King Mindaugas II.
kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.o: Germany recognised Lithuanian independence in March 1918 on condition of close ties with the German Empire, and plans circulated to unite the crown with Prussia or Saxony. To avoid this, the Council of Lithuania on 11 July 1918 proclaimed a constitutional monarchy and invited Prince Wilhelm of Urach, a Catholic from Wurttemberg, to be king.
kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.r: Wilhelm accepted and took the name Mindaugas II, after the medieval king of the Kingdom of Lithuania, but he never came to Lithuania and the German authorities did not recognise his election. In practice the country remained under German military occupation, while the council prepared Lithuanian institutions.
kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.e: As Germany's defeat approached, the Council revoked the election on 2 November 1918 and adopted provisional republican principles. The state continued as the Republic of Lithuania (1918-1940). Wilhelm never set foot in the country, and the episode is remembered as a curiosity of Lithuanian state-building.

kingdom-of-vannius.t: A Roman client kingdom of the Quadi north of the Danube, set up to house the followers of the fallen kings Maroboduus and Catualda.
kingdom-of-vannius.o: After Maroboduus and his successor Catualda were driven out in 19, their followers were settled by Rome north of the Danube between the March (Morava) and Váh rivers. Drusus the Younger installed Vannius, of the Quadi, as their king, creating a buffer state opposite the Roman frontier in Pannonia and Noricum.
kingdom-of-vannius.r: Vannius ruled for some thirty years as a client of Rome. Tacitus says he was at first respected, then grew arrogant, enriching himself through raiding and tolls on traders. The kingdom grew wealthy on commerce along the Amber Road between the Baltic and Carnuntum, and Roman goods reached its elite graves.
kingdom-of-vannius.e: In 50 Vannius was overthrown by his nephews Vangio and Sido with the help of the Hermunduri and Lugii. Emperor Claudius refused to intervene but gave him refuge in Pannonia. The nephews divided the kingdom and stayed loyal to Rome; Sido fought for Vespasian in 69.

kingdom-of-strathclyde.t: British kingdom of the Clyde, first centred on Dumbarton Rock and later at Govan, which outlasted the other northern Brittonic realms until absorbed into Scotland.
kingdom-of-strathclyde.o: The kingdom grew from the British people of the Clyde, descendants of the Damnonii, after Roman influence ended. Its early king Ceretic, probably the Coroticus whom St Patrick rebuked for slave-raiding in the 5th century, ruled from Alt Clut, the fortress on Dumbarton Rock.
kingdom-of-strathclyde.r: Rhydderch Hael, a king of the late 6th century, appears in the lives of Columba and Kentigern, the patron saint of Glasgow. In 642 Owain son of Beli defeated and killed Domnall Brecc of Dál Riata at Strathcarron. Society rested on cattle farming, and its people spoke Cumbric, a northern form of Brittonic. After 870 the royal centre moved to Govan, where a fine collection of carved stones survives.
kingdom-of-strathclyde.e: In 870 Viking kings from Dublin took Dumbarton after a four-month siege. The renewed kingdom, often called Cumbria, expanded south into Cumbria in the 10th century. Its last known king, Owain the Bald, may have died around 1018, and it was absorbed into the kingdom of Scotland during the 11th century.

kingdom-of-phrygia.t: Phrygia, the Iron Age kingdom of Gordion in central Anatolia, home of King Midas and the Gordian knot.
kingdom-of-phrygia.o: The Phrygians, probably migrants from the Balkans after the Late Bronze Age collapse, settled the plateau west of the Kızılırmak. By the 9th century BCE they had built a fortified capital at Gordion on the Sakarya river, with a citadel of megaron halls. Assyrian texts call the people Mushki.
kingdom-of-phrygia.r: Phrygian kings ruled from Gordion and built huge burial mounds; Tumulus MM held a king with bronze vessels and fine wooden furniture. Midas, the Mita of Assyrian records, was a rival of Sargon II and sent gifts to Delphi. The Phrygians wrote in an alphabet adapted from Greek and worshipped the mother goddess Matar, later Cybele.
kingdom-of-phrygia.e: Cimmerian invaders sacked Gordion in the early 7th century BCE, and Greek tradition says Midas killed himself. Phrygia then fell under the Kingdom of Lydia and the Achaemenid Empire, though its language and cults survived for centuries.

kingdom-of-atholl.t: A Pictish kingdom in the central Highlands whose name, 'New Ireland', hints at Gaelic influence, later a Scottish earldom.
kingdom-of-atholl.o: Atholl, Athfotla, appears in Irish annals from the 8th century, when a king of Atholl was drowned by Oengus son of Fergus, king of the Picts, in 739. The name is usually interpreted as 'New Ireland', suggesting Gaelic settlement or influence in the Pictish highlands of Perthshire. Fotla is also one of the seven Pictish provinces.
kingdom-of-atholl.r: Atholl seems to have had its own kings within the Pictish overkingship. Its lands in the valleys of the Tay, Tummel and Garry were pastoral and thinly peopled. Dunkeld, on its edge, became a major church centre in the 9th century.
kingdom-of-atholl.e: Atholl was absorbed into the Kingdom of Scotland as a mormaerdom and later an earldom. Its rulers produced Crinan, abbot of Dunkeld, father of King Duncan I, linking Atholl with the royal house.

kingdom-of-seisyllwg.t: A Welsh kingdom of Ceredigion and Ystrad Tywi, named after King Seisyll, which merged with Dyfed to form Deheubarth.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.o: Seisyllwg was created when Seisyll ap Clydog of Ceredigion added Ystrad Tywi, the Tywi valley, to his realm in the 8th century. The new territory was named after him. Little else is known of its early rulers beyond genealogies.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.r: The kingdom covered much of later Cardiganshire and Carmarthenshire, a land of upland pasture and coastal farms with important churches such as Llanbadarn Fawr. Its last native king, Gwgon, drowned in 871, and it passed by marriage to Rhodri the Great of Gwynedd, whose son Cadell inherited it.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.e: Cadell's son Hywel Dda united Seisyllwg with Dyfed around 920, creating the Kingdom of Deheubarth. The name Seisyllwg fell out of use, though Ceredigion persists as a county.

kingdom-of-morgannwg.t: A south-east Welsh kingdom formed by the union of Glywysing and Gwent, whose name survives in Glamorgan.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.o: Morgannwg, 'Morgan's land', is traditionally named after Morgan Hen ab Owain, who united the older kingdoms of Glywysing and Gwent around 942. Earlier rulers of the region are known from the charters of the Book of Llandaff.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.r: The kingdom covered the fertile vale and uplands between the Tywi and the Wye, with churches such as Llandaff and Llancarfan. Its kings dealt with English rulers, and Morgan Hen attended Aethelstan's court. After his death in 974 Gwent and Glywysing separated again at times, and the kingdom was later ruled by Gruffydd ap Llywelyn and then Caradog ap Gruffydd.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.e: Iestyn ap Gwrgant, the last native ruler, was overthrown around 1090 by the Norman Robert Fitzhamon, who created the Lordship of Glamorgan. The name survives in the counties of Glamorgan.

kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.t: Tiny Welsh kingdom between the Wye and the Ithon whose rulers claimed descent from Vortigern, the British ruler blamed for inviting the Saxons.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.o: Gwrtheyrnion means 'the land of Gwrtheyrn', the Welsh form of Vortigern. The Historia Brittonum, written in 829 or 830, says that after Vortigern's fall his son Pascent was granted Buellt and Gwrtheyrnion by Ambrosius, and that its ruler in the author's day, Fernmail, descended from him. The territory lay around Rhayader in what became Radnorshire.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.r: Almost nothing is known of its government beyond this genealogy. It was a small upland territory of river valleys and hill pasture, often ruled together with the neighbouring Kingdom of Buellt, and its dynasty used its link with Vortigern, whatever its truth, to assert ancient legitimacy.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.e: Gwrtheyrnion was absorbed by more powerful Welsh kingdoms, probably in the 10th century, and later formed a cantref of the Middle March between Wye and Severn, held by Welsh and Anglo-Norman lords such as the Mortimers.

kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.t: The dual kingdom of Ibn Saud, uniting the holy cities with Najd, and the immediate forerunner of Saudi Arabia.
kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.o: After conquering the Kingdom of Hejaz, Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud was proclaimed King of the Hejaz in Mecca in January 1926 while remaining Sultan of Nejd. In 1927 Nejd was also raised to a kingdom, and the two realms were ruled in personal union.
kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.r: The Hejaz kept its own administration and consultative council under Ibn Saud's son Faisal as viceroy, while Najd was ruled directly. The Treaty of Jeddah in 1927 brought British recognition of full independence. The Ikhwan, angry at modern innovations and limits on raiding, rebelled; Ibn Saud defeated them at the Battle of Sabilla in 1929 and crushed the revolt by 1930.
kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.e: On 23 September 1932 a royal decree unified the dual kingdom as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, named after the ruling family.

kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.t: A small Anglian sub-kingdom on the Welsh border in Herefordshire and Shropshire, ruled by Merewalh's dynasty under Mercia.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.o: The Magonsaete, perhaps named after Magnis (Kenchester), emerged in the mid 7th century in the borderlands west of the Severn. Their first known ruler was Merewalh, whom later tradition made a son of Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia, though this is uncertain.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.r: Merewalh's family was noted for piety: his daughter Mildburh founded the abbey of Much Wenlock, and other children became saints. A bishopric at Hereford served the people. The rulers were sub-kings under Mercian overlordship, and the population included many Britons.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.e: The dynasty disappears from record in the 8th century, and the territory was absorbed directly into Mercia. Its outline survived as the diocese of Hereford.

kingdom-of-limerick.t: A Norse town-kingdom on the Shannon estuary whose fall to the Dal Cais opened the way for Brian Boru's rise.
kingdom-of-limerick.o: Vikings had raided the Shannon since the 9th century, and in 922 Tomrair mac Ailchi established a permanent fleet base at Limerick, Hlymrekr. The settlement competed with the Kingdom of Dublin for control of the Irish Sea trade and raided deep into Connacht and Munster.
kingdom-of-limerick.r: Limerick was a fortified trading port on an island in the Shannon, dealing in slaves and plunder. Its kings were rivals of Dublin's dynasty, losing a war with them in 937. In the 960s Ivar of Limerick allied with Irish kings of Munster against the rising Dal Cais.
kingdom-of-limerick.e: Mathgamain and Brian Boru of the Dal Cais defeated the Norse at Sulcoit in 967 and sacked the town. Brian killed Ivar and his sons on Scattery Island in 977. Limerick became the O'Brien capital and later the seat of the Kingdom of Thomond.

kingdom-of-brittany.t: Breton kingdom forged in the 9th century by Nominoe and his successors, who won independence from the Carolingian Franks.
kingdom-of-brittany.o: Louis the Pious appointed the Breton noble Nominoe as his representative in Brittany in 831. After Louis's death Nominoe broke with Charles the Bald, defeating him at Ballon in 845. His son Erispoe won again at Jengland in 851, and the Treaty of Angers recognised him as king with Rennes, Nantes and the Pays de Retz.
kingdom-of-brittany.r: The kingdom united Domnonée, Cornouaille and Broërec with the Frankish marches. Salomon, who killed Erispoe and took the throne in 857, gained the Cotentin and Avranchin in 867. The kings ruled through local machtierns and monasteries such as Redon, and set up a Breton church province at Dol.
kingdom-of-brittany.e: After internal conflict Alan the Great defeated the Vikings at Questembert around 888, but after his death in 907 Vikings overran Brittany. Alan Barbetorte returned from England in 936 and expelled them by 939, ruling as duke and founding the Duchy of Brittany.

kerma.t: The first great kingdom of Nubia, centred on Kerma at the Third Cataract and for centuries a rival to pharaonic Egypt.
kerma.o: Kerma culture developed in Upper Nubia from about 2500 BCE, with its centre at Kerma near the Third Cataract of the Nile. The town grew from a farming and cattle-herding settlement into the capital of a kingdom that Egyptian texts called Kush, controlling the river trade in gold, ivory, ebony and cattle.
kerma.r: The rulers lived in a walled city dominated by the Western Deffufa, a massive mud-brick temple. Kings were buried under huge circular tumuli, some with hundreds of sacrificed attendants. Kerma potters made distinctive polished black-topped red ware. At its height, in the 17th century BCE, Kerma raided as far as Elkab in Egypt and allied with the Hyksos of the Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt against Thebes.
kerma.e: The New Kingdom pharaohs struck back. Thutmose I sacked Kerma around 1500 BCE, and Egypt annexed Nubia as the Viceroyalty of Kush. Kerma traditions survived beneath Egyptian rule and fed into the later Kushite Empire of Napata and Meroë.

kingdom-of-barwe.t: A Shona kingdom of central Mozambique whose rulers, the Makombe, resisted Portuguese conquest into the 20th century.
kingdom-of-barwe.o: Barwe emerged around 1500 between the Mutapa lands and the Kingdom of Manyika, ruled by a dynasty related to the Mutapa house. Its rulers, titled Makombe, controlled routes between the Zambezi and the gold-bearing highlands.
kingdom-of-barwe.r: The Makombe was a sacred king whose installation required ritual approval, including holy water sent from the Kingdom of Uteve, and spirit mediums held great influence. The kingdom traded with Portuguese posts at Sena and Tete and frequently fought Afro-Portuguese prazo holders and neighbouring states. In the 19th century it fought off the Gaza Nguni and the warlords of the Zambezi.
kingdom-of-barwe.e: After repeated campaigns, Portuguese forces occupied Barwe in 1902, ending its independence. A major rising in 1917, led by Barwe nobles and spirit mediums, was crushed, and the area was absorbed into Portuguese Mozambique.

kingdom-of-odoacer.t: Kingdom of the barbarian general Odoacer, who deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in 476 and ruled Italy until 493.
kingdom-of-odoacer.o: Odoacer, an officer of Germanic origin in the Roman army in Italy, led a mutiny of soldiers demanding land. In 476 he defeated the general Orestes and deposed his son, the young emperor Romulus Augustulus, sending the imperial regalia to Zeno in Constantinople. His soldiers proclaimed him king.
kingdom-of-odoacer.r: Odoacer ruled from Ravenna as king while nominally recognising the eastern emperor. He kept the Roman administration and the Senate, appointing Roman consuls and officials, and gave his soldiers land, traditionally a third of estates. An Arian Christian, he tolerated the Catholic Church. He gained Sicily from the Vandals by treaty, took Dalmatia and destroyed the Rugian kingdom on the Danube in 487.
kingdom-of-odoacer.e: Zeno sent Theodoric and the Ostrogoths against Odoacer in 489. After defeats on the Isonzo and at Verona, Odoacer held out in Ravenna for three years. He agreed to share power in 493 but was killed by Theodoric at a banquet days later, and the Ostrogothic Kingdom replaced his.

kurin-khanate.t: A khanate created by Russia in the Lezgin lands of southern Dagestan, which lasted until the end of the Caucasian War.
kurin-khanate.o: In 1812 the Russian authorities formed the Kurin Khanate from Lezgin communities in the Samur river area of southern Dagestan, which had been free societies. They placed it under Aslan Khan, a member of the Kazikumukh ruling family, as a Russian ally, with its seat at Kurakh.
kurin-khanate.r: The khanate governed Lezgin villages of farmers and herders under Russian supervision. Its khans held Russian military rank and pensions, collected taxes and supplied troops. Aslan Khan also gained the Kazikumukh Khanate, and the two were often ruled together. Kurakh had a Russian fort, and the khanate remained loyal during the wars with the Caucasian Imamate.
kurin-khanate.e: After the defeat of Shamil and the stabilisation of Dagestan, the Russian Empire abolished the khanate in 1864 and incorporated it into the Kyurin district of the Dagestan Oblast. The area remains the heartland of the Lezgin people in southern Dagestan.

kanyok-kingdom.t: A Luba-related kingdom of the southern Kasai, long a rival of the Luba Empire, whose history is known mainly from oral tradition.
kanyok-kingdom.o: The Kanyok lived between the Lubilash and Mbuji-Mayi rivers in the southern Kasai and shared many institutions and origin stories with their Luba neighbours. A centralised kingship under the Mwen a Kanyok had formed by the 17th century, according to oral traditions.
kanyok-kingdom.r: The Mwen a Kanyok was a sacred ruler who governed through titled officials and village chiefs. Kanyok traditions recall repeated wars with the Luba Empire, sometimes as rival and sometimes as tributary. In the 19th century the kingdom was drawn into regional trade and raiding linked to the Chokwe and other slave traders.
kanyok-kingdom.e: The Congo Free State extended its authority over the Kanyok in the 1890s, ending the kingdom's independence. Its history has been reconstructed by historians largely from oral traditions collected in the 20th century.

kingdom-of-sai.t: One of the three kingdoms carved from the Qin heartland in 206 BCE, held by the former Qin officer Sima Xin, which fell to Liu Bang within months.
kingdom-of-sai.o: Sima Xin had been chief clerk under the Qin general Zhang Han and surrendered with him to Xiang Yu in 207 BCE. Xiang Yu divided the Guanzhong region among three former Qin commanders to block Liu Bang, giving Sima Xin the kingdom of Sai east of Xianyang, with its capital at Yueyang.
kingdom-of-sai.r: Sai's population resented its new king, since Xiang Yu had massacred some 200,000 surrendered Qin soldiers at Xin'an while sparing their commanders. The kingdom had no time to develop any administration of its own.
kingdom-of-sai.e: When Liu Bang broke out of Hanzhong in 206 BCE, Sima Xin surrendered and his land became Han territory. He later fled back to Xiang Yu and killed himself after a Chu defeat at Chenggao in 203 BCE.

kazikumukh-shamkhalate.t: The leading Muslim state of medieval Dagestan, ruled by shamkhals from the Lak village of Kumukh, which later divided into Tarki and Kazikumukh.
kazikumukh-shamkhalate.o: The Laks of Kumukh were among the first peoples of mountainous Dagestan to adopt Islam, and their village became a religious centre. By the 14th century a ruler with the title shamkhal, claiming descent from early Arab commanders, headed a state there that spread its authority over neighbouring communities and the Kumyk plain.
kazikumukh-shamkhalate.r: The shamkhals ruled with Lak and Kumyk nobles, promoting Islam among neighbours and leading campaigns against Georgian and Circassian lands. The state lived from herding, crafts and trade and was tributary to the Golden Horde before Timur's invasion of 1395. In the 16th century it was the strongest power in Dagestan, courted by the Ottomans and Safavid Empire.
kazikumukh-shamkhalate.e: Internal quarrels and pressure from Persia weakened it, and by about 1642 the shamkhals had moved their seat to Tarki on the Caspian coast, founding the Shamkhalate of Tarki, while Kumukh itself became the Kazikumukh Khanate.

kingdom-of-ireland.t: The kingdom created when Henry VIII took the title King of Ireland in 1542, ruled by English monarchs until the Act of Union of 1800.
kingdom-of-ireland.o: The Crown of Ireland Act of 1542, passed by the Irish Parliament, replaced the Lordship of Ireland with a kingdom. Henry VIII pursued 'surrender and regrant', converting Gaelic chiefs into earls, while the Tudor and Stuart conquests extended English authority across the island.
kingdom-of-ireland.r: Ireland was governed by a lord deputy or lord lieutenant at Dublin Castle and its own Parliament. Plantations in Munster and Ulster settled English and Scottish Protestants. After the Williamite war of 1689 to 1691, the Penal Laws excluded Catholics from land and office, creating the Protestant Ascendancy. Grattan's Parliament gained legislative independence in 1782.
kingdom-of-ireland.e: After the United Irishmen rebellion of 1798, the Acts of Union of 1800 merged Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1 January 1801.
kingdom-of-ireland.re: Christianity; Catholic majority, Anglican established church

kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.t: Autonomous Croatian kingdom within the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary, where modern Croatian institutions and the idea of South Slav unity took shape.
kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.o: The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868, known as the Nagodba, joined the kingdoms of Croatia and Slavonia into one autonomous unit within the Lands of the Hungarian Crown. Croatia kept its own Sabor and control of internal affairs, justice and education, while finance and defence were common with Hungary. The former Military Frontier was added in 1881.
kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.r: A ban appointed on the Hungarian prime minister's advice headed the government in Zagreb. Ban Ivan Mažuranić modernised schools and courts in the 1870s, while Ban Károly Khuen-Héderváry, from 1883 to 1903, ruled by playing Serbs against Croats. Bishop Strossmayer founded the Yugoslav Academy and helped open the University of Zagreb in 1874. Fiume remained under Hungary.
kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia.e: From 1905 the Croat-Serb Coalition dominated politics. On 29 October 1918 the Sabor broke all ties with Austria-Hungary and joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, which in December merged into the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

kingdom-of-cappadocia.t: Cappadocia, a Hellenistic kingdom of the central Anatolian plateau ruled by Iranian-descended kings who became loyal allies of Rome.
kingdom-of-cappadocia.o: Ariarathes, the Persian satrap, defied Alexander's successors until Perdiccas killed him in 322 BCE. His adopted son Ariarathes II regained the land c. 301 BCE, and his heirs took the title king, ruling the plateau from Mazaca beneath Mount Argaeus.
kingdom-of-cappadocia.r: The Ariarathid kings ruled a rural country of large estates and temple domains, such as the shrine of the goddess Ma at Comana. Iranian traditions mixed with Greek culture; Ariarathes V was a patron of philosophers. The kingdom supplied horses, slaves and grain and allied with Rome against the Seleucid Empire.
kingdom-of-cappadocia.e: After Pontic interference, Rome installed Ariobarzanes I in 95 BCE. The last king, Archelaus, was summoned to Rome by Tiberius and died there in 17 CE, and Cappadocia became a Roman province.

kingdom-of-karasahr.t: The oasis kingdom of Agni on the northern Silk Road, one of the homes of the Tocharian languages and of Central Asian Buddhism.
kingdom-of-karasahr.o: Karasahr, called Yanqi in Chinese and Agni in its own documents, grew around the Bosten Lake oasis on the north-eastern edge of the Tarim Basin. It enters Chinese records in the 2nd century BCE as one of the city-states of the Western Regions, alternating between Xiongnu and Han control.
kingdom-of-karasahr.r: Its people spoke Tocharian A, an Indo-European language preserved in Buddhist manuscripts. Ruled by its own kings, Karasahr lived from irrigated farming, fishing, salt and Silk Road trade, and its monasteries at Shikshin followed the Sarvastivada school. The pilgrim Xuanzang passed through in 630. The Han general Ban Chao subdued it in 94, and the Tang Dynasty conquered it in 644 and made it one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi.
kingdom-of-karasahr.e: After Tang power in the Tarim faded in the late 8th century, Karasahr passed under Tibetan and Uyghur influence. Uyghurs fleeing the fall of the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 settled there, and the region became part of the Kingdom of Qocho, where Tocharian gave way to Old Uyghur.

kingdom-of-undi.t: The western Chewa kingdom of the Undi, an offshoot of Maravi whose lands held gold mines worked by Portuguese traders.
kingdom-of-undi.o: The Undi dynasty was founded in the 17th century by a member of the Phiri ruling clan of the Kingdom of Maravi who, according to tradition, quarrelled with the Kalonga and led followers west. He established his capital at Mano near the Kapoche river, on the borderlands of present-day Mozambique, Zambia and Malawi.
kingdom-of-undi.r: The Undi ruled through kin and territorial chiefs who sent tribute and recognised his ritual primacy, including over rain shrines. The kingdom traded ivory and cloth with the Portuguese at Tete and Zumbo, and in the 18th century Portuguese and Goan miners worked gold deposits in Undi territory under licence. Chewa culture, including the Nyau masked societies, flourished.
kingdom-of-undi.e: Decline set in during the 19th century as Afro-Portuguese warlords and, from the 1830s, Ngoni invaders raided its lands. By around 1880 central authority had collapsed. The Undi title survives as a Chewa paramount chieftaincy in Zambia.

kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.t: Interwar Hungarian kingdom without a king, ruled by Regent Miklós Horthy, which sought to undo the Treaty of Trianon and was drawn into the Second World War.
kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.o: After the fall of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, a national assembly restored the monarchy in 1920 but, with the Habsburgs barred, elected Admiral Miklós Horthy regent on 1 March. The Treaty of Trianon in June 1920 took two-thirds of the former Kingdom of Hungary (1867-1918). Former king Charles IV twice tried to return in 1921 and failed.
kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.r: Prime Minister István Bethlen stabilised the conservative regime in the 1920s, with restricted voting and dominance of landowners. Revision of Trianon was the central aim, and through the Vienna Awards of 1938 and 1940 Hungary regained southern Slovakia and northern Transylvania with German and Italian support. Antisemitic laws began with the numerus clausus of 1920 and tightened from 1938.
kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.e: Hungary joined the war against the Soviet Union in 1941. Germany occupied it in March 1944, and around 437,000 Jews were deported, most to Auschwitz. Horthy's attempt to leave the war in October 1944 led to Ferenc Szálasi's Government of National Unity. The monarchy was abolished in February 1946.

kingdom-of-cyrene.t: The Greek kingdom of the Battiad dynasty in eastern Libya, enriched by silphium, horses and grain.
kingdom-of-cyrene.o: According to Herodotus, colonists from the island of Thera, sent by the oracle of Delphi, founded Cyrene around 631 BCE under a leader who became King Battus I. The site, on a fertile plateau above the coast of Cyrenaica, was shown to them by local Libyans, with whom the settlers intermarried.
kingdom-of-cyrene.r: Eight kings, alternately named Battus and Arcesilaus, ruled for nearly two centuries. Battus II brought new settlers and defeated an Egyptian army sent by Apries at Irasa around 570 BCE, and the reformer Demonax of Mantinea later limited royal power. The economy rested on silphium, a medicinal plant shown on the city's coins, and on horses and grain. Cyrene paid tribute to the Achaemenid Empire from 525 BCE.
kingdom-of-cyrene.e: Royal power provoked repeated conflict, including Barca's secession. Arcesilaus IV, whose chariot victory at Delphi in 462 BCE was celebrated by Pindar, was overthrown around 440 BCE, and the monarchy gave way to the Republic of Cyrene.

kingdom-of-moray.t: A powerful northern Scottish realm whose rulers, styled kings or mormaers, contested the Scottish throne, most famously through Macbeth.
kingdom-of-moray.o: Moray emerged in the 10th century in the lands around the Moray Firth after the decline of the Pictish kingdom of Fortriu. Its ruling family, probably from Cenel Loairn by later genealogies, sometimes appear in Irish annals as kings of Alba, reflecting their claims to the Kingdom of Scotland.
kingdom-of-moray.r: Moray's rulers commanded a rich coastal plain and highland hinterland. Macbeth, mormaer of Moray, killed Duncan I in 1040 and ruled Scotland until 1057, making a pilgrimage to Rome. His stepson Lulach briefly succeeded him. The house of Moray clashed repeatedly with Norse earls of Orkney and with the line of Malcolm III.
kingdom-of-moray.e: After Angus of Moray died in battle at Stracathro in 1130, David I annexed the province, planting burghs and Flemish settlers. Revolts by MacWilliam claimants continued into the 13th century.

kingdom-of-hadramawt.t: The frankincense kingdom of south Arabia, ruling the Wadi Hadramawt from Shabwa and controlling the Dhofar groves and the port of Qana.
kingdom-of-hadramawt.o: Hadramawt is named in Sabaean inscriptions of the 7th century BCE, when it was first an ally and then a rival of the Kingdom of Saba. Its kings ruled the long Wadi Hadramawt and its tributaries from Shabwa, a walled town where all incense had to be brought for taxing before caravans set off west.
kingdom-of-hadramawt.r: Its wealth came from frankincense, gathered in Dhofar where Hadramawt founded the port of Sumhuram (Khor Rori), and shipped through Qana on the Indian Ocean coast, a port described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. The kingdom worshipped the moon god Sayin and wrote Hadramitic, a south Arabian language. It absorbed much of the Kingdom of Qataban in the 2nd century CE.
kingdom-of-hadramawt.e: In the early 3rd century CE Saba sacked Shabwa, and around 300 CE the Himyarite Kingdom under Shammar Yahrish conquered Hadramawt outright. The name survived as a region, and the valley's later sultanates, such as the Kathiri Sultanate and the Qu'aiti Sultanate, inherited it.

kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.t: The leading western Rus' state after the Mongol invasion, whose ruler Daniel was crowned King of Rus' and founded the city of Lviv.
kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.o: In 1199 Roman Mstislavich of the Principality of Volhynia took Halych and united it with his own lands. After his death in battle in 1205 Galicia fell into decades of strife involving Hungary and Poland. His son Daniel won back both lands by 1238 and made the state one of the most powerful in Eastern Europe.
kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.r: Daniel submitted to Batu Khan in 1245 but looked to the West for help, and in 1253 he was crowned King of Rus' by a papal legate at Dorohychyn. He founded Kholm and Lviv, which he named after his son Leo, and welcomed German, Armenian and Jewish settlers to the towns. Orthodox, Catholic and steppe influences met in its court.
kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.e: The direct dynasty ended in 1323, and Yuri II Boleslaw, a Masovian Piast, was poisoned by boyars in 1340. Poland and Lithuania then divided the kingdom, with Casimir III taking Galicia by 1349 and the Duchy of Volhynia going to Lithuania.

kushan-empire.t: An empire of Yuezhi origin stretching from the Amu Darya to the Ganges, a crossroads of Rome, China and India that carried Buddhism into Central Asia.
kushan-empire.o: Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Kushan branch of the Yuezhi, united the five Yuezhi chiefdoms of Bactria in the 1st century CE and pushed south across the Hindu Kush, taking lands from the Indo-Parthians and Indo-Greeks. His successors Vima Takto and Vima Kadphises extended rule deep into northern India.
kushan-empire.r: Under Kanishka the Great in the 2nd century, the empire was ruled from Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, using Bactrian written in Greek script. Gold coins showed Greek, Iranian and Indian gods side by side. The Kushans controlled Silk Road trade between Han China, Parthia and Rome, and patronised Gandharan and Mathuran art, which produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha. Mahayana Buddhism spread northward under their rule.
kushan-empire.e: In the 3rd century the Sasanians conquered the western lands, creating the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom, while the Gupta Empire and local rulers took the Indian territories. Small Kushan kingdoms lingered in Gandhara and Kashmir until overrun by the Kidarite Kingdom in the 4th century.

kingdom-of-ergyng.t: A small British kingdom in the Wye valley around the Roman town of Ariconium, whose name survives in Archenfield, a Welsh-speaking district of Herefordshire.
kingdom-of-ergyng.o: Ergyng emerged after Roman rule ended, its name derived from Ariconium, an iron-working town near Ross-on-Wye. It appears in the 6th and 7th centuries in the charters of the Book of Llandaff, which name local kings such as Peibio, associated in legend with the birth of Saint Dubricius.
kingdom-of-ergyng.r: Ergyng was a Christian British kingdom in which churches and monasteries, many linked to Dubricius, held land through royal grants. Its rulers were at times linked to the dynasties of Gwent and Glywysing. Little else is reliably known of its government.
kingdom-of-ergyng.e: From the 7th century the kingdom was absorbed by Gwent, and English settlement from Mercia advanced into the area. By the 10th century it was the district of Archenfield, under English lordship but still Welsh in law and speech; Domesday Book recorded its Welsh customs.
